title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
Opposites, sitting near each other. That is not a bug. They appear in near-identical contexts ("I feel ___ today"), and the embedding captures how a word is used , not what it means to a person. Antonyms are used almost interchangeably, grammatically speaking. king / man scores 0.068 — 1.6σ below chance. The single most repeated example in every explanation of embeddings, and in this model those two words are unusually far apart . The folklore is not wrong exactly, but it is not what the numbers say either. ### What the nearest neighbours look like Taking one token and finding the eight closest of all 49,152, purely by these numbers: ```
king → King, King, kings, queen, Kings, Queen, kingdom, king
Monday → Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Monday, Sunday
seven → eight, six, nine, seven, five, Seven, four, eleven
Paris → Paris, London, France, French, Madrid, London, Berlin
red → Red, Red, red, blue, RED, green, yellow, reds
```

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
```
king → King, King, kings, queen, Kings, Queen, kingdom, king
Monday → Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Monday, Sunday
seven → eight, six, nine, seven, five, Seven, four, eleven
Paris → Paris, London, France, French, Madrid, London, Berlin
red → Red, Red, red, blue, RED, green, yellow, reds
``` Nobody told it about the days of the week. Nobody grouped the numbers, or the colours, or European capitals. **Those groupings fell out of predicting text**, and they are sitting in the file right now, measurable with twenty lines of code. ### And the famous one The classic claim is that *directions* carry meaning too — that the step from `man` to `king` is the same step as from `woman` to `queen`.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
The classic claim is that *directions* carry meaning too — that the step from `man` to `king` is the same step as from `woman` to `queen`. So subtract one and add the other: ```
king − man + woman → queen, kings, King, queens, princess
walking − walk + swim → swimming, Swimming, swimmers, swam, swimmer
``` It works, on a 360-million-parameter model 
 The first is the textbook example, and it lands on queen as the top result. The second is the more interesting one: it is not about meaning at all but about grammar — the -ing ending — and that direction has its own consistent geometry. Not everything works. Paris − France + Italy returns Italian words but not Rome ; the model is too small and the tokens too fragmented.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: Paris − France + Italy returns Italian words but not Rome ; the model is too small and the tokens too fragmented. This is reported because it failed. A guide that only showed the successful analogy would be lying by selection. ## The problem this cannot solve The embedding gives every token a fixed position. That is already a problem, and one sentence shows why: > the **bank** of the river · the **bank** approved my loan Same token. Same row of the table. **Identical 960 numbers**, both times. Yet the meanings share nothing, and any model relying on that fixed row would have to average the two and be permanently confused. Words do not have fixed meanings. They have meanings **in context** — and a lookup table has no way to know the context.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
They have meanings **in context** — and a lookup table has no way to know the context. ## Attention: the room of people This is the mechanism that solves it, and it is the one idea in this guide worth slowing down for. Picture a conference room. Everyone holds three things: Q, K, V, O — the four letters, spelled out Letter Stands for In the room What it is 
 Q · q_proj Query the question you walk in with What this token needs to know — "am I financial or geographic?" 
 K · k_proj Key the name badge everyone wears What this token offers as a label — "I am about rivers" . Queries are matched against these. V · v_proj Value what they actually say The content handed over if you decide to listen.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
V · v_proj Value what they actually say The content handed over if you decide to listen. A badge gets you noticed; the value is what you take away. O · o_proj Output the write-up afterwards Fifteen heads each held their own conversation. O is what combines them — see below, because it is the one everybody forgets. All four are matrix multiplications — the same weighted-sum operation from chapter 03 . Q, K and V are applied to the same input with three different grids; O is applied afterwards, to the result. Their real shapes, from the file Shape Parameters, per layer 
 q_proj [960, 960] 921,600 full width 
 k_proj [320, 960] 307,200 a third — 5 key/value heads, not 15 
 v_proj [320, 960] 307,200 a third 
 o_proj [960, 960] 921,600 full width, back to where it started

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
Shape Parameters, per layer 
 q_proj [960, 960] 921,600 full width 
 k_proj [320, 960] 307,200 a third — 5 key/value heads, not 15 
 v_proj [320, 960] 307,200 a third 
 o_proj [960, 960] 921,600 full width, back to where it started K and V are smaller because fifteen attention heads share five sets of badges and contents — grouped-query attention, met in chapter 02 as a shape on disk and in chapter 05 as a cache three times cheaper than it would otherwise be. ### Why O exists, since nobody ever explains it The room is not one conversation. It is **fifteen simultaneous ones** — fifteen *attention heads*, each with its own slice of the numbers, each asking about something different. One head might track grammatical agreement, another which noun a pronoun refers to.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
One head might track grammatical agreement, another which noun a pronoun refers to. Nobody assigns them these jobs; they differentiate during training. So after attention, there are fifteen separate answers sitting side by side, **and none of them has met the others.** Head 3 does not know what head 11 found. `o_proj` is the grid that fixes that. It takes all fifteen results at once and produces one blended output — every number in it drawing on every head. Without O, the heads never talk 
 Remove o_proj and the fifteen heads' answers would simply be stacked next to each other and passed on, never combined. Each head's findings would stay quarantined in its own slice of the numbers for the rest of the model.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: Each head's findings would stay quarantined in its own slice of the numbers for the rest of the model. O is the only thing in the attention block that mixes across heads — and it costs the same 921,600 parameters as Q. That price is not for the looking-up; it is for the putting-together. The procedure, for one token: Ask everyone. Compare your question against every badge in the room. A dot product per person — one number saying how relevant each is. Decide how much to listen. Turn those scores into proportions summing to 1 — the step called softmax , which exaggerates as it normalises: the largest score takes most of the weight and small ones are pushed toward nothing. Highly relevant people get most of your attention; the rest get a sliver.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
Highly relevant people get most of your attention; the rest get a sliver. Take a weighted blend. Add up everyone's content , weighted by how much you are listening. One list of numbers comes back. Update yourself. Add that blend to your own position. You have moved. And the crucial part: **every token does this at the same time, about every other token.** Hence *self*-attention — the room is asking itself. ### Watch `bank` move Now the two sentences resolve. Both `bank` tokens start at the identical row of the table. Then: ```
"the bank of the river" bank asks: what am I? river's badge matches strongly
 bank absorbs river-ness, and moves "the bank approved my loan" bank asks: what am I? loan and approved match strongly
 bank absorbs finance-ness, and moves elsewhere
```

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
loan and approved match strongly
 bank absorbs finance-ness, and moves elsewhere
``` **Same starting point, different destinations.** The fixed lookup table became context-dependent, and it happened through nothing but dot products and weighted sums. And then `o_proj` does its job: fifteen heads' separate findings, blended into one result the next layer can use. And this is where the memory goes 
 Every token's badge and content — its key and value — must be kept, because every future token will need to ask about them. That store is the KV cache — K for keys and V for values, the badges and the contents — and it is now identifiable as a thing rather than a term: the badges and contents of everyone already in the room.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: That store is the KV cache — K for keys and V for values, the badges and the contents — and it is now identifiable as a thing rather than a term: the badges and contents of everyone already in the room. Add a token and one more of each is kept, forever, which is why it grows with every word and why chapter 07 's wall is where it is. ## Wait — how does it know the word order? Read the room-of-people procedure again and something is missing. Every token asks every other token; badges are matched, contents are blended. **Nothing in that anywhere mentions who came first.** That is not an oversight in the description. Attention as described is genuinely **order-blind**. Shuffle the words and every question, every badge, every blend comes out identical:

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
Shuffle the words and every question, every badge, every blend comes out identical: > the dog bit the man  ·  the man bit the dog Same tokens, same embeddings, same keys and values. A model with attention alone could not tell those apart — which would make it useless for language, where order carries much of the meaning. ### The fix: rotate, don't append The obvious repair is to add a "position number" to each token's numbers. Early models did roughly that. Modern ones, including this one, do something neater. RoPE — rotary position embedding Term What it means 
 RoPE Ro tary P osition E mbedding. The method this model uses to inject word order. rotary It literally rotates . Each token's query and key are turned through an angle before they meet.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: Each token's query and key are turned through an angle before they meet. the angle Proportional to the token's position . Token 1 turns a little, token 50 turns fifty times as much. Take the query and key as arrows. Rotate each by an angle set by where its token sits in the sentence. Now when two arrows are compared, the result depends on the difference between their angles — which is the distance between the two tokens. The analogy is **two clock hands.** Compare an hour hand at 3 o'clock with one at 5 o'clock and the answer is "two hours apart" — and it stays two hours apart at 9 and 11. The comparison naturally measures a *gap*, not two absolute positions. That is exactly the property wanted.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
That is exactly the property wanted. A token five words back should feel five words back whether the sentence started at word 1 or word 900. ### And it costs nothing Here is the part worth sitting with. Searching the file for anything storing position information: ```
rotary/position tensors in the file: NONE
total tensors: 290
``` **Not one parameter.** The rotation angles are computed from a single number in the configuration — `rope_theta: 100000` — by a formula fixed in advance. Nothing about position was learned, nothing about it is stored, and it adds nothing to the 723,674,912 bytes. This also explains a number in the configuration that looks like a hard limit and is not. `max_position_embeddings: 8192` says what the model was *trained* on.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: `max_position_embeddings: 8192` says what the model was *trained* on. Since the angles are computed rather than looked up, positions beyond 8,192 can still be calculated — the model has simply never seen arrows turned that far, and its answers degrade. **The wall is in the training, not in the file**, which is why techniques exist to stretch a model's context beyond what it was trained for, and why they work imperfectly. ## Doing it thirty-two times One round of asking is not enough. In `the bank of the river was steep`, the word `steep` matters to `bank` too — but on the first pass `bank` did not yet know it was geographic, so it did not know to care. So the whole block repeats. **Thirty-two times**, each layer working on the output of the last:

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
**Thirty-two times**, each layer working on the output of the last: ```
layer 1 crude grouping — parts of speech, obvious associations
layers 2-8 phrases cohere, references start resolving
mid layers the abstract work: relationships, structure, whatever is being tracked
final layers converging on an answer — what comes next? ``` Those descriptions are **the honest state of knowledge**, not a specification. Broad patterns like this have been found by researchers probing real models, but nobody hands a layer a job and nobody can fully say what layer 17 does. The blocks are identical in shape and differ only in their numbers. Chapter 03 counted the cost: 9,830,400 multiplications per token per layer, 32 layers deep.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: Chapter 03 counted the cost: 9,830,400 multiplications per token per layer, 32 layers deep. ## And then, a score for every token After the last layer, one token's worth of numbers — still 960 of them — has to become a prediction over the whole vocabulary. One final matrix multiplication against the output head, `960 × 49,152`, gives **49,152 numbers: one score per possible token.** In this model that grid is [the embedding read backwards](02-a-file-of-numbers.html) — the same dictionary, used in the other direction. Those scores are turned into probabilities, one is chosen, and it is appended to the input. Then the entire thing runs again for the next token, exactly as [chapter 01](01-what-is-an-llm.html) described.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text: Then the entire thing runs again for the next token, exactly as [chapter 01](01-what-is-an-llm.html) described. ## So why does it work? The mechanism is now completely laid out. The honest answer to *why it produces good text* is thinner than anyone would like. **What is solidly understood:** predicting the next token across trillions of words is a genuinely hard task, and a system optimised hard enough for it is forced to represent grammar, facts, and structure. The measurements above are that representation, visible. The days of the week grouped themselves because grouping them helps prediction. **What is not understood:** why capability appears as *sharply* as it does with scale. Why a model of one size cannot do arithmetic and a larger one can.

title: 04 · Why That Predicts Language
text:
Why a model of one size cannot do arithmetic and a larger one can. What any particular parameter contributes. Whether the internal representations correspond to anything a person would call a concept. The honest position 
 Everything in this chapter is measurable, and most of it was measured here. The gap is not in the mechanism — it is in the explanation of why the mechanism suffices. This guide will not paper over that. What it can do is keep putting real numbers on the parts that are knowable: how much memory, how much arithmetic, how much time. Those are answerable, and the rest of it is answered honestly by saying nobody knows. ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter 
 embedding cosine similarity attention self-attention query · key · value context softmax KV cache 
 If the room of people makes sense — questions, badges, contents, and a weighted blend — then attention is understood, and with it the reason the KV cache exists at all.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
# What Running It Means Everything so far has been static: a file, its shapes, its arithmetic. This chapter puts the model in motion for the first time, times it, and finds it running at 2.8% of what the hardware allows. Four chapters of preparation. The file has been opened and counted, the arithmetic derived, the card benchmarked, the embedding measured. **Nothing has actually been run.** So it was. The model from chapter 02 loaded onto one card, handed a prompt, and timed. What came back is the most useful result in this guide so far — not because it was fast, but because it was not. ## The prompt ```
The three most important things to know about running a large language
model on a small graphics card are
```

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
```
The three most important things to know about running a large language
model on a small graphics card are
``` Nineteen tokens in. The model was asked to continue, and it did — coherently, and rather on the nose. It reaches for the abbreviation **GPU**, for *graphics processing unit*, which is the card described in [chapter 06](06-the-box.html): > *…are:* **1. GPU-specific optimizations**: Large language models require specialized hardware to run efficiently. GPUs are specifically designed for parallel processing… That is a 360-million-parameter model, running on a second-hand gaming graphics card, writing plausible prose about itself. It is worth registering as remarkable before taking it apart.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
It is worth registering as remarkable before taking it apart. ## Two phases that share nothing but weights Generating text is not one activity. It is two, and they behave so differently that measuring them together produces a number describing neither. Prefill and decode Prefill Decode 
 What it does reads the prompt writes the answer 
 How many tokens all of them, at once one 
 Can it parallelise? yes — every token is already known no — each depends on the last 
 Weights read once, for the whole prompt once, per token 
 Limited by arithmetic memory 
 Felt by a user as the pause before anything appears the speed of the stream The analogy is **reading a letter versus writing a reply.** Reading, your eyes take in whole lines at once and the page is already there in front of you.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
The analogy is **reading a letter versus writing a reply.** Reading, your eyes take in whole lines at once and the page is already there in front of you. Writing, each word has to be decided before the next can be — and you cannot write the fifth word until the fourth exists, however fast your hand is. Same person, same desk, two completely different rates. ### Timed, on the box Measured 2026-09-13 — SmolLM2-360M on one RTX 3060 Ti graphics processing unit, weights in bf16 (brain float, 16-bit) Phase Time Rate 
 Prefill — 19 prompt tokens 65 ms total · 3.4 ms/token 292 tokens/sec 
 Decode — 60 generated tokens 62.1 ms per token (median) 16.1 tokens/sec Prefill is 18× faster per token than decode , running exactly the same weights on exactly the same card.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Prefill is 18× faster per token than decode , running exactly the same weights on exactly the same card. This is why any honest benchmark reports **time to first token** and **tokens per second** separately, and why a single "speed" figure for a model is close to meaningless. They measure different machines wearing the same hat. ## The distribution, seen for real Chapter 01 claimed a forward pass produces a score for every token in the vocabulary, not a word. Here is that claim, printed: ```
next-token distribution over 49,152 tokens:
 72.48% ':'
 3.61% ' that'
 2.48% ' the'
 2.19% ' as'
 0.81% '...'
 0.71% ' ['
 0.71% ' ('
 0.63% ' how'
 ... 49,144 more, sharing 16.39%
``` One confident favourite, a handful of plausible alternatives, and a very long tail of almost-nothing sharing the remainder.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text: One confident favourite, a handful of plausible alternatives, and a very long tail of almost-nothing sharing the remainder. **The model did not choose `:`** — it produced this table, and something else picked the top entry. That something is the **sampler**, and it is the one place where a decision gets made. Taking the maximum every time is *greedy* decoding, which is what was used here and what every measurement in this guide uses, because it is reproducible. Sampling in proportion to the probabilities instead gives variety, and a *temperature* setting flattens or sharpens the table before choosing. **Temperature zero means take the top entry** — no randomness, same answer every time. ## The cache, and why anything is cached at all

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
## The cache, and why anything is cached at all The **KV cache** has been mentioned in three chapters now. The letters stand for *keys and values* — which explains precisely nothing on its own, and that is the problem with how this thing is usually introduced. So rather than another definition, here is the situation it exists to fix. ### A meeting that has been going for three hours You are taking notes at a long meeting. Someone asks you a question, and to answer it properly you have to take account of **everything anyone has said so far**. The obvious approach, and why it is unbearable 
 Play back the whole recording from the beginning, listen to all three hours, then answer. Then the next question arrives — and you play back the recording again.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Then the next question arrives — and you play back the recording again. Now it is three hours and one minute long. Then again, three hours and two minutes. Every answer costs more than the last, and you spend the afternoon re-listening to a speech you already heard forty times. Nothing about the early part of that recording changes. The work of understanding it was already done, and thrown away, and done again. ### So write an index card The alternative: as each person speaks, listen **once** and write a single index card. Two lines per card — and they are the K and the V On the card What it holds Its real name 
 the top line what this person was talking about — the topic, so you can tell at a glance whether they are relevant the key 
 the body what they actually said — the content you take away if you decide they matter the value

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
On the card What it holds Its real name 
 the top line what this person was talking about — the topic, so you can tell at a glance whether they are relevant the key 
 the body what they actually said — the content you take away if you decide they matter the value Now a question arrives. You flick through the cards, read the top lines, decide who is relevant, and take what those people said. You never replay the recording. That stack of index cards is the KV cache . One card per person who has spoken. This is the same room from [chapter 04](04-predicting-language.html), seen from a different angle: the top line is the name badge and the body is what they say. What is new here is the reason for keeping them — **not to be organised, but to avoid doing the work twice.**

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text: What is new here is the reason for keeping them — **not to be organised, but to avoid doing the work twice.** ### Why the questions are not written down The obvious follow-up: if keys and values are kept, why not queries? Because **a question is asked once and answered once.** Nobody will ever need to look up what you asked twenty minutes ago. But what people *said* — that gets consulted again by every question that follows. So keys and values accumulate and queries evaporate. That asymmetry is the whole reason the thing is called a KV cache and not a QKV cache. ### Thirty-two note-takers, in a row One complication, and it is where the size comes from. There are not one but **32 note-takers**, seated in a line.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
There are not one but **32 note-takers**, seated in a line. The first listens to the actual speech. The second listens to the first one's summary, the third to the second's, and so on. Each keeps **their own stack of cards**. So a single spoken word produces 32 cards, not one — which is exactly where the 32 in the formula comes from, and why a deeper model has a more expensive memory. Predicted, then weighed 
 The formula from chapter 07 , with this model's real configuration — 32 layers, 5 key/value heads, head dimension 64, two bytes per number: 
 2 × 32 × 5 × 64 × 2 = 40,960 bytes per token 
 The cache after 79 tokens weighed 3.09 MiB , which is 40,960 bytes per token . Exact. Conversation length Cards on the table 
 4,096 tokens 0.16 GiB 
 32,768 tokens 1.25 GiB 
 131,072 tokens 5.00 GiB

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Conversation length Cards on the table 
 4,096 tokens 0.16 GiB 
 32,768 tokens 1.25 GiB 
 131,072 tokens 5.00 GiB This model is unusually frugal — 5 key/value heads and a head dimension of 64. Llama-3-8B costs 131,072 bytes per token, 3.2× more , which is the difference between a long conversation fitting on an 8 GB card and not. ### What happens if you burn the cards All of that is reasoning. It can be tested: generate the same text twice, once keeping the cards and once throwing them away after every single word. Measured — same model, same prompt, same output Conversation so far With the cards Burning them each time Cost of burning 
 200 tokens 16.0 tok/s 14.7 tok/s 1.1× 
 1,000 tokens 15.7 tok/s 14.6 tok/s 1.1× 
 3,611 tokens 14.3 tok/s 6.1 tok/s 2.3× 
 8,000 tokens 11.0 tok/s 2.5 tok/s 4.4×

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Conversation so far With the cards Burning them each time Cost of burning 
 200 tokens 16.0 tok/s 14.7 tok/s 1.1× 
 1,000 tokens 15.7 tok/s 14.6 tok/s 1.1× 
 3,611 tokens 14.3 tok/s 6.1 tok/s 2.3× 
 8,000 tokens 11.0 tok/s 2.5 tok/s 4.4× The output was identical in every case. The cache changes nothing about what the model says — it only avoids redoing work that was already done. Two things in that table are worth more than the headline. **At short lengths the cache barely helps.** At 200 tokens it is worth 1.1×, which is nearly nothing. The first attempt at this measurement used a 50-token conversation and found **no difference at all** — a result that looked like a broken experiment and was not.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
The first attempt at this measurement used a 50-token conversation and found **no difference at all** — a result that looked like a broken experiment and was not. With so little to re-read, the per-token overhead from the next section swamps everything. **The cache only pays when there is real work to skip.** **Its value grows with the conversation.** 1.1× → 2.3× → 4.4×, and still climbing at the end. This is the shape that matters: with the cards, each word costs the same as the last. Without them, each word costs a little more than the last, forever. At 8,000 tokens that is 2.5 tokens per second — slower than typing. The trade being made 
 The cache buys time with memory. Keep the cards and every word costs the same; burn them and you pay the whole conversation again, each time.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text: Keep the cards and every word costs the same; burn them and you pay the whole conversation again, each time. But the cards pile up . At 40,960 bytes each they are cheap in this model and ruinous in a larger one, and they are the thing that eventually fills the card — not the weights, which never grow. That is the wall chapter 07 measures, and nearly everything a serving engine does cleverly is about managing this stack of index cards — paging it, sharing it between conversations that begin the same way, storing it in fewer bytes, deciding whose cards to throw away when the table is full. ## The 36× gap Here is the finding, and it reframes everything that follows. Chapter 03 measured this card reading a model's weights: **0.72 GB in 1.71 ms**.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Chapter 03 measured this card reading a model's weights: **0.72 GB in 1.71 ms**. Since one token requires reading every weight once, that sets a hard ceiling of about **584 tokens per second**. The measurement above came in at **16.1**. 2.8% of what the hardware allows Memory-bound ceiling (measured) 584 tok/s 
 What actually happened 16.1 tok/s 
 Slower by a factor of 36× Per token: the hardware needs 1.71 ms to move the weights. The run took 62.1 ms . So 60.4 ms of every single token — 97% of the time — was spent on something that is not memory and is not arithmetic. Where does it go? Into the machinery around the multiplication — and that machinery has a name that this guide will lean on for the rest of its length, so it gets one properly.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text: Into the machinery around the multiplication — and that machinery has a name that this guide will lean on for the rest of its length, so it gets one properly. ### What a kernel is — one program the card runs A graphics card is not a fast processor. It is **thousands of slow ones**, and they cannot be given instructions individually — there is no time to walk around a factory floor of five thousand workers handing each a task. So they are given one instruction, together. A **kernel** is a single short program the card runs — posted where all of them can read it, so every worker runs it at the same moment on a different piece of the data: *"take the number in your slot, multiply it by the number in that other slot, put the answer back."* Five thousand multiplications, one instruction.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
A **kernel** is a single short program the card runs — posted where all of them can read it, so every worker runs it at the same moment on a different piece of the data: *"take the number in your slot, multiply it by the number in that other slot, put the answer back."* Five thousand multiplications, one instruction. The word, and the word next to it Term What it is In the factory On this card 
 kernel One small program that every processor on the card runs at once, each on its own slice of the data. The instruction sheet pinned to the wall. one matrix multiply, one normalisation, one softmax 
 launch Handing that program to the card and telling it to begin. Walking over and pinning the sheet up.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Walking over and pinning the sheet up. a few microseconds, whatever the job size 
 launch overhead The cost of the walk, paid once per kernel, doing no useful work. Fine for one big job. Ruinous for a thousand tiny ones. the 60.4 ms below The crucial property is in the third column of the middle row: pinning up the sheet costs the same whether the job takes an hour or a second. A kernel that multiplies two enormous matrices amortises its launch to nothing. A kernel that adds two small vectors is almost entirely launch. Now the 60.4 ms has an explanation. Every operation in every layer is a separate kernel, launched one at a time by a Python program, and each launch has a fixed cost unrelated to the size of the work.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Every operation in every layer is a separate kernel, launched one at a time by a Python program, and each launch has a fixed cost unrelated to the size of the work. With 32 layers and several operations each, a single token becomes **hundreds of small kernels** — hundreds of walks to the wall, each carrying overhead, each waiting for the last. The card spends its time being told what to do rather than doing it. This is the entire reason Part I exists 
 If the naive approach reached the hardware limit, there would be nothing to learn: every serving engine would be a thin wrapper and the choice between them cosmetic. Instead there is a 36× gap between what the card can do and what straightforward code achieves.

title: 05 · What Running It Means
text:
Instead there is a 36× gap between what the card can do and what straightforward code achieves. Everything the engines in Part I do — batching, fusing operations, avoiding round trips, capturing whole graphs of commands — is an attempt to close it. The prediction this guide now carries: those engines will land somewhere between 16 and 584 tokens per second. Where, exactly, is the question Part I exists to answer, and this is the number they will be measured against. ## The whole journey, end to end Everything in the Foundations chapters, in the order it happens: ```mermaid

 F -.->|"append and run again — 62 ms each time"| D
 D -.->|"keys and values kept"| H["KV cache 40,960 bytes per token"]

```

title: 06 · The Box
text:
# The Box Three graphics cards that cost about $200 each, a pair of decade-old server CPUs, and one wiring detail that decides what is possible. Everything in this guide runs on one machine. It is worth knowing it properly, because almost every limit encountered later traces back to a number on this page — and because the most consequential fact about it is not the one anyone would guess. Hardware attracts abbreviations, so here is the whole alphabet before it appears. The letters on this page, in plain words Short Stands for What it is 
 GPU Graphics Processing Unit The graphics card. Built for drawing games, it turns out to be built for exactly the arithmetic a model needs. CPU Central Processing Unit The main processor.

title: 06 · The Box
text: CPU Central Processing Unit The main processor. Runs the program that tells the GPU what to do. VRAM Video RAM Memory on the graphics card . Fast, and the thing that runs out. The whole project is shaped by having 8 GB of it per card. RAM Random Access Memory Main system memory, on the motherboard. Far larger here (125 GB), far slower to reach from the GPU. PCIe Peripheral Component Interconnect Express The wiring that connects cards to the motherboard, and to each other. The bottleneck discussed below. NVLink NVIDIA Link A much faster direct card-to-card connection. This machine does not have it, and that absence shapes Part IV. CUDA Compute Unified Device Architecture NVIDIA's system for running general-purpose programs on a GPU.

title: 06 · The Box
text: CUDA Compute Unified Device Architecture NVIDIA's system for running general-purpose programs on a GPU. Effectively the language everything here is spoken in. bf16 brain float, 16-bit A number format: each number takes 2 bytes. The default for modern models. FP8 floating point, 8-bit A smaller format, 1 byte per number. Newer cards support it; these do not . sm_86 streaming multiprocessor, version 8.6 NVIDIA's generation code. It determines which software features the card supports. TFLOPS tera floating-point operations per second Raw arithmetic speed — trillions of calculations per second. OS operating system Linux, here. The obvious headline is 24 GB of video memory. The fact that actually shapes the project is **how the three cards are wired to each other**.

title: 06 · The Box
text:
The fact that actually shapes the project is **how the three cards are wired to each other**. ## What is in it Measured on **2026-09-11**, read off the machine rather than a spec sheet. dalang-Z9PE-D8-WS GPU 3× NVIDIA RTX 3060 Ti — 8192 MiB each, 24 GB total 
 GPU arch Ampere sm_86 · bf16 tensor cores yes · FP8 no 
 Bandwidth 448 GB/s per card 
 Interconnect PCIe only — no NVLink 
 Driver 595.84 
 CPU 2× Intel Xeon E5-2665 — 32 threads 
 RAM 125 GB 
 Disk 879 GB, 585 GB free 
 OS Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS Nothing here is new. The 3060 Ti launched as a mid-range gaming card; the Xeons are from a server generation long since retired. That is the point — this is hardware that can be bought used, not a rented datacenter instance.

title: 06 · The Box
text:
That is the point — this is hardware that can be bought used, not a rented datacenter instance. ## The number that predicts the most Of everything above, one figure will come up in nearly every chapter that follows: 448 GB/s 
 Each card can read its own memory at roughly 448 gigabytes per second. Generating a token requires reading the model's active weights once . Those two facts together set a hard ceiling on generation speed that no software can cross — only work within. Chapter 08 turns this into a formula that predicts real measurements. It is the single most useful piece of arithmetic in this guide. Note what it is *not*. It is not the compute figure. For generating text one token at a time, these cards spend most of their time waiting on memory, not calculating — so the number that matters is how fast memory moves, not how fast the arithmetic units run.

title: 06 · The Box
text:
For generating text one token at a time, these cards spend most of their time waiting on memory, not calculating — so the number that matters is how fast memory moves, not how fast the arithmetic units run. ## The wiring, which matters more than it should Three cards in one machine are not the same as one card with three times the memory. How they are connected decides how much worse. GPU0 
 GPU1 
 GPU2 SYS 
 PHB 
 SYS 
 fast 
 GPU1 and GPU2 share a host bridge. GPU0 does not. Traffic to GPU0 crosses the CPU interconnect — the slow path. `nvidia-smi topo -m` reports `PHB` between GPU1 and GPU2 — they share a PCIe host bridge. Between GPU0 and either of the others it reports `SYS`, meaning the data has to cross the link between the two physical CPUs to get there.

title: 06 · The Box
text:
Between GPU0 and either of the others it reports `SYS`, meaning the data has to cross the link between the two physical CPUs to get there. So the three cards are not peers. **Two of them are neighbours and the third lives across town.** When this bites, in order 
 Serving one request at a time: barely at all. The cards take turns; little crosses between them. Splitting one model across cards: noticeably. Pieces of every layer must be recombined, and some of that traffic takes the slow road. It is possible that using all three cards is slower than using the two neighbours — an outcome to measure rather than assume. Training: hardest of all. Every training step ends by averaging gradients across all cards.

title: 06 · The Box
text: Every training step ends by averaging gradients across all cards. That is a large transfer, and it happens thousands of times. Without NVLink, the wiring — not the GPU — may well set the pace. This is the asymmetry worth remembering: **inference tolerates a slow interconnect; training punishes it.** ## The 125 GB of RAM is a feature It looks like a leftover from a retired server, and in a sense it is. It is also the reason one of the most instructive experiments in this guide is possible at all. A model too large for 24 GB of video memory can still be held in 125 GB of system memory and fed to the GPU a piece at a time. It is slow — chapter 11 measures exactly how slow, and explains where the time goes.

title: 06 · The Box
text: It is slow — chapter 11 measures exactly how slow, and explains where the time goes. But it runs, and the fact that it runs *at all* is the entire reason one of the serving engines in Part I exists. The same generosity has a second use much later: a training run needs somewhere to stage data, and 125 GB is a comfortable staging area. ## Two absences worth naming **No FP8.** These are Ampere cards. The 8-bit floating-point formats that newer hardware uses for fast, accurate quantization need an Ada or Hopper generation GPU. Several techniques described in modern serving literature are simply unavailable here, and the guide will say so when it reaches them rather than quietly using something else.

title: 06 · The Box
text: Several techniques described in modern serving literature are simply unavailable here, and the guide will say so when it reaches them rather than quietly using something else. **No NVLink.** Covered above, and the reason it keeps returning. Both are consequences of choosing affordable hardware. Neither is a defect. They are the shape of the constraint, and the constraint is the subject. ## What was already installed The machine arrived at this project with a working PyTorch — `2.11.0+cu128` — left behind by the sibling video project, along with its virtual environment. Reusing it saves a multi-gigabyte download. Everything else this guide needs was absent: no serving engines, no container runtime, no CUDA compiler.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text: # What Fits — the Memory Math A model's size tells you whether it loads. It does not tell you whether it runs, and the difference is where most people's estimates fall apart. Ask how large a model fits in 8 GB and the usual answer is arithmetic on the weights: so many billion parameters, so many bytes each, divide. That calculation is correct and it is not enough. A model can load perfectly and then fail the moment a long conversation is handed to it — not because the weights grew, but because something else did. This chapter derives both halves. The second half is the one that matters. ## The budget Everything competing for a card's memory. **VRAM** stands for *Video Random Access Memory* — the memory on the graphics card itself, as distinct from the system RAM on the motherboard.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
**VRAM** stands for *Video Random Access Memory* — the memory on the graphics card itself, as distinct from the system RAM on the motherboard. The four things below fight over it, and two of the four are abbreviations worth spelling out immediately: the **KV cache** holds *keys and values*, and the **CUDA context** is the working state of *CUDA*, NVIDIA's Compute Unified Device Architecture for running programs on a graphics card. ```
VRAM = weights + KV cache + activations + CUDA context
``` - **Weights** — the model. Fixed the moment it loads and never changes. - **KV cache** — *keys and values*: working memory for the conversation. **Grows with every token.**
- **Activations** — scratch space for the calculation in flight.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
**Grows with every token.**
- **Activations** — scratch space for the calculation in flight. Small during generation. - **CUDA context** — roughly 0.5–1 GB the driver takes just to exist, before a single weight is loaded. Unavoidable overhead. That last one is why an 8 GB card is really about **7.6 GB** of usable space. The gap is not a rounding error; at the edge it is the difference between running and not. ## Part one: the weights The easy half. $$\text{weight bytes} = \text{params} \times \text{bytes per param}$$ Every term, in plain words Term What it means Typical value 
 weight bytes How much space the model occupies once loaded. The answer being sought. — 
 params Parameters — the count of individual numbers in the model.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
— 
 params Parameters — the count of individual numbers in the model. This is the "8B" in a model's name: 8 billion of them. 8,000,000,000 
 bytes per param How much space one of those numbers takes. Set by the number format, and the only part that can be changed after training. 0.55 – 2.0 
 × Ordinary multiplication. Nothing is hiding here — this really is as simple as it looks. — So an 8B model at 2 bytes each is 8,000,000,000 × 2 = 16,000,000,000 bytes ≈ 16 GB . Squeeze each number down to about half a byte and the same model becomes ≈ 4.5 GB. The parameter count never changes — only the cost of storing each one. The names in the table below are number formats — how many bytes one weight costs.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text: The names in the table below are number formats — how many bytes one weight costs. ([Binary-docs](../binary-docs/floats.html) takes these apart bit by bit; the [calculator](../vram-calculator.html) runs the arithmetic in this chapter for any model and card.) **fp16** (*floating point*, 16-bit) and **bf16** (*brain float*, 16-bit) are two flavours of the same size — 2 bytes per number; **int8** is an 8-bit *integer*, 1 byte; and the `Q`-names are compressed formats averaging well under a byte. What "bytes per param" can be is the entire subject of quantization — storing each number in fewer bits, accepting a small loss of precision in exchange for a large saving in space. Storage cost per parameter

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
Storage cost per parameter Format Bytes/param A 7B model 
 fp16 / bf16 — full precision 2.0 14 GB 
 int8 / fp8 1.0 7 GB 
 Q5_K_M ~0.7 ~4.9 GB 
 Q4_K_M — the workhorse ~0.55 ~3.9 GB 
 Q3_K_M ~0.43 ~3.0 GB Those sub-1-byte figures are averages, not a uniform bit-width. A modern 4-bit format stores most weights in 4 bits, keeps a handful of sensitive ones at higher precision, and adds a scaling factor per small group of numbers. The average lands a little above 4 bits per weight — hence 0.55 bytes rather than 0.5. Quantization below roughly 4 bits is where quality starts to visibly suffer. Part I measures that rather than repeating it as folklore. ## Part two: the KV cache, which is the real story

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
## Part two: the KV cache, which is the real story Here is the part the simple calculation misses. Generating text one token at a time would be hopelessly wasteful if the model re-read the entire conversation for every new word. So it does not. It keeps the intermediate results for every token it has already seen — two tensors per token per layer, called the keys and the values — and reuses them. That store is the **KV cache** — **KV** for *keys and values*, the two things being kept — and its cost is: $$\text{bytes per token} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{kv heads} \times \text{head dim} \times \text{dtype bytes}$$ Every term, in plain words Term What it means 8B example 
 bytes per token The cost of remembering one token of the conversation.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
Term What it means 8B example 
 bytes per token The cost of remembering one token of the conversation. Multiply by the context length for the total. 131,072 
 2 Not a fudge factor — there are literally two things stored per token: a key and a value . Hence the name "KV cache". 2 
 layers A model is the same block of machinery repeated. Each repetition is a layer, and each one keeps its own cache . 32 
 kv heads Within a layer the work is split into parallel "heads". Only the heads that store keys and values count here — which is why this number is often smaller than the head count. 8 
 head dim How many numbers each head stores per token. The width of one head's slice. 128 
 dtype bytes Space per stored number, exactly as in the weights formula.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
128 
 dtype bytes Space per stored number, exactly as in the weights formula. 2 for 16-bit, 1 for 8-bit — halving this halves the whole cache . 2 Every term is a multiplication, so every term is a lever. Three of them — layers, kv heads, head dim — are fixed by whoever designed the model and cannot be touched. Only the last one is ours to change , which is why quantizing the KV cache appears later as a real technique rather than a footnote. The leading 2 is for the keys and the values. ### Worked, for an 8B model Take a Llama-3-8B-shaped model: 32 layers, 8 key/value heads, head dimension 128, cached in 16-bit. $$2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072 \text{ bytes} = \mathbf{128\ KB\ per\ token}$$

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
$$2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072 \text{ bytes} = \mathbf{128\ KB\ per\ token}$$ Which number is which Number Term Where it comes from 
 2 keys and values fixed — there are two of them, always 
 32 layers this model's architecture 
 8 kv heads this model's architecture 
 128 head dim this model's architecture 
 2 dtype bytes our choice — 16-bit. Drop to 8-bit and this becomes 1 Two of those numbers are the digit 2 and they mean entirely different things. The first is structural and permanent; the last is a setting, and it is the only one on the line that can be changed without changing the model. 128 kilobytes does not sound alarming. Then it is multiplied by a context length:

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
Then it is multiplied by a context length: The same model, four conversation lengths Context KV cache Plus 4.5 GB of Q4 weights 
 4,000 tokens 0.5 GB 5.0 GB — comfortable 
 8,000 tokens 1.0 GB 5.5 GB — fine 
 32,000 tokens 4.2 GB 8.7 GB — does not fit 
 128,000 tokens 16.8 GB larger than two whole cards The weights never moved. The model that ran happily at 8,000 tokens fails at 32,000, and the reason has nothing to do with how many parameters it has. The rule worth memorising 
 Doubling the context costs more than doubling the parameters. Weights are a one-time cost. The KV cache is a per-token cost, and it is charged on every token in the conversation, not just the new one. ### Why this is the centre of the whole field

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text: ### Why this is the centre of the whole field Once the shape of that table is clear, a great deal of otherwise confusing engineering falls into place. Nearly everything a serving engine does cleverly is aimed at this one number: - **Paging it** — allocate the cache in small blocks instead of one reserved slab, so nothing is wasted on conversations that end early. - **Sharing it** — if fifty requests begin with the same long instruction, store that prefix once. - **Quantizing it** — keep the cache in 8-bit instead of 16-bit and it halves. - **Evicting it** — decide which conversations keep their cache and which are recomputed later. Those four ideas are, respectively, most of what distinguishes the engines compared in Part I.

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
Those four ideas are, respectively, most of what distinguishes the engines compared in Part I. They are not competing philosophies. They are four attacks on the table above. A note on why 8 key/value heads, not 32 
 The model has 32 attention heads but only 8 sets of keys and values, shared between them. That is grouped-query attention , and it exists precisely to shrink this cache — four-to-one, in this case. An older model of the same size with one key/value set per head would need 512 KB per token , and 32,000 tokens of context would cost 16.8 GB instead of 4.2. When a model's context window seems implausibly generous for its size, this is usually why. ## Putting both halves together Estimates — not yet measured on this box

title: 07 · What Fits — the Memory Math
text:
## What this chapter cannot tell you It answers *whether it fits*. It says nothing about *how fast it goes* — and the two are almost independent. A model can fit comfortably and generate at a crawl; another can sit at the edge of memory and be quick. Speed is set by a different number entirely, and there is only one that matters. ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter 
 KV cache quantization Q4_K_M context length grouped-query attention CUDA context activations bytes per parameter

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text: # How Fast It Can Possibly Go There is a ceiling on generation speed that no software can cross. Finding it takes one division — and finding out that the software is nowhere near it takes a stopwatch. Chapter 05 measured a model generating at 16.1 tokens per second and noted, without explaining, that the hardware allowed 584. This chapter is the explanation: where that number comes from, why nothing beats it, and why almost nothing reaches it. ## The one division Every token requires reading every active weight out of memory. That is not a rule of thumb — [chapter 03](03-what-numbers-do.html) counted it: each weight is used in exactly one multiplication per token, so each must make the trip from memory to the arithmetic units.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
That is not a rule of thumb — [chapter 03](03-what-numbers-do.html) counted it: each weight is used in exactly one multiplication per token, so each must make the trip from memory to the arithmetic units. So the speed limit is a question about moving bytes: $$\text{tokens per second} \le \frac{\text{memory bandwidth}}{\text{bytes read per token}}$$ Every symbol, in plain words Term What it means On this box 
 memory bandwidth How fast the graphics card reads its own memory. A property of the hardware, not the model. Measured, not quoted — the advertised figure was 448. 423.9 GB/s 
 bytes read per token The size of the weights that take part. For a dense model that is all of them; for a sparse one, only the parts that activate.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
For a dense model that is all of them; for a sparse one, only the parts that activate. 0.72 GB 
 ≤ Less than or equal to — and the equality is never reached. This is a ceiling, not a prediction. — For the model in this guide: 423.9 ÷ 0.72 = 585 tokens per second , and the direct measurement agreed — reading those weights took 1.71 ms , which is 584 per second. The formula is indifferent to how clever the software is. **The bytes have to arrive.** ## Why bandwidth and not arithmetic The instinct is that a bigger model is slower because there is more *maths* to do. Chapter 03 measured that instinct wrong. The two costs, side by side Per token, this model Cost Time on this card 
 Arithmetic — 0.72 billion operations 0.72 GFLOP 0.02 ms 
 Moving the weights — 0.72 GB 0.72 GB 1.71 ms

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
Per token, this model Cost Time on this card 
 Arithmetic — 0.72 billion operations 0.72 GFLOP 0.02 ms 
 Moving the weights — 0.72 GB 0.72 GB 1.71 ms Fetching the numbers takes 85× longer than using them. Each weight makes a long journey to be multiplied once and thrown away. The analogy is a kitchen where every ingredient lives in a warehouse across town. Chopping an onion takes seconds; fetching it takes an hour. **Hiring a faster chef changes nothing** — and this is why quantization makes models faster even though unpacking compressed numbers is extra work. Fewer bytes to fetch beats more arithmetic to do, because the arithmetic was never the problem. ## Prefill obeys a different formula

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
## Prefill obeys a different formula That ceiling applies to **decode** — writing one token at a time. Prefill, reading a prompt, is a different machine. All the prompt's tokens are known, so they go through the grids together. **The weights are fetched once and used for all of them**, so the cost per token collapses: $$\text{prefill tokens per second} \approx \frac{\text{compute throughput}}{2 \times \text{parameters}}$$ Every symbol, in plain words Term What it means On this box 
 compute throughput How many arithmetic operations the card performs per second — measured in TFLOPS , tera floating-point operations per second , meaning trillions. Measured here, not quoted. 36.59 TFLOPS 
 2 × parameters The operations one token costs: one multiply and one add per weight, from chapter 03 .

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
36.59 TFLOPS 
 2 × parameters The operations one token costs: one multiply and one add per weight, from chapter 03 . 0.72 GFLOP 
 the division How many tokens' worth of arithmetic fit into one second. ~50,000/s Note what is absent : bandwidth does not appear. Prefill reads the weights once for the whole prompt, so the fetch stops being the per-token cost and arithmetic takes over. That permits roughly **50,000 tokens per second** — and chapter 05 measured 292. Both phases fall far short of their ceilings, which is the actual subject of this chapter. ## Three limits, and a fourth that keeps winning Any given moment is bounded by whichever of these binds first. The ratio that decides between the first two has a name — **arithmetic intensity**, the number of operations performed per byte fetched.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
The ratio that decides between the first two has a name — **arithmetic intensity**, the number of operations performed per byte fetched. Low intensity means memory decides; high intensity means the arithmetic units do. What could be the bottleneck Limit Set by Per step, here 
 Memory weights ÷ bandwidth 1.71 ms 
 Compute operations ÷ throughput 0.02 ms at batch 1 
 Capacity weights + cache vs 7.6 GiB not binding at this size 
 Overhead the cost of asking the card to do things 63.8 ms The fourth row is not a physical limit at all, and on this box it is **thirty-seven times larger than the largest real one.** Every layer is a separate instruction issued from a Python program; with 32 layers and several operations each, one token becomes hundreds of small commands, each with a fixed cost unrelated to the size of its work.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text: The fourth row is not a physical limit at all, and on this box it is **thirty-seven times larger than the largest real one.** Every layer is a separate instruction issued from a Python program; with 32 layers and several operations each, one token becomes hundreds of small commands, each with a fixed cost unrelated to the size of its work. That is the 36× gap from chapter 05, named. **The card is not slow. It is idle, being told what to do.** ## The prediction that tests all of this If decode really is limited by fetching weights rather than by arithmetic, a strong claim follows: > Serving many requests at once should be **nearly free.** The weights arrive once per step regardless of how many requests are waiting, so they can serve all of them.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
> Serving many requests at once should be **nearly free.** The weights arrive once per step regardless of how many requests are waiting, so they can serve all of them. Each individual stream should stay exactly as slow as it was. Total throughput should climb almost in step with the batch size. Here is that prediction measured. Three things in that table are worth separating. **A single stream never gets faster.** A **stream** here is one conversation — one request being answered, start to finish. Sixteen people asking at once is sixteen streams, and "per stream" measures what any one of them experiences while the others are also being served.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text: Sixteen people asking at once is sixteen streams, and "per stream" measures what any one of them experiences while the others are also being served. It is the number a user feels; total throughput is the number the machine reports. 16.2 at batch 1, 15.7 at batch 64. Each token still waits for the whole 0.72 GB to arrive, and nothing about a crowd makes the journey shorter. **Batching buys throughput, never latency** — a fact that decides how a serving engine should be configured, and one that disappoints everyone the first time they meet it. **The last column is the formula being satisfied.** Bytes read per token falls as one over the batch size. The weights are fetched once per *step*; spread across 64 requests, each token's share is 0.011 GB instead of 0.724.

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text: The weights are fetched once per *step*; spread across 64 requests, each token's share is 0.011 GB instead of 0.724. **And the "ceiling" was exceeded.** 1,002 tokens per second against a stated limit of 585. Not a contradiction — the ceiling is **per stream**. Weights are read once per step, not once per token, so total throughput is bounded by bandwidth ÷ (weights ÷ batch), which grows. ## Why it scaled so cleanly, and where it would stop Near-perfect scaling to 64× is suspiciously good. The reason is the overhead from earlier: at 63.8 ms per step against a memory floor of 1.71 ms, **nothing physical was binding at any batch size tested.** There was enormous slack, and batching spent it. Working out where each limit would finally bite:

title: 08 · How Fast It Can Possibly Go
text:
Working out where each limit would finally bite: The batch sizes at which each wall arrives Memory becomes binding at batch 37 if the overhead were gone 
 Compute becomes binding at batch 3,227 far away 
 Capacity — the cache fills the card at ~199,000 tokens of total context across all requests On a properly optimised engine the memory wall would arrive at about batch 37, and scaling would flatten there. This measurement sailed past it only because the overhead was so dominant that memory never got a chance to be the problem. A faster engine would scale less impressively and finish far sooner — which is the right trade, and not an obvious one. ## What this predicts for Part I Every figure needed to predict the engines is now measured.

 Batching raises total throughput, never single-stream speed measured above, 16.2 → 15.7 
 A well-optimised engine stops scaling around batch 37 where memory finally binds 
 Quantizing to 4-bit roughly doubles the ceiling halves the bytes; the extra unpacking is free That last one is worth stating plainly, because it sounds wrong: **making a model less accurate makes it faster, and the arithmetic needed to decompress it costs nothing.** The card has arithmetic to spare and no bandwidth to spare.

 That completes the Foundations. A model is a file of numbers; the numbers get multiplied; that predicts language; running it costs one full read of the weights per token; and the ceiling that sets is a division anyone can do.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text: # What a Serving Engine Does The model does the thinking and the card does the arithmetic. So what is a serving engine for — and why are there five of them? Everything in the Foundations was about the model and the machine. Neither of those is a serving engine, and after eight chapters it is reasonable to ask what is left to write. The answer was measured in [chapter 05](05-running-it.html): running a model the obvious way reached **16.1 tokens per second** on hardware that permits **584**. **A serving engine is whatever closes that gap** — and the reason there are five is that they disagree about how. ## What is actually left to do The arithmetic is fixed. Given the same weights and the same prompt, every engine must compute the same thing.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
Given the same weights and the same prompt, every engine must compute the same thing. What differs is everything around it. The jobs an engine takes on Job What it means Chapter that set it up 
 Load the weights Read the file, place tensors on the right card, convert formats if needed. 02 
 Issue fewer commands Fuse many small operations into few large ones. This is where most of the 36× lives. 05 
 Manage the cache Allocate, grow, share and evict the keys and values. The thing that actually fills the card. 05 
 Batch requests Serve many conversations from one fetch of the weights. 08 
 Schedule Decide who runs next, who waits, and who gets dropped when memory runs out. — 
 Speak a protocol Accept requests over HTTP and stream tokens back, through an API — an application programming interface , the agreed shape of those requests.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
— 
 Speak a protocol Accept requests over HTTP and stream tokens back, through an API — an application programming interface , the agreed shape of those requests. Every engine here speaks the same one. — Not one of those is arithmetic. An engine is a memory manager and a scheduler wearing a web server. The maths was settled before it started. That is why five of them can exist without any being wrong. They are answers to *how should the waiting be organised*, and different answers suit different situations. ## One card, on purpose Before any of that: **every measurement in this part uses a single graphics card.** The box has three; two of them sit idle throughout. Why deliberately waste two thirds of the machine 
 Because one variable at a time .

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
Why deliberately waste two thirds of the machine 
 Because one variable at a time . Adding a second card changes what an engine does, how memory is divided, and how much traffic crosses between them — and any of those could explain a difference that gets credited to the engine instead. It is also the honest learning order. Serving a model on one card is the thing to understand first; splitting one across three is a different subject with its own failure modes, and it gets its own part — chapters 15 to 18. The constraint is enforced, not assumed . The engine is pinned to card 0 and the others are made invisible to it — and the harness records memory on all three, so a run that quietly spread would be visible in the results.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
The engine is pinned to card 0 and the others are made invisible to it — and the harness records memory on all three, so a run that quietly spread would be visible in the results. And pinning is harder than it looks 
 Setting the usual environment variable hid the other two cards from CUDA — NVIDIA's Compute Unified Device Architecture , the normal way programs reach a graphics card — and the engine found them anyway through Vulkan , a second interface it also supports. Both had to be shut off. An engine will use hardware it can see. "I only set one card" is not the same as "it only used one card", and the only way to know is to look at every card's memory afterwards. ## Measuring them without measuring the wrong thing

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
## Measuring them without measuring the wrong thing Comparing engines is easy to do badly. The failure is always the same: **two things change at once** and the difference gets attributed to the interesting one. The methodological hole, stated before it is patched 
 The plan was "control the model, vary the engine". It cannot be done literally. llama.cpp reads GGUF — the GPT-Generated Unified Format , a container built for it — while vLLM reads safetensors. The same file cannot go through both, so something must differ. If one engine runs 4-bit weights and another 16-bit, the comparison measures quantization and reports it as engine quality. That is the trap, and most published comparisons fall into it.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
That is the trap, and most published comparisons fall into it. The way out is to control the **numbers** rather than the file: Two tracks, asking two different questions Control track Capability track 
 Question Which engine is faster? What is the best that runs here? Precision 16-bit everywhere whatever each engine does best 
 Weights numerically identical across engines different by design 
 Fair? yes — the only variable is the engine no, and it is not trying to be A GGUF file at 16-bit is a repack of the same numbers, not a different model. Container differs, values do not — so the control track compares engines and nothing else. That claim needed checking, and it was not quite true 
 "The same numbers" assumes the conversion is lossless.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
That claim needed checking, and it was not quite true 
 "The same numbers" assumes the conversion is lossless. Two engines here read GGUF at F16 ( floating point , 16-bit); the other two read safetensors at bf16 ( brain float , 16-bit). Those are different formats — F16 spends its 16 bits as 1 sign, 5 exponent and 10 mantissa; bf16 as 1, 8 and 7. Wider range, coarser precision. Checked against the real file, all 361,821,120 weights: survive bf16 → F16 → bf16 exactly 361,811,290 99.9973% 
 changed 9,830 0.0027% Nothing overflowed — the largest weight is 7.47 and F16 reaches 65,504. The damage is at the other end: 117,192 weights sit below F16's smallest normal value of 6.1×10⁻⁵, and the smallest in the model is 3.9×10⁻¹⁰.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text: The damage is at the other end: 117,192 weights sit below F16's smallest normal value of 6.1×10⁻⁵, and the smallest in the model is 3.9×10⁻¹⁰. Those lose precision going across. The fix is one flag. vLLM and SGLang are loaded with dtype=float16 , so they perform the same conversion the GGUF file already went through — leaving all four engines holding the same numbers, including the same 9,830 degraded ones. Without that, the comparison would have measured engines and number formats and reported the sum as engine quality — which is the exact trap named at the top of this section, committed while writing the section that names it. ## The six metrics, and why exactly these Every engine reports the same six numbers, produced by the same script.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
Every engine reports the same six numbers, produced by the same script. Nothing is measured by hand. What each one is for Metric What it captures Why it cannot be skipped 
 TTFT — time to first token How long before anything appears. What a user experiences as lag. Governed by prefill, which is a different machine from decode. decode tok/s Streaming speed, one stream. The number bounded by bandwidth ÷ weights . Comparable to a ceiling that is already known. concurrent tok/s Total output with many requests at once. A completely different quantity, and the one that decides whether an engine can serve more than one person. VRAM peak per card video random access memory How much memory was really used.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text: VRAM peak per card video random access memory How much memory was really used. No engine reports this honestly about itself. Sampled externally. context ceiling Where it stops working. The capacity limit, as opposed to the speed limit. output hash at temperature 0 Exactly what was produced. The correctness column. See below — it is the one everybody omits. That last one deserves its own paragraph, because a speed comparison with no correctness column is not a comparison at all. **An engine that is fast and wrong should lose**, and without hashing the output there is no way to notice. At temperature 0 the model always takes its highest-scoring token, so the same prompt must give the same text every time.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
At temperature 0 the model always takes its highest-scoring token, so the same prompt must give the same text every time. Two engines running numerically identical weights should therefore produce **identical output**. If they do not, something differs — a different attention implementation, a different rounding order, a silently different default — and that is worth far more than a few tokens per second either way. ## Frozen, on purpose The prompt set cannot change 
 Four prompts, fixed on 2026-09-13: a short one to isolate fixed overhead, a medium one for the everyday case, a long one of about 2,850 tokens for prefill cost at length, and a code-generation one because that is what Part II will care about.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
The prompt set cannot change 
 Four prompts, fixed on 2026-09-13: a short one to isolate fixed overhead, a medium one for the everyday case, a long one of about 2,850 tokens for prefill cost at length, and a code-generation one because that is what Part II will care about. Changing a prompt invalidates every measurement taken before the change. To add one, add a new identifier and keep the old. The long prompt's filler is deliberately repetitive so its content cannot flatter one engine over another. The table in this guide is **generated** from the result files, never written by hand. A number that was not measured cannot appear in it, and a number that was measured cannot quietly go stale.

title: 09 · What a Serving Engine Does
text:
## A caution, already paid for The harness first estimated token counts from character length, dividing by four. Against the first engine's own reported counts, that estimate was **wrong by 1.43×** — real output averaged 5.71 characters per token, not 4. What that would have cost 
 Every tokens-per-second figure in Part I would have been 43% too high , consistently, across every engine. The comparison between engines would still have looked sensible, because the same error applied to all of them — which is exactly what makes this class of mistake survive. The fix: ask the engine. The protocol has a field for real token counts, and the harness now records which source each count came from , because a number is only as trustworthy as its origin.

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text:
# L0 · Ollama — the Baseline One command to install, one to run. Its job here is not to win anything — it is to be the reference the next four engines have to match, token for token. Ollama is the easiest way to run a language model locally, and that is the whole reason it goes first. It hides everything, which makes it a good control: whatever it does internally, the output it produces is what the other engines will be checked against. Deliberately, **its internals are not examined in this chapter.** It is the reference, not the subject. ## Getting it running ```
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama pull smollm2:360m
``` One detail matters and is easy to get wrong. By default the server listens only on the machine it runs on, which makes it unreachable from anywhere else:

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text:
By default the server listens only on the machine it runs on, which makes it unreachable from anywhere else: ```
Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434"
``` Bind to the network, not to localhost 
 A server on 127.0.0.1 can only be reached by programs on the same machine. Every measurement in this project is taken from a laptop across the room, so the endpoint has to be reachable at the box's own address. This is the single most common reason a locally-hosted model "works on the server and not from anywhere else", and it is one line. ## What it downloaded ```
architecture llama
parameters 361.82M
context length 8192
embedding length 960
quantization F16
``` **361.82M parameters** and **F16** — 16-bit floating point.

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text:
**361.82M parameters** and **F16** — 16-bit floating point. That is the same model [chapter 02](02-a-file-of-numbers.html) opened, at the same precision, in a different container. Its copy is 725 MB against the original file's 723.7 MB. This matters more than it looks: it puts Ollama squarely on the **control track** from [chapter 09](09-what-an-engine-does.html). The numbers are the same numbers. Any difference the next engines show is theirs, not the weights'. ## Measured Four prompts, three repeats each, median reported. Token counts come from the engine itself, never estimated. L0 · Ollama 0.34.0 · SmolLM2-360M F16 · one RTX 3060 Ti · 2026-09-13 Prompt TTFT time to first token Decode Tokens out

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text: Sixteen users get the same total output as one, divided sixteen ways. Compare the raw batching experiment from chapter 08 , on the same card with the same model: batch 16 gave 250 tok/s and batch 64 gave 1,002 — scaling almost perfectly. The prediction was not wrong about the hardware. **Ollama simply does not batch by default** — it processes requests one after another. Chapter 08 proved the card can serve sixteen requests for almost the price of one; this engine declines to. That is a legitimate choice for the thing Ollama is: a single-user tool on a laptop, where the simplicity is worth more than throughput nobody will use. It is also precisely the gap [chapter 12](12-vllm.html) exists to fill, and it means the two engines are not really competing at the same task.

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline

It is also precisely the gap [chapter 12](12-vllm.html) exists to fill, and it means the two engines are not really competing at the same task. ### The first token is faster than it should be `longctx` sends about 2,850 tokens and came back in **52.5 ms**. [Chapter 05](05-running-it.html) measured prefill at 292 tokens per second, which would predict nearly ten seconds. The engine's logs explain it: `prompt cache`. Those tokens had been sent before, in an earlier repeat, and their keys and values were still held — so most of the prompt was never recomputed. The request reported **34 of 35 prompt tokens cached**. A measurement of the harness, not of the engine 
 This is a real effect and a real feature, but as measured it is an artefact of repeating the same prompt three times.

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text:
A measurement of the harness, not of the engine 
 This is a real effect and a real feature, but as measured it is an artefact of repeating the same prompt three times. The first repeat paid full price; the median reported the cached ones. It is recorded here rather than quietly corrected, because it identifies a flaw in the harness: repeats interact with prefix caching , and an engine with a good cache will look better than it is at long prompts. Chapter 13's engine is built entirely around this behaviour, so the harness will need a cold-start mode before that comparison can be trusted. ## Where the remaining gap is Ollama reached **51%** of the ceiling. Something still costs roughly half of every token.

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text:
Something still costs roughly half of every token. The account so far tok/s ms per token 
 Hardware limit 584 1.71 moving 0.72 GB of weights 
 Ollama 298 3.36 1.65 ms unaccounted 
 The obvious approach 16.1 62.1 60.4 ms unaccounted The overhead per token fell from 60.4 ms to 1.65 ms — a 37× reduction — and what remains is the same kind of thing, just less of it: work that is neither moving weights nor multiplying them. Whether 1.65 ms is the floor for a careful implementation, or whether another engine halves it again, is the question the next three chapters answer. ## The checkpoint Every level in Part I has a question that must be answerable before moving on. For this one: Where did the weights go, in what format, and what holds the card?

title: 10 · L0 · Ollama — the Baseline
text: Where did the weights go, in what format, and what holds the card? Where: /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models , as content-addressed blobs — named by the hash of their contents rather than by model name, so two models sharing a layer store it once. What format: GGUF — the GPT-Generated Unified Format — at F16. The same numbers as the original safetensors file, repacked. What holds the card: a persistent ollama process, started by the system at boot, that keeps the model resident after the first request and unloads it after a period of inactivity. That is why the first request of the day is slow and the rest are not — and why peak memory stayed at 1,073 MB between runs rather than returning to zero.
