title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit
text: # L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit This is not a new engine. It is the one chapter 10 was already using, with the lid taken off — which makes the comparison unusually sharp. Ollama is a wrapper. Underneath it, doing the actual work, is **llama.cpp**. Running them side by side therefore measures something specific: not "which engine is better", but **what the wrapper costs and what it hides.** And because the same file can be used — the identical bytes, not a re-download — the comparison has no room for the usual excuses. ## The same file, guaranteed Ollama stores weights as **content-addressed blobs**: files named by the hash of their contents rather than by model name. That blob is already a **GGUF** file — the *GPT-Generated Unified Format* — which is what llama.cpp reads.

title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit
text:
That blob is already a **GGUF** file — the *GPT-Generated Unified Format* — which is what llama.cpp reads. So rather than downloading a second copy, it was **hard-linked**: ```
models/gguf/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct-F16.gguf
 same inode as ollama's blob? YES
 725,553,792 bytes
 sha256: 7d23be4097d67c5c43c3df62ebc19609... ``` One file, one inode, two engines 
 A hard link is not a copy. There is one set of bytes on the disk with two names pointing at it, so the two engines cannot possibly be running different weights — not "the same model", not "the same quantization", the same bytes . Note also that the blob's filename is its sha256. Ollama names files by content, which is why two models sharing a layer store it once, and why this check was free.

title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit
text:
Ollama names files by content, which is why two models sharing a layer store it once, and why this check was free. ## Building it llama.cpp needs a compiler for **CUDA**, NVIDIA's *Compute Unified Device Architecture*, which the graphics driver alone does not provide: ```
apt-get install -y cmake ccache nvidia-cuda-toolkit # ~3 GB
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86 ... ``` Why the architecture number matters 
 86 is this card's compute capability — the generation code from chapter 06 , written sm_86 for streaming multiprocessor version 8.6, meaning Ampere. Naming it means the compiler emits code for this card and nothing else. Left out, the build compiles for every architecture llama.cpp supports, which takes several times longer and produces a binary full of code this machine will never run.

title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 build/bin/llama-server \
 -m models/gguf/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct-F16.gguf \
 -ngl 99 -c 8192 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
``` `-ngl 99` is the flag this chapter is really about — how many layers go on the graphics card. Ninety-nine means all of them, and the next chapter in this part takes that number apart properly. ## Measured L1 · llama.cpp 37b3a9e · same GGUF as L0 · one card · 2026-09-13 L0 Ollama L1 llama.cpp

This is [chapter 08's prediction](08-how-fast.html) arriving on schedule. Decode is limited by fetching weights; the weights arrive once per step regardless of how many requests are waiting; therefore serving several at once should be nearly free. Ollama declines to. llama.cpp does it by default, and the server log says how: `n_slots = 4`. Two details in that table repay attention. **862 tokens per second exceeds the 584 ceiling** from chapter 08 — and does not break it.

title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit
text: **862 tokens per second exceeds the 584 ceiling** from chapter 08 — and does not break it. That ceiling is **per stream**. With four requests sharing one fetch of the weights, each token's share of the memory traffic is a quarter, and the aggregate limit moves accordingly. Chapter 08 said exactly this would happen. **Batch 16 is slower than batch 4.** Because there are four slots. Sixteen requests do not run sixteen at a time — they queue in groups of four, and the extra twelve wait. The engine's concurrency is a configured number, not an unlimited one, and going past it costs rather than gains. ## The engines disagree — on one prompt in four The harness hashes every completion at temperature 0.

What that means, and what it does not 
 Not a bug in either engine. At that position the model's scores for two tokens were nearly tied, and the two engines computed those scores in slightly different ways — a different **kernel** — the small program every processor on the card runs at once, [chapter 05](05-running-it.html) — a different order of summation, a different rounding at the last bit. The arithmetic differs in the final decimal place; the tie tips one way or the other. This is why the hash column exists. A speed comparison without it would have reported these engines as interchangeable. They are very nearly interchangeable — and "very nearly" is exactly the thing a measurement should be able to say precisely.

Neither is wrong; they are not the same measurement, and **the comparison in this chapter only ever uses figures from the same tool.** ## The model that does not fit The offload model above has one more use, and it is the reason llama.cpp exists at all: **it predicts what happens to a model too large for the card.** The test uses the same 8-billion-parameter model chapter 01 built its parameter budget from, in two quantizations that land either side of the line:

Each Llama-3-8B layer at Q8 is 231 MB against SmolLM2's 19.7 MB, and the sweep measured the link moving those at an effective 12.2 GB/s — so one layer left in system memory costs about 19 ms per token here, against 1.61 ms there. title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit
text:
Read those two rows together, because the shape of the answer is the point: A 4% overflow is predicted to cost 80% of the speed 
 The Q8 file is 1.7× the size of the Q4 one, which sounds like it should be somewhat slower. The prediction says five times slower — and not because of its size, but because of where the line falls. Everything up to 8.16 GB is free. The 0.35 GB past it is charged at the speed of the PCIe link rather than the card's own memory, on every token, forever. The penalty for not fitting is not proportional to how badly you miss. It is a cliff, not a slope. That is the single most useful thing to take from this level, and it explains a great deal of otherwise strange advice: why people obsess over squeezing a model under a memory limit, why the difference between two quantizations can be enormous or nothing at all depending on the card, and why "it still runs" and "it is still usable" are separate questions.

title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit

It is also why llama.cpp is the engine that runs *anywhere*. It will not refuse a model that does not fit — it will spill the remainder into system memory and keep going. Whether the result is usable is left to the person running it, which is the right division of responsibility and the opposite of what [chapter 12's engine](12-vllm.html) does.

 -ngl 99 — put everything on the card — failed outright : 
 failed to create context with model 'Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf' 
 But -ngl 32 worked. The difference is that 99 also tries to place the embedding and output layers, and those were the straw. llama.cpp does not spill automatically. It does exactly what it is told, and if what it is told does not fit, it stops. The "runs anywhere" reputation is earned by the -ngl flag existing, not by the engine being clever.

The cost of a spilled layer was predicted at **19.0 ms** and measured at **9.6 ms** — the prediction was twice as pessimistic as reality. Why: big transfers are more efficient 
 The 19.0 ms came from scaling SmolLM2's measurement, which implied an effective link rate of 12.2 GB/s . Llama-3-8B's larger layers imply 24.1 GB/s — twice as fast, on the same wire. That is not the bus speed: chapter 17 measures the raw link at 4.87–5.81 GB/s.

title: 11 · L1 · llama.cpp — Making It Fit
text: That is not the bus speed: chapter 17 measures the raw link at 4.87–5.81 GB/s. It is an effective rate — layer bytes divided by the per-token cost — and it runs ahead of the wire because the transfer overlaps computation and not every byte crosses every token. The number to predict with is this effective one; the raw bus speed would over-count the cost. Nothing about the hardware changed. A 231 MB transfer amortises the fixed cost of starting a transfer in a way a 19.7 MB one cannot. The small model was paying overhead the large one spreads thin. So the constant in that formula is not a property of the machine — it depends on how much is moved at once. Fitted on a small model it under-states the link; the honest version of the rule carries the transfer size with it.

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
# L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast The first engine here built for more than one person at a time. On the same card and the same weights it produced ten times the throughput of the baseline — and charged for it. The two engines so far were designed for a person running a model on their own machine. vLLM was designed for a machine serving many people, and the difference shows up in exactly one column of the results. ## Getting it running was the hard part Worth recording, because none of it is in the documentation and all of it cost time. Three failures, in order 
 1 · Its own environment. vLLM installs torch 2.13.0+cu130 — built against CUDA 13.0, NVIDIA's Compute Unified Device Architecture — this project's environment has 2.11.0+cu128 .

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text: vLLM installs torch 2.13.0+cu130 — built against CUDA 13.0, NVIDIA's Compute Unified Device Architecture — this project's environment has 2.11.0+cu128 . Sharing one would break both, which is why the plan gives every engine its own. The install is 7.6 GB . 2 · FileNotFoundError: 'ninja' . vLLM compiles kernels when it starts and shells out to the ninja build tool. Installing it into the environment was not enough — the environment's bin has to be on PATH , because the compile runs as a subprocess. 3 · nvcc fatal : Unknown option '--compress-mode=size' . The real one. vLLM's attention library compiles with a flag that requires CUDA 12.8 or newer , and the toolkit available from this system's package manager is 12.0 .

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
vLLM's attention library compiles with a flag that requires CUDA 12.8 or newer , and the toolkit available from this system's package manager is 12.0 . That third failure is the kind of thing that stops a project. The options were to install a newer toolkit from the vendor — several more gigabytes — or to find the piece that needed it and switch it off: ```
VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0
``` The failing compile was for **sampling** kernels, not attention. vLLM has its own sampler that needs no compilation, so turning the optional one off costs nothing measurable here and the engine starts. Worth generalising 
 An error deep in a build log usually names one component. Read which part actually failed before reaching for the large fix.

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
Read which part actually failed before reaching for the large fix. Here the difference was one environment variable against a multi-gigabyte toolkit upgrade — and the failing component turned out to be optional. Then, on one card and at 16-bit to stay on the control track: ```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve models/hf/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct \
 --dtype float16 --max-model-len 8192 \
 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
``` `--dtype float16` is not cosmetic. The weights on disk are brain float; the other two engines read a file already converted to 16-bit floating point. Without this flag the comparison would measure engines **and** number formats — [chapter 09](09-what-an-engine-does.html) has the full accounting, including the 9,830 weights that do not survive that conversion.

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
Without this flag the comparison would measure engines **and** number formats — [chapter 09](09-what-an-engine-does.html) has the full accounting, including the 9,830 weights that do not survive that conversion. ## Measured Three engines · same model · same card · 2026-09-13 Engine Alone Time to first token 16 at once Card memory Host memory 
 L0 Ollama 297.5 tok/s 11.2 ms 288.1 tok/s 1,091 MB 739 MB 
 L1 llama.cpp 283.6 tok/s 13.7 ms 772.6 tok/s 1,255 MB 635 MB 
 L2 vLLM 312.9 tok/s 33.1 ms 3,029.1 tok/s 6,979 MB 1,294 MB Alone, all three are the same engine to within a few percent — as they must be, since the hardware limit is the same and none of them is near it. **Everything interesting is in the fourth column.**

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
**Everything interesting is in the fourth column.** ### The scaling Total throughput as requests arrive together Engine 1 4 16 gain at 16 
 L0 Ollama 279.5 289.0 288.1 1.0× 
 L1 llama.cpp 276.2 862.4 772.6 2.8× 
 L2 vLLM 266.2 955.9 3,029.1 11.4× Ollama gains nothing. llama.cpp gains until its four slots are full and then stops. vLLM keeps going. This is [chapter 08's argument](08-how-fast.html) fully realised. Decode is limited by fetching weights from memory; the weights arrive once per step whatever the number of waiting requests; so requests served together are nearly free. Chapter 08 measured that ceiling at 584 tokens per second **for one stream** — and vLLM produced 3,029, which is not a contradiction but the point.

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
Chapter 08 measured that ceiling at 584 tokens per second **for one stream** — and vLLM produced 3,029, which is not a contradiction but the point. The mechanism has a name: **continuous batching**. Rather than collecting a fixed group, running it, and collecting another, vLLM adds a new request to the batch as soon as one finishes, so the machine never idles waiting for a slow generation to complete. llama.cpp's four slots are a simpler version of the same idea with a hard limit. ## And what it costs Nothing here is free vs Ollama 
 Throughput at 16 concurrent 10.5× better 
 Time to first token 3.0× worse — 33.1 ms against 11.2 
 Card memory 6.4× more — 6,979 MB against 1,091 
 Host memory 1.8× more — 1,294 MB against 739

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
vs Ollama 
 Throughput at 16 concurrent 10.5× better 
 Time to first token 3.0× worse — 33.1 ms against 11.2 
 Card memory 6.4× more — 6,979 MB against 1,091 
 Host memory 1.8× more — 1,294 MB against 739 **The memory is the more interesting cost**, because it is not waste. vLLM claims 85% of the card at startup and manages that pool itself — the log says `Available KV cache memory: 5.15 GiB`. The model is 0.7 GB; almost everything else is a reservation for the keys and values of conversations it has not been asked to have yet. That reservation **is** the batching. Sixteen simultaneous conversations need sixteen caches, and an engine that allocates them on demand will eventually fail mid-request.

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text: Sixteen simultaneous conversations need sixteen caches, and an engine that allocates them on demand will eventually fail mid-request. vLLM takes the memory in advance and rations it. The full mechanism — treating the cache as pages, the way an operating system treats memory — is what the [PagedAttention paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) describes. **The latency is the more practical cost.** Three times the wait before the first word appears. For a person typing at a chat box, that is the number they feel; for a job processing ten thousand documents overnight, it is irrelevant. **There is no best engine here, only a question about who is waiting.** ## The engines still disagree — and Ollama is the odd one

title: 12 · L2 · vLLM — Making It Fast
text:
## The engines still disagree — and Ollama is the odd one Output hashes, all three engines Prompt L0 Ollama L1 llama.cpp L2 vLLM

 medium 8c88988b… 8c88988b… 8c88988b…

 code 9e34bfd3… 7e10b432… 7e10b432… Three of four prompts identical across three engines, three file formats and two number formats. On the fourth, vLLM agrees with llama.cpp — and Ollama is alone. Chapter 11 found this divergence with two engines and could only say they differed. With a third it becomes a **vote**: two engines write `def` immediately and one writes `import os` first. That does not prove Ollama wrong — there is no right answer to a near-tie — but it does move the question from "they differ" to "one of them differs from the others", which is a more useful thing to know.

It also means the agreement on the other three prompts is stronger evidence than it was. title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
# L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart The fastest single stream measured in this project — and then, at eleven concurrent requests, a collapse to a tenth of its speed. The collapse is the more valuable half. SGLang is built for workloads where requests share structure: many conversations beginning with the same long instruction, an agent re-sending its whole history every turn. That is exactly what Part III will run, which is why it is here. What it actually produced was a sharper lesson about something else. ## The install was the hardest yet Chapter 12 hit a compiler that was too old and worked around it by switching off an optional component. SGLang does not offer that escape. Same error, no easy exit 
 nvcc fatal : Unknown option '--compress-mode=size' 
 In vLLM this came from the sampler , which is optional.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
Same error, no easy exit 
 nvcc fatal : Unknown option '--compress-mode=size' 
 In vLLM this came from the sampler , which is optional. In SGLang it comes from attention , which is not. The flag needs CUDA — NVIDIA's Compute Unified Device Architecture — at version 12.8 or newer; this box has 12.0. The way out was a different attention implementation entirely — Triton , which compiles through a different path that does not involve nvcc : 
 --attention-backend triton --sampling-backend pytorch So this is not SGLang as intended 
 Everything below runs a fallback backend . SGLang's own default is flashinfer, and it could not be compiled on this machine. The numbers are real measurements of a real configuration, and they are not a fair statement of what this engine does on a properly provisioned box.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text: The numbers are real measurements of a real configuration, and they are not a fair statement of what this engine does on a properly provisioned box. This is recorded prominently rather than buried, because the temptation to present a fallback measurement as the engine's performance is exactly how misleading benchmarks get written. One more thing bit before any of it ran: **vLLM was still holding 6,859 MB of the card.** SGLang failed with `Loaded weights leave no GPU memory for the KV cache` — no room on the **GPU** (*graphics processing unit*) for the **KV** (*keys and values*) cache — which reads like a model-too-large error and was nothing of the sort. **One engine at a time, and check the card before blaming the configuration.**

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
**One engine at a time, and check the card before blaming the configuration.** ## Measured Four engines · same model · same card · 2026-09-13 Engine Alone First token 16 at once Card Host 
 L0 Ollama 297.5 11.2 ms 288.1 1,091 MB 739 MB 
 L1 llama.cpp 283.6 13.7 ms 772.6 1,255 MB 635 MB 
 L2 vLLM 312.9 33.1 ms 3,029.1 6,979 MB 1,294 MB 
 L3 SGLang 374.9 49.8 ms 357.8 7,253 MB 5,434 MB The fastest single stream of the four — 374.9 tokens per second, 26% above Ollama — and the slowest to produce a first token, at 4.5× Ollama's wait. And the host column, which the earlier chapters did not measure: 5,434 MB of system memory , 8.6× what llama.cpp uses. Its total footprint across both kinds is 12.7 GB — more than the graphics card holds in total.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
Its total footprint across both kinds is 12.7 GB — more than the graphics card holds in total. That trade is consistent with everything before it: the engines built for throughput make one person wait longer. SGLang takes it furthest in both directions. The last column is where it gets strange. ## The cliff Total throughput as requests arrive together Concurrent Total Per stream CUDA graph? 1 310.7 310.7 yes 
 2 547.1 273.6 yes 
 4 1,106.5 276.6 yes 
 8 2,069.0 258.6 yes 
 10 239.9 24.0 no 
 12 286.7 23.9 no 
 16 377.5 23.6 no Between 8 and 10 concurrent requests, throughput falls by a factor of 8.6 . Per stream it falls from 258.6 to 24.0. Up to eight, SGLang scales better than anything else measured — 2,069 tokens per second at batch 8, against vLLM's 955.9 at batch 4.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
Up to eight, SGLang scales better than anything else measured — 2,069 tokens per second at batch 8, against vLLM's 955.9 at batch 4. Past eight it becomes the slowest engine in the project. The server log names the cause in one line, printed at startup: ```
Capture target decode CUDA graph begin. backend=full, num_tokens_per_req=1, bs=[1, 2, 4, 8], avail mem=0.64 GB
``` CUDA graphs, and what happens without them 
 A CUDA graph records the whole sequence of commands a forward pass issues — hundreds of them, one per operation per layer — and replays the recording as a single instruction. The work is identical; the cost of asking for it collapses. SGLang captures one graph per batch size, in advance, and each costs memory.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text: SGLang captures one graph per batch size, in advance, and each costs memory. After the model and its cache there was 0.64 GB left, enough for four: batch 1, 2, 4 and 8 . A request arriving at batch 10 finds no recording, so the engine issues every command individually — and speed per stream drops from 258.6 to 24.0 tokens per second . The graphs are worth 10.8× . ### Which is the answer to chapter 05 That number should look familiar. [Chapter 05](05-running-it.html) measured a plain PyTorch loop at **16.1 tokens per second** against a hardware ceiling of 584, and attributed the 36× gap to *the overhead of issuing hundreds of small commands*. That was an inference from where the time was not going.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
That was an inference from where the time was not going. Here the same effect is visible **by switching it off**: The same gap, three ways Plain PyTorch loop, no graphs ( ch.05 ) 16.1 tok/s 
 SGLang past its graph limit, per stream 24.0 tok/s 
 SGLang within its graph limit, per stream 258.6 tok/s A production engine, running without command recordings, lands in the same territory as a naive loop. The difference between 16 and 300 tokens per second was never the arithmetic — it was how many times the card had to be told what to do, and this is that claim measured directly rather than inferred. ### And why the cliff is here rather than elsewhere The limit is **memory**, not a design choice. SGLang captures graphs for as many batch sizes as it can afford, and on this card 0.64 GB bought four.

title: 13 · L3 · SGLang — Making It Smart
text:
SGLang captures graphs for as many batch sizes as it can afford, and on this card 0.64 GB bought four. On a larger card it would buy more and the cliff would move — which means **this measurement is about the hardware as much as the engine.** It also suggests a configuration worth trying: reserving less memory for the cache would leave more for graphs, trading maximum context for a higher batch ceiling. That is a real decision this project now knows how to reason about, and there is no universally right answer to it. ## The engines still agree All four produce identical text on three prompts of four. On the fourth, vLLM, llama.cpp and SGLang agree with each other and Ollama does not. Three of four prompts, four engines, byte-identical 
 Across three file formats, two number formats, four independent implementations and a fallback attention backend, the output hashes match exactly.

 A later re-run of vLLM and SGLang measured them at 27 and 26 tok/s — and an earlier draft of this section reported those as the engines' speed, blaming a missing CUDA developer toolkit ( nvcc , which flashinfer needs to compile its kernels). That was wrong. The re-run had CUDA graphs disabled by hand ( --enforce-eager , --disable-cuda-graph ) to sidestep that compile, and on a tiny model graph replay is most of the speed — so the 27/26 were an artifact of the configuration, not the engines.

title: 14 · Four Engines, Compared
text: The re-run had CUDA graphs disabled by hand ( --enforce-eager , --disable-cuda-graph ) to sidestep that compile, and on a tiny model graph replay is most of the speed — so the 27/26 were an artifact of the configuration, not the engines. SGLang in particular needs no nvcc at all: its Triton backend captures graphs, which is exactly how the 374.9 above was measured. The lesson is the one the whole guide runs on — a measurement is only as good as the configuration it was taken in, and this one was quietly crippled. The engines separate by workload , and the published designs say how. **llama.cpp is the generalist.** Its C++ core has the lowest first-token latency and the least setup friction, it reads GGUF, and it is the only one of the three that will run on the CPU (central processing unit) or spill an oversized model to host memory — the 90 GB model in chapter 31 ran on it and on nothing else here.

title: 14 · Four Engines, Compared
text: **llama.cpp is the generalist.** Its C++ core has the lowest first-token latency and the least setup friction, it reads GGUF, and it is the only one of the three that will run on the CPU (central processing unit) or spill an oversized model to host memory — the 90 GB model in chapter 31 ran on it and on nothing else here. Its bottleneck is the crowd: it batches requests through a rigid fixed set of slots rather than reorganising them, so it cannot fill the hardware when many arrive at once. At peak concurrent load, vLLM has been measured serving 35× the requests and 44× the output tokens per second . **vLLM is the throughput engine.** PagedAttention stores the key-value cache in non-contiguous pages so memory is not wasted on reservations, and continuous batching re-forms the running batch every step so a finished request frees its slot at once.

title: 14 · Four Engines, Compared
text: **vLLM is the throughput engine.** PagedAttention stores the key-value cache in non-contiguous pages so memory is not wasted on reservations, and continuous batching re-forms the running batch every step so a finished request frees its slot at once. On this box its total climbed past 1,200 tok/s at sixteen concurrent streams . The cost is the format — it reads only safetensors, not GGUF (see the format divide ) — and that at a single stream, with no crowd to schedule, the paging and reshuffling are overhead it cannot amortise. **SGLang is the prefix engine.** RadixAttention keeps every cached prefix in a radix tree and reuses it across requests automatically, so any two requests that begin with the same tokens share that computation.

title: 14 · Four Engines, Compared
text:
**SGLang is the prefix engine.** RadixAttention keeps every cached prefix in a radix tree and reuses it across requests automatically, so any two requests that begin with the same tokens share that computation. On this box its total reached 2,098 tok/s at eight streams , and on workloads where a fixed system prompt leads every request — agents — reported cache hit rates run 75 to 95 percent, opening a clear lead over vLLM. Its bottleneck is that this only pays when prefixes overlap; with unique prompts the tree is bookkeeping that earns nothing. It, too, reads only safetensors. This project has already felt all three 
 The agent battle in Part III sends the same system prompt to every task — SGLang's exact sweet spot, and the reason a prefix cache mattered enough that chapter 30 's benchmark had to erase it between tasks: a reused prefix on llama.cpp changed the answer, which is the same cache SGLang is built to exploit deliberately.

And the reason the app loads llama.cpp by default is not that it is fastest — it is that every model on the box is GGUF, which only llama.cpp reads. title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
# L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam Four engines have been measured. This chapter writes a fifth from an empty file, because reading about a mechanism and being able to build it are different claims, and only one of them can be tested. In progress 
 All five steps are built and measured, on the box, 2026-09-13 and 2026-09-14 . The engine serves over the network and has a row in the same table as the other four. ## What "engine" means here, and what it does not An engine is the code between a file of numbers and a stream of text. Chapter 09 described the job; four chapters then measured other people's answers to it. **Ours is allowed `torch` and nothing above it** — the matrix multiplications are a solved problem and rewriting them teaches nothing.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
**Ours is allowed `torch` and nothing above it** — the matrix multiplications are a solved problem and rewriting them teaches nothing. Everything that makes those multiplications into a *language model* gets written by hand. The line, drawn precisely Allowed Not allowed 
 torch matrix multiply, softmax, the card any serving framework — vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp

 the reference implementation, as a thing to be checked against the reference implementation, as a thing to call ## The exam, stated before we start A test written after the result is known is not a test. So the standard is fixed here, in advance:

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
So the standard is fixed here, in advance: The pass condition 
 At temperature 0, our engine must produce token-identical output to the L0 reference — same prompt, same model, same numbers. Not similar. Not close. The same tokens in the same order. Temperature 0 means no randomness: at every step the highest-scoring token wins, so two correct implementations must agree. Any divergence is a real bug, not a rounding difference to be waved through. This standard is known to be reachable, which is what makes it fair. [Chapter 14](14-four-engines-compared.html) ran four independent engines over the frozen prompt set and found **three of four prompts byte-identical across all of them**. Four separate teams, four codebases, same tokens.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
Four separate teams, four codebases, same tokens. The bar is not theoretical. ## The five steps L4, broken down Step What it has to do State 
 L4a weights open the file, parse its header, put tensors on the card done — passes 
 L4b forward turn a list of tokens into a score for every possible next token done — passes 
 L4c cache remember the work already done, so token two costs less than token one done — and it changed what the exam means 
 L4d sampler choose a token from the scores done — checked against 200,000 draws 
 L4e serve a batching loop and an endpoint other programs can call done — 16.3 tok/s, measured by the same harness They are in dependency order. Nothing later works until everything earlier is exactly right, which is the point of building in this direction.

### RMSNorm — keeping the numbers in range Thirty-two blocks each add to the same running vector. Without a brake, those values drift — a little larger each layer, until the arithmetic runs out of range. Normalisation is that brake, applied before each block reads the stream. $$\text{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 + \epsilon}} \odot w$$ Every symbol Symbol Reads as What it is Here

The model must be told position, and the obvious method — add a position number to the vector — has an obvious problem: it corrupts the vector.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text: The model must be told position, and the obvious method — add a position number to the vector — has an obvious problem: it corrupts the vector. The numbers meant *what the word is*, and now they mean what-the-word-is-plus-where-it-sits, mixed together beyond separating. Rotary position embedding does not add anything. It takes the 960 numbers in pairs and **rotates each pair by an angle set by the position** — a clock hand turning. The vector's length is unchanged, so nothing about *what the word is* has been damaged. Only its direction moves. The payoff is what happens when two rotated vectors are compared. Comparing is a dot product, and a dot product depends on the angle between the two.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
Comparing is a dot product, and a dot product depends on the angle between the two. Rotate one by its position and the other by its position, and the angle between them is the **difference** of the two positions. Absolute positions went in; relative distance came out, without being asked for and without being stored anywhere. Every term in the rotation Term What it is Here

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam

The mechanism is short. The mistakes were not. Bug 1 — every layer but the first thought the past was longer than it was 
 The cache reports its length so the rotation can be applied at the true position. Ours asked the cache directly, inside the layer loop — and the cache answers with layer 0's stack, which has already been appended to by the time layer 1 runs. Layers 1 through 31 each saw a past five tokens too long. It surfaced as a shape mismatch, which was lucky. The same class of error in the rotation alone would have produced fluent, confident, wrong text and no error at all. The length has to be captured once, before the loop, and handed to every layer. Bug 2 — the first exam was rigged in our favour 
 The first run of the test reported all four prompts identical .

That line is also the only reason any two engines can be compared at all — it is the setting under which output is supposed to be reproducible. Temperature 0 is a limit, not a value 
 Temperature works by dividing every score before the softmax. Divide by 0.5 and the differences double, concentrating the probability. Divide by 2 and they halve, spreading it. Divide by zero and there is no arithmetic to do at all. Temperature Probability of the leading token 
 1.0 0.181616 
 0.1 0.998053 
 0.01 1.000000 As the temperature falls, all the probability collects on the single highest score. "Temperature 0" names the limit that approaches , and every engine — ours included — special-cases it to taking the maximum directly.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
"Temperature 0" names the limit that approaches , and every engine — ours included — special-cases it to taking the maximum directly. It is not a temperature the formula can accept. Above zero, three knobs interact, and the order they are applied in is not arbitrary. Every knob, and why this order Order Knob What it does 
 1 temperature Reshapes the whole distribution — sharper or flatter. 2 top-k Keeps the k highest and discards everything else. A fixed count. 3 top-p Keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. An adaptive count. 4 draw One sample from whatever survived. Cutting before scaling would truncate a different distribution than the one the temperature was asked to produce, so the shape must be set first and the cut made second.

The difference between the two knobs is in those numbers. top-k ignores how confident the model is — 40 tokens whether the answer is obvious or wide open. top-p adapts : 8 tokens where the model is sure, 231 where it is not. That is the whole argument for preferring it. A sampler is easy to write and easy to get subtly wrong, and wrong here is invisible — the text still reads fine. So it is checked by drawing from it 200,000 times per setting and comparing what came out against what was intended. The sampler draws the distribution it claims to. ## L4e · The engine The last step is the one that makes this a service rather than a script: requests arriving over the network, batched together, answered in a shape other programs already understand. Static batching, which is not what chapters 12 and 13 measured 
 Requests that arrive at the same moment are served together, sharing one forward pass per step. The batch is fixed when it starts, and the whole batch finishes before the next one begins.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text: The batch is fixed when it starts, and the whole batch finishes before the next one begins. That is static batching. Continuous batching — what vLLM and SGLang do — evicts a finished sequence mid-flight and gives its slot to a waiting request immediately. Ours does not. A batch of sixteen where fifteen finish early keeps running at the pace of the sixteenth, with fifteen slots idle. The gap that opens is measurable and appears in the table below. Batching sequences of different lengths requires them to line up. Ours are **left-padded**, so every sequence's newest token sits in the same column and one cache tensor can serve them all. The cost is that a token's real position is now its column minus that sequence's own padding — and that number must reach the rotation, or the model silently believes every prompt begins at position zero.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
That is the honest result and it is also the most useful number on the page. ### 16.3 against 16.1 Chapter 05 measured naive PyTorch — a loop with no cache, no batching, no engine at all — at **16.1 tok/s**, against a memory-bandwidth ceiling of 584. It called that gap 36× and said the rest of Part I would be about closing it. This engine has a cache, a sampler, batching, and a fused attention kernel. It runs at **16.3 tok/s**. What that means, stated plainly 
 Writing the entire serving path by hand, correctly, and changing nothing else lands within 1% of the naive baseline. Everything built in this chapter bought correctness , and almost no speed. The 36× was never in the algorithm. It is in launch overhead, kernel fusion, memory layout and command recording — the engineering the four other engines spend their entire existence on, and which chapter 13 measured directly when SGLang without command recordings fell to 24 tok/s per stream.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text: It is in launch overhead, kernel fusion, memory layout and command recording — the engineering the four other engines spend their entire existence on, and which chapter 13 measured directly when SGLang without command recordings fell to 24 tok/s per stream. Ours is permanently in that state. It does batch, though, and that is visible: **15.9 → 61.0 → 118.7** tok/s at 1, 4 and 16 concurrent. Ollama, the fastest single-stream engine here, does not batch at all — 285.8 at four, 291.0 at sixteen. A slow engine that batches overtakes a fast one that does not, given enough concurrent requests; ours would need about 26. And it uses **40 MB of host memory**, sixteen times less than anything else in the table.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text: And it uses **40 MB of host memory**, sixteen times less than anything else in the table. There is nothing clever in that. It is what is left when an engine has no scheduler, no paging, no graph capture and no server framework. ### The correction: command recording was the missing piece "Permanently in that state" did not survive the next day. The one optimisation the four other engines have and this one lacked is exactly the one [chapter 13](13-sglang.html) measured on SGLang: **command recording** — a **CUDA** (*Compute Unified Device Architecture*) graph that captures the hundreds of launches a single forward pass issues and replays them as one. Adding it changed nothing about the arithmetic and everything about the speed.

title: 15 · L4 · Our Own Engine — the Exam
text:
Adding it changed nothing about the arithmetic and everything about the speed. Measured · the same harness, one card, after command recording Our engine Alone vs 16.1 naive baseline Output 
 eager — one launch at a time 16.3 tok/s 1.0× the exam, passed 
 with command recording 132.8 tok/s 8.1× byte-identical to the eager run 16.3 → 132.8, and not one token changed. The recording replays the identical operations in the identical order, so the output hash is unchanged — the speed was always being spent on asking for the work, never on the work itself. This is the SGLang cliff run backwards: that engine lost 10.8× when it fell below its graph limit; ours gained 8.1× the moment it finally captured one.

text: The template is not the explanation, and the split is not ours against everyone — it is four independent serving engines on one side, and the reference implementation plus us on the other . That is worth stating without softening. This chapter graded itself against the reference and passed. **The reference is the minority opinion** — four separately written engines, in different languages, using different kernels, agree with each other and disagree with it. It does not follow that the reference is wrong. Four engines agreeing may mean four engines share a family of attention kernels rather than four independent confirmations. What does follow is narrower and harder to dismiss: **"produces the right tokens" is not a property any single implementation can confer.** Chapter 14 opened by treating agreement across engines as evidence.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text:
# What Parallelism Means There are three ways to put more than one graphics card to work on a language model, they solve different problems, and choosing between them comes down to one number that nobody has measured yet. Part I used one card, deliberately, so that only the engine varied. Two cards sat idle for fourteen chapters. This part turns them on — and the first thing to establish is that "use three cards" is not one idea. ## Decoding the word **Parallelism** here does not mean "faster". It means *splitting something up*, and what gets split is the whole question. Three things that can be split Split Name What each card ends up holding 
 the requests data parallelism a complete copy of the model 
 the layers pipeline parallelism some whole layers, and none of the others 
 each layer itself tensor parallelism a slice of every layer

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text:
Split Name What each card ends up holding 
 the requests data parallelism a complete copy of the model 
 the layers pipeline parallelism some whole layers, and none of the others 
 each layer itself tensor parallelism a slice of every layer The names are unhelpfully abstract and all three get called "multi-GPU" — multiple Graphics Processing Units — in the same breath. They are not variations on a theme. They answer different questions and they cost wildly different amounts. ## The restaurant Three cooks have arrived, and there is one kitchen's worth of orders. Three ways to use three cooks Arrangement In the kitchen What it fixes What it cannot fix 
 data Three cooks, three complete kitchens, three different orders at once.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text:
Arrangement In the kitchen What it fixes What it cannot fix 
 data Three cooks, three complete kitchens, three different orders at once. Nobody speaks to anybody. Throughput. Three times the orders. Any one order is no faster — and every kitchen needs the entire set of equipment. pipeline One order, one bench, three stations. Cook one preps, hands the tray to cook two, who hands it to cook three. Equipment. Each station needs only its own third. Two handoffs per order, and while cook one works cooks two and three are waiting. tensor One order, and all three cooks work on the same step at the same time , each doing part of it, then comparing notes before the next step can start. Equipment and the speed of a single order.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text: Equipment and the speed of a single order. They must compare notes after every single step. Nothing proceeds until all three have finished and spoken. The last row is the one worth sitting with. Tensor parallelism is the only arrangement that makes a single request faster, and it buys that by requiring the cooks to talk constantly. ## What each one asks of the link The cooks talking is the part that costs. In a kitchen, talking is free. Between graphics cards it is not — every conversation is bytes crossing a wire, and this is where the three arrangements stop being comparable. A **crossing** is one handoff of data from one card to another. Counting them per forward pass is structural: it depends only on how the work was split, not on how fast anything is.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text:
Counting them per forward pass is structural: it depends only on how the work was split, not on how fast anything is. Crossings per forward pass, for a 32-layer model on 3 cards Strategy Crossings Why that many 
 data 0 Each card answers its own request from start to finish. Nothing is shared, so nothing is sent. pipeline 2 Cutting 32 layers into 3 consecutive pieces makes exactly two seams . The activations cross at each seam, once. tensor 64 Every layer is split, so the pieces must be recombined — twice per layer , once after attention and once after the feed-forward block. 32 × 2. Zero, two, and sixty-four. Not a difference of degree. Tensor parallelism does thirty-two times more communicating than pipeline, per pass, forever.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text: Tensor parallelism does thirty-two times more communicating than pipeline, per pass, forever. ### Why tensor parallelism has to talk that often Chapter 15 established that fifteen attention heads each hold a separate conversation, and the **output** projection — `o_proj` — is the only thing in the block that mixes across them. Split those heads across three cards and each card computes five heads' worth, but that output projection needs **all fifteen**. The pieces are meaningless separately; they have to be added together before anything else can happen. The same is true in the feed-forward block. Split the widening across cards and each holds part of a sum that is not a number until the parts are added.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text:
Split the widening across cards and each holds part of a sum that is not a number until the parts are added. So the recombination is not overhead that a cleverer implementation could remove. **It is the arithmetic.** A sum split across three places is not a sum until the three places agree. ## Which one you want depends on what is wrong Matching the problem to the split The problem The answer Because 
 Many users, model fits one card data No communication at all, and three cards means three times the work done. Model does not fit one card pipeline Each card holds a third, and pays only two crossings per pass. Model does not fit, and one request must be fast tensor The only arrangement that puts three cards on a single token — at the price of 64 crossings.

title: 16 · What Parallelism Means
text: Model does not fit, and one request must be fast tensor The only arrangement that puts three cards on a single token — at the price of 64 crossings. Model fits, one user, wants it faster none of them Data does not help one request; the other two cost more in crossings than they save in compute unless the link is very fast. That last row is the one most often ignored. More cards is not a speed-up for a model that already fits. ## The number this all hangs on Zero, two and sixty-four crossings only become times once there is a price per crossing. That price is the speed of the link between the cards, and it is the single number that decides whether tensor parallelism is the obvious choice or an expensive mistake.

The structure of this part follows from that. Chapter 17 establishes the price of a crossing. Chapter 18 takes the three strategies above and measures what they actually do, against predictions made from that price. Chapter 19 runs one sequence across all three cards. ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter

 Three ways to split, costing zero, two and sixty-four crossings a pass. What a crossing costs is the next chapter, and it decides everything above.

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
# The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink These cards talk over PCIe — Peripheral Component Interconnect Express — and not over NVLink , NVIDIA Link , which is what every guide to using several cards quietly assumes. Chapter 16 counted the crossings each strategy needs: zero, two, sixty-four. This chapter measures what one costs, and the answer is nearly five times worse than this project has been claiming. A correction, first 
 Since the planning document was written, four pages of this project have stated that these cards are connected at roughly 25 GB/s . The index page said it and added the words "Measured, not assumed." 
 It was assumed. Nobody had run the measurement. The real figure is 4.87 to 5.81 GB/s , and this chapter is where it got checked.

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
The real figure is 4.87 to 5.81 GB/s , and this chapter is where it got checked. Every page has been corrected. ## Decoding the names The two ways cards are wired together Name Stands for What it is On this box 
 PCIe Peripheral Component Interconnect Express The general-purpose slot standard every expansion card plugs into — graphics cards, network cards, drives. Traffic goes card → motherboard → wherever. yes , Gen 3, 16 lanes 
 NVLink NVIDIA Link A dedicated cable from one card directly to another, bypassing the motherboard entirely. no 
 P2P peer to peer One card reading another's memory directly, without the data passing through system memory first. no — and that turns out to be the whole story

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
no — and that turns out to be the whole story ## What the machine says about itself Measured · nvidia-smi topo and link state · 2026-09-14 card 0 card 1 card 2 
 card 0 — SYS SYS 
 card 1 SYS — PHB 
 card 2 SYS PHB — PHB means the two cards share a PCI Host Bridge — the same doorway onto the motherboard. SYS means the traffic has to cross between processor sockets to get there, a longer route. Card 0 is the odd one out, exactly as chapter 06 found. One detail worth knowing before reading any such report. At rest, the cards announce **Gen 1** — a quarter of the speed they are capable of. Ask them to move something and they announce Gen 3. The link idles down When Reported Theoretical rate 
 nothing moving Gen 1, 16 lanes 4.0 GB/s 
 under load Gen 3, 16 lanes 15.8 GB/s

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
Getting 5.3 means something is wrong, and there are three candidates. They can be separated by measurement rather than argument. Measured · source/17b_why_so_slow.py · 2026-09-14 Route Rate Share of Gen 3 × 16 
 host → card, ordinary memory 5.60 GB/s 36% 
 host → card, pinned memory 11.75 GB/s 75% 
 card → host, ordinary memory 3.39 GB/s 21% 
 card → host, pinned memory 10.89 GB/s 69% 
 card → card 5.81 GB/s 37% One hop, done properly, reaches 11.75 GB/s . So the bus is not the problem. And card-to-card comes in at almost exactly half of one good hop. Half of one hop is the shape of two hops. Which raises the question of why a card-to-card copy is taking two hops at all — and the machine answers it directly when asked:

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
Which raises the question of why a card-to-card copy is taking two hops at all — and the machine answers it directly when asked: Measured · asking the driver to enable peer access 
 cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess(1) returns 217 , which is cudaErrorPeerAccessUnsupported . These cards refuse. GeForce hardware has peer-to-peer over PCIe disabled in the driver — it is a product decision separating consumer cards from data-centre ones, not a limitation of the bus or the slot. The bus would carry it. The driver will not. So the chain is complete, and each link of it is measured rather than inferred: Why 5 GB/s, in four steps Step Evidence 
 1 These cards refuse peer access error 217, returned by the driver 
 2 So a card-to-card copy must route through system memory — out and back the only remaining path 
 3 One hop, pinned, runs at 11.75 GB/s measured directly 
 4 Two hops give about half that 5.81 measured against 5.88 predicted

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
Step Evidence 
 1 These cards refuse peer access error 217, returned by the driver 
 2 So a card-to-card copy must route through system memory — out and back the only remaining path 
 3 One hop, pinned, runs at 11.75 GB/s measured directly 
 4 Two hops give about half that 5.81 measured against 5.88 predicted The arithmetic closes to within 1%. Nothing here is a mystery, and nothing here is fixable by configuration. ### Pinned memory, since it turned up A side result worth carrying forward. **Pinned** memory is host memory the operating system has promised not to move. The card can read it directly; ordinary memory has to be copied into a staging buffer first, so the bus is paid twice for one hop.

title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
The card can read it directly; ordinary memory has to be copied into a staging buffer first, so the bus is paid twice for one hop. The difference is not small — **5.60 against 11.75 GB/s** outbound, **3.39 against 10.89** inbound. Anything that moves data between host and card and does not pin it is leaving half the bus unused, and chapter 11's offload results were measured without it. ## What a crossing costs Measured · the fixed price of any transfer, however small Route Latency 
 card 0 → card 1 43.8 µs 
 card 0 → card 2 44.4 µs 
 card 1 → card 0 43.6 µs About 44 microseconds before a single useful byte moves. Small transfers pay this in full, which is why many tiny crossings are far worse than one large one carrying the same total.

text: For an 8B-shaped model, where each layer's activations are 16.78 MB rather than 3.93, the same arithmetic gives pipeline 1.12× and tensor 6.29× . **Tensor parallelism spends more time moving data than computing.** 66 ms of link against 51.5 ms of work, to run a model that already fits on one card. That is not a tuning problem. The prediction, recorded before chapter 18 measures it Tensor parallelism will be slower than one card for this model — around 2.3× — and the gap will widen for wider models. Pipeline parallelism will be close to one card , within a few percent, and will not be faster. Data parallelism will scale nearly linearly in throughput and do nothing for single-request latency.

No arrangement of three cards will answer one request faster than one card does , for a model that fits on one card. Written down now so chapter 18 can score them. title: 17 · The Interconnect — PCIe, Not NVLink
text:
The second row is the one that explains the literature. On an NVLink machine, moving a tensor to another card is cheaper than reading it from the card's own memory . Every piece of advice about tensor parallelism was written in a world where communication is effectively free — and on this box it costs eighty times what the guides assume. This is not a complaint about the hardware. It is the reason Part II is a separate part rather than a footnote in Part I: **the standard answers are correct, on the machine they were measured on, and this is not that machine.** ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter

 A crossing costs 44 microseconds plus a fifth of a gigabyte per second of patience.

title: 18 · Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured
text:
# Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured All four predictions held. Then the one that held by the widest margin turned out to be right for a reason the prediction never mentioned, and chasing that is most of this chapter. Chapter 16 counted crossings. Chapter 17 priced them and wrote down four claims. This runs the three strategies on the three cards. Why this is possible at all 
 Tensor and pipeline parallelism here are modifications to a forward pass we wrote ourselves in chapter 15 — not flags on somebody else's scheduler that may or may not do what their names suggest. When a number is surprising, the code that produced it can be read. That is the return on the engine, and it arrives one chapter after it was built.

title: 18 · Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured

That matters more than the timings: a fast wrong answer is not a result, and splitting a model across cards is exactly the kind of change that can silently alter one. The crossing count needs one clarification.

title: 18 · Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured
text:
The crossing count needs one clarification. Chapter 16 said tensor parallelism needs 64 recombinations. It does — but each recombination requires a **transfer from every card that is not doing the summing**, which with three cards is two. **64 recombinations, 128 transfers.** Both numbers are right; they count different things. The four predictions from chapter 17, scored Claim Outcome 
 1 tensor slower than one card, around 2.3× HELD — 3.18× 
 2 pipeline within a few percent, not faster HELD — 1.02× 
 3 data scales throughput, nothing for latency HELD — 0 crossings, one request unchanged 
 4 no split beats one card on a single request HELD — best was 1.02× Four for four. The direction was right every time — and one of the magnitudes was not.

title: 18 · Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured
text:
The direction was right every time — and one of the magnitudes was not. Predicted against measured Strategy Predicted Measured Error

 tensor 2.28× 3.18× +39% A model that predicts one row to within 1% and misses the other by 39% is not slightly wrong. It is missing a term , and the term is missing from the row with more of everything. ## Chasing the 39% The obvious suspect was the cost model for the recombination. Chapter 17 used the textbook figure: a **ring** all-reduce, where each card passes data to its neighbour and the sum assembles as it travels, moving about 1.33 times the tensor rather than three copies of it. A ring requires each card to hand data directly to the next one.

title: 18 · Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured
text:
A ring requires each card to hand data directly to the next one. **That is peer access, and chapter 17 established these cards refuse it.** So there is no ring — every shard is carried to one card, which does the summing. Bandwidth in its most pessimistic honest form accounts for 1.48× of a 3.18× slowdown — less than half . The link was never the main cost. That is the useful failure. Two chapters of this part treated the interconnect as the thing that decides multi-card performance, and on the strategy where it should matter most, it explains under half the damage.

Our hand-written tensor parallelism measured 3.18× slower . A real implementation of the same strategy on the same three cards is 6.5% faster than one card. The 3.18× was a property of this chapter's code, not of the hardware. What survives: the shard-inefficiency measurement, which was taken on a single card with no transfers at all and is a fact about matrix shapes. What does not: the conclusion that tensor parallelism is ruinous here. It is roughly break-even — better single-stream, 15% worse at sixteen concurrent (153.0 against 180.9), and its real return is capacity, not speed. And a limit neither this chapter nor chapter 17 anticipated

title: 18 · Tensor, Pipeline, Data — Measured
text:
And a limit neither this chapter nor chapter 17 anticipated 
 vLLM refused tensor parallelism outright — not on bandwidth, not on peer access, but on arithmetic : 
 assert self.total_num_kv_heads % tp_size == 0 
 SmolLM2-360M has 5 key-value heads , and 5 does not divide by 3. Tensor parallelism splits heads across cards, so the head count must be divisible by the number of cards. --tensor-parallel-size 2 was refused too: 15 attention heads do not divide by 2 either. Llama-3-8B has 32 heads and 8 key-value heads , so three cards would be rejected for it as well. A three-card box cannot run vLLM tensor-parallel on most mainstream models , and the reason has nothing to do with the interconnect this part spent two chapters measuring.

Split three ways they become 853 × 960, which is too small to fill a card. A model with matrices ten times wider would shard into pieces that are still large enough to be efficient, and the 36% would not appear. title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text:
# Three Cards, One Sequence Pipeline parallelism costs 2% per request and leaves two thirds of the hardware idle. The obvious fix is to keep it busy with more requests. That did not work, and the reason turns out to be the same thing that has been limiting this project since chapter 05. ## The number chapter 18 could not show Chapter 18 timed a single forward pass through the pipeline: 1.02× the cost of one card. A good number. It is also the wrong question, and the right one is visible as soon as the stages are timed separately. Measured · source/19_pipeline_under_load.py · 2026-09-14 Stage Layers held Busy for Share of the pass 
 card 0 11 ~20 ms 33% 
 card 1 11 ~20 ms 33% 
 card 2 10 ~20 ms 33%

title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text:
Stage Layers held Busy for Share of the pass 
 card 0 11 ~20 ms 33% 
 card 1 11 ~20 ms 33% 
 card 2 10 ~20 ms 33% Each card works for a third of the pass and waits for the rest of it. This is occupancy — how much of the card is filled — and it reads 33% each — which is not a subtlety, it is two thirds of the hardware standing still for the entire request. A pipeline is stations in a row. While station one preps, stations two and three have nothing to do: the work has not reached them. The journey takes the same time it always did — the work is the same work, in the same order, merely spread across hardware that takes turns. What pipeline parallelism is actually for 
 It does not make a request faster, and it never could.

title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text:
What pipeline parallelism is actually for 
 It does not make a request faster, and it never could. What it buys is that a model too large for one card runs at all , at close to single-card speed, with each card holding a third. Chapter 18's 1.02× was the journey time for one request. True, and not the number a server cares about. ## The fix that did not work The idle stages have an obvious remedy. While card 0 starts request N, card 1 can be finishing N−1 and card 2 finishing N−2. Nothing waits, provided there is always another request. This is how every real pipeline is kept full. Measured · requests in flight, as a wavefront Requests Wall time Per request Throughput

The pipeline did not fill at all — the stages took turns exactly as they had for a single request, and the extra work simply queued. That is a result that should not be published without an explanation, because "pipelines do not fill" contradicts every serving system in existence. The likelier story is a fault in the code. ### Ruling things out Measured · can these cards work at the same time at all? Work Time Against one

title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text:
## What actually serialises it Large **kernels** — each one program the card runs across all its processors, [chapter 05](05-running-it.html) — overlapped. A pipeline stage did not. The remaining difference is the **shape** of the work: one enormous operation against a long sequence of modest ones. Measured · source/19d_where_overlap_stops.py · same work on one card versus three Work given to each card One card Three cards Ratio 
 one 4096 × 4096 matrix multiply 4.63 ms 4.81 ms 1.04× overlaps 
 one 1024 × 1024 matrix multiply 0.20 ms 0.39 ms 1.92× partial 
 50 × 1024 × 1024 matrix multiplies 4.44 ms 9.04 ms 2.04× partial 
 200 × 512 × 512 matrix multiplies 9.07 ms 27.28 ms 3.01× serialises The last row is three cards delivering exactly one card's throughput.

title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text: The last row is three cards delivering exactly one card's throughput. Note that rows three and four give each card more total work than row one, and overlap worse. It is not the amount. It is the size of the pieces. One large operation keeps a card busy long enough that the driver can hand work to the next card while the first is still running. A long run of small operations does not: the process spends its time **issuing** rather than waiting, and issuing is one thread doing one thing at a time. The cards are not competing for the bus or for memory. They are queueing for the attention of a single program. A transformer layer is a long run of modest operations — precisely the bottom row. So the pipeline could not fill, and the cause is not parallelism, or the interconnect, or the strategy.

title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text:
So the pipeline could not fill, and the cause is not parallelism, or the interconnect, or the strategy. ## Which closes Part II onto Part I The same cause, measured three times in this project Where Symptom Measured 
 chapter 05 naive PyTorch against the memory ceiling 16.1 tok/s against 584 — a 36× gap 
 chapter 13 SGLang with command recording switched off 258.6 → 24.0 tok/s per stream

Chapter 15 concluded that its 36× gap was launch overhead rather than algorithm. This is the same gap, wearing a different costume, and it is now blocking a strategy rather than just slowing one down.

title: 19 · Three Cards, One Sequence
text:
This is the same gap, wearing a different costume, and it is now blocking a strategy rather than just slowing one down. What would fix it, and is not built here Fix What it does Evidence it works 
 command recording Capture a whole sequence of operations once and replay it with a single instruction, so issuing costs nothing per operation. chapter 13 — SGLang loses 10× without it

It has shown that it cannot be filled by a single Python process issuing operations one at a time, and identified what to build instead.

It is still slower than one card — 140.4 tok/s against 314.1, and 992 against 3,010 at sixteen concurrent — so the chapter's practical conclusion stands. What does not stand is the mechanism: the stages were never unable to overlap. The single-threaded issuing measured here was ours alone. ## What Part II actually established Four chapters, measured Question Answer Chapter

It was measured, it was five times worse than claimed, and it turned out not to be the thing standing in the way of either strategy that failed. title: 20 · The Endpoint
text:
# The Endpoint Parts I and II measured single questions. An agent does not ask single questions — it holds a conversation that re-sends itself in full, every turn, forever. This measures what that does to a server, and finds one of them quietly solving it. ## The interface was already built Chapter 15 ended with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — `/v1/chat/completions`, streaming, token counts from the engine itself. Every engine in Part I speaks the same surface, which is why one benchmark script drove all five without modification. Why this shape, and not something better Property What it buys 
 One interface every engine implements The engine underneath can be swapped without touching anything above it — and this project has now swapped it five times .

title: 20 · The Endpoint
text:
Property What it buys 
 One interface every engine implements The engine underneath can be swapped without touching anything above it — and this project has now swapped it five times . Stateless requests Any request can go to any instance. No session to lose, no affinity to maintain. Somebody else's design Every existing client already speaks it. Nothing above has to be written. The second row is the interesting one. Statelessness is what makes serving simple, and it is exactly what makes an agent expensive. ## What a conversation costs The server remembers nothing between requests. So turn two must re-send turn one, turn three must re-send both, and so on. Eight turns of a short conversation, each question about the same size:

title: 20 · The Endpoint
text:
Eight turns of a short conversation, each question about the same size: Measured · source/20_agent_traffic.py · 2026-09-14 Turn Tokens sent New that turn Cumulative sent 
 1 43 43 43

 6 429 77 1,417 
 8 583 78 2,505 The eighth question is the same size as the first and costs 13.6× as much to ask . Across eight turns the server received 2,505 tokens to be told eight things — a waste factor of 4.6×, on a conversation short enough to fit on one screen. Each turn costs roughly *n* times the first, so a conversation of *n* turns costs about *n²* rather than *n*. Double the conversation and quadruple the work. **This is why an agent is a pathological workload** — and an agent is worse than this example, because its turns carry file contents and command output rather than one-line questions.

Still paid every turn Saved by the cache 
 Sending the tokens over the network Re-reading them through 32 layers 
 Holding them in the context window The keys and values, recomputed from scratch 
 The 4.6× waste factor in what is transmitted Most of what that waste would have cost The quadratic growth in traffic is real and unchanged. What the cache removes is the quadratic growth in work , which is the half that was going to hurt. ## A correction to Part I Chapter 14 measured Ollama as the engine that does not batch — 285.8 tokens per second at four concurrent requests, 291.0 at sixteen, flat. That was true and it made Ollama look like the least sophisticated engine in the table. Part I asked the wrong question of this engine 
 Ollama does prefix-cache, measured above at up to 4.87×, and it does it without being configured to.

title: 20 · The Endpoint
text:
Part I asked the wrong question of this engine 
 Ollama does prefix-cache, measured above at up to 4.87×, and it does it without being configured to. Part I never saw this because every prompt in the frozen set is independent — the benchmark was built to compare engines fairly on single questions, and a fair single-question benchmark cannot see a feature that only helps repeated ones. For an agent, prefix caching matters more than batching. A benchmark measures what it was built to measure, and nothing else. That is not a flaw in chapter 14's numbers; they are correct for what they measured. It is a limit on what those numbers licence anyone to conclude, and it is the reason this part exists: **a workload nobody has run is a workload nobody has measured.**

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
# The Agent Loop The loop fits on a page. Run against two locally served models, the small one failed in ways impossible to miss and the large one failed in ways impossible to see — and the second is the dangerous one. ## The loop All of it Step 
 1 Tell the model what tools exist. 2 Send the conversation. 3 Read the reply. If it asks for a tool, run the tool. 4 Append the result to the conversation and go back to 2. 5 Stop when it answers instead of asking. That is the whole idea, and it explains chapter 20's measurement exactly: step 4 is why an agent conversation grows . Every tool result is appended and re-sent forever. Four tools, deliberately dull: list a directory, read a file, search for a pattern, count the lines in a file.

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
Four tools, deliberately dull: list a directory, read a file, search for a pattern, count the lines in a file. Written by hand rather than taken from a framework, so that when something goes wrong it is visible rather than swallowed. **Everything difficult is in step 3.** The model produces text. Text has to become an action. That means parsing something a language model wrote, which means it will eventually be wrong in a way nothing anticipated. ## Two models, the same three tasks Each task has a verifiable answer, which turns out to matter more than expected. Measured · source/21_agent.py · 2026-09-14 · both served on one card Model Tasks answered Steps Tokens sent Generated Unparseable replies 
 SmolLM2-360M 0 of 3 24 7,588 154 10 of 24 
 Llama-3-8B, 4-bit 3 of 3 11 3,750 76 1 of 11

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
Model Tasks answered Steps Tokens sent Generated Unparseable replies 
 SmolLM2-360M 0 of 3 24 7,588 154 10 of 24 
 Llama-3-8B, 4-bit 3 of 3 11 3,750 76 1 of 11 Read that table the obvious way and the larger model wins outright: it finished everything, in half the steps, with a tenth of the parse failures. ### How the small model failed It never produced a valid action for two of the tasks, and on the third it did this, eight times in a row: Measured · the same step, repeated until the budget ran out Step What it asked for 
 2 TOOL: list_files DIR 
 3 TOOL: list_files DIR 
 … … 
 8 TOOL: list_files DIR The tool description says TOOL: list_files DIR , where DIR is a placeholder. The model copied the placeholder — asking, literally, for the directory named DIR — and never noticed that the answer came back the same every time.

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
The model copied the placeholder — asking, literally, for the directory named DIR — and never noticed that the answer came back the same every time. This is a bad failure and a harmless one. It produces nothing, loudly, and no one could mistake it for working. ### How the large model failed Measured · the answers, against ground truth Task It answered The truth 
 How many files are in source/ ? 159 39 wrong 
 Does bench/ contain run.py ? yes yes right 
 How many prompts in bench/prompts.json ? 39 4 wrong Three of three answered. One of three correct. And the wrong answers are not noise — they are the output of the wrong tool, reported with complete confidence. The 159 is the giveaway. Asked to count files, the model ran `list_files` — which worked — then abandoned the result and tried `count_lines` on a directory, then on a pattern, then on `README.md`.

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
Asked to count files, the model ran `list_files` — which worked — then abandoned the result and tried `count_lines` on a directory, then on a pattern, then on `README.md`. **`README.md` is 159 lines long.** It answered with the last number it happened to see. The second wrong answer is the same mistake: asked how many prompts a file lists, it counted the file's **lines** (39) and answered 39. The question was about entries in a list; the tool it reached for measures something else entirely. The two failure modes, side by side SmolLM2-360M Llama-3-8B 
 What it does loops, gives up completes every task 
 How wrong produces nothing 2 of 3 answers wrong 
 How visible unmissable invisible without checking 
 What a dashboard shows 0% completion — alarming 100% completion — fine

title: 21 · The Agent Loop

SmolLM2-360M Llama-3-8B 
 What it does loops, gives up completes every task 
 How wrong produces nothing 2 of 3 answers wrong 
 How visible unmissable invisible without checking 
 What a dashboard shows 0% completion — alarming 100% completion — fine A system watching completion rates would report the second model as working perfectly. The more capable model has the more dangerous failure , because it produces exactly the shape of output that success produces. ## What the loop costs Measured · the accounting the checkpoint asked for Model Generated Sent Read-to-spoken ratio Wall clock 
 SmolLM2-360M 154 7,588 49× 1.6 s 
 Llama-3-8B, 4-bit 76 3,750 49× 1.7 s Both models were read to roughly fifty times more than they spoke , and arrived at that ratio independently.

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
Both models were read to roughly fifty times more than they spoke , and arrived at that ratio independently. An agent is overwhelmingly a prefill workload — which is why chapter 20's prefix caching matters more here than any amount of generation speed. It also explains something from Part I that looked like an oddity. Time to first token — the cost of reading the prompt — was treated as a secondary metric in chapter 14, well behind tokens per second. **For an agent it is the primary one**, because 98% of the tokens involved are being read rather than written. ## Which is the whole argument for chapter 22 What this chapter cannot tell you 
 Everything above about correctness required knowing the right answer in advance .

title: 21 · The Agent Loop
text:
What this chapter cannot tell you 
 Everything above about correctness required knowing the right answer in advance . There were three tasks and the answers were checked by hand. That does not scale, and it does not survive contact with a real question. A model that completes every task and is wrong two thirds of the time is indistinguishable — from logs, from timings, from token counts, from anything this chapter measured — from one that works. The only thing that separates them is a scored test. That is chapter 22, and it is the instrument Part V will be judged with. ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter 
 agent loop tool call tool-call parsing step budget silent failure prefill-dominated workload ground truth 
 The loop is five steps and the hard part is the one that turns text into an action.
