title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
# Evaluation — the Hardest Part Chapter 21 showed a model completing every task and getting most of them wrong, with nothing able to tell the difference. This builds the thing that can — and then finds that two thirds of what it says is solid and one third is not. ## Why this chapter exists before any model is trained Part V trains a model. Without this chapter, the only available judgement of that model would be reading its output and forming an impression. The thing an eval is for 
 Training produces a model that finished training. Nothing about finishing indicates learning. The loss curve says the optimiser did its job; it says nothing about whether the result is useful. A scored test is the only instrument that distinguishes a model that learned something from one that merely stopped.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
A scored test is the only instrument that distinguishes a model that learned something from one that merely stopped. Which is why the instrument is built before the thing it measures — and measured itself, on models whose quality is already known. ## Three design decisions, each load-bearing And what each one prevents Decision What it prevents 
 Ground truth is computed, never stored. Every task carries a function that works the answer out from the repository at the moment the test runs. A stored answer key rots the first time a file is added. During this chapter's own work the correct answer to one task changed from 39 to 40 — because writing the harness added a file to the directory it counts.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text: During this chapter's own work the correct answer to one task changed from 39 to 40 — because writing the harness added a file to the directory it counts. Tasks come from our own repository. Questions about files no public model has ever seen. Contamination — a model that saw the answers during training scores well without being able to reason. It is the reason published benchmark numbers are so hard to trust, and it is unfalsifiable from the outside: nobody can prove what was in a training set. Grading is exact and mechanical. The answer is a number or a yes, compared to what the filesystem says. A model judging another model, which imports the judge's failures into the score and cannot be audited.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
A model judging another model, which imports the judge's failures into the score and cannot be audited. Ten tasks, four tools, eight steps allowed each. Every answer is checkable by a program, and [the harness itself is written out here](the-harness.html). ## The scores Measured · source/22_eval.py · 2026-09-14 · one card Model Correct Answered but wrong Gave up Completion rate Accuracy 
 SmolLM2-360M 0 / 10 0 10 0% 0% 
 Llama-3-8B, 4-bit 5 / 10 4 1 90% 50% 
 Llama-3-8B, 8-bit 6 / 10 3 1 90% 60% The two rightmost columns are the chapter. Completion says 90%. Accuracy says 50%. Every system that monitors whether a request succeeded — every log, every dashboard, every uptime check — reads the first number.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text: Every system that monitors whether a request succeeded — every log, every dashboard, every uptime check — reads the first number. Four of ten answers were confidently wrong. Not refused, not errored, not flagged: **answered**, in the correct format, with a plausible number. `files_bench` expected 6 and got 273. `n_prompts` expected 4 and got 39. Nothing short of checking the content distinguishes those from the six that were right. ## Then the ranking has to be defended The harness produces an order: 360M, then 4-bit, then 8-bit. The checkpoint for this chapter was a ranking **defensible from the data rather than from vibes**, and defending it means asking whether the gaps could have come from chance.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
The checkpoint for this chapter was a ranking **defensible from the data rather than from vibes**, and defending it means asking whether the gaps could have come from chance. Measured · source/22b_is_the_ranking_defensible.py Comparison Gap Verdict 
 SmolLM2-360M against either 8B model 0% against 50–60% defensible — no sample size makes 0 of 10 a close call 
 8-bit against 4-bit 6 of 10 against 5 of 10 NOT defensible — p = 1.00 The two models disagreed on exactly one task out of ten . A one-task gap is precisely what chance produces between two equally good models. The harness ranked them and the data does not support the ranking. This is the honest answer to the checkpoint, and it is more useful than a clean ordering would have been.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
This is the honest answer to the checkpoint, and it is more useful than a clean ordering would have been. **Two of the three comparisons are solid. The interesting one is not**, and only running the significance check revealed which was which. And they failed identically 
 Both 8B models got the same four tasks wrong: files_source , py_source , n_prompts , files_bench . All four require counting things , and both models reached for a tool that measures something else — the same wrong-tool failure chapter 21 diagnosed. Doubling the precision of every weight changed the score by one task and changed the failure mode not at all . Whatever is wrong is not a rounding problem. ## What this instrument still cannot do

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
## What this instrument still cannot do Stated so that Part V does not over-trust it Limit Consequence 
 Ten tasks is too few. The significance test above is the proof — a one-task difference is invisible. Only large gaps can be detected. Part V needs far more tasks to see a small improvement. Every task is a lookup. Count files, read a field, check existence. It measures tool use and instruction following, not reasoning or code generation. One sample per task, at temperature 0. No pass@k — no measure of whether a model that fails once would succeed given several attempts, which is how coding agents are actually used. And chapter 15 showed temperature 0 is not even reproducible under batching.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
And chapter 15 showed temperature 0 is not even reproducible under batching. Our repository is small. Tasks can be exhausted, and a model tuned against them would overfit to this particular directory tree. A benchmark measures what it was built to measure. Chapter 20 learned that the expensive way, when Part I's frozen prompt set turned out to be structurally unable to see prefix caching. The same limit applies here and is written down in advance this time. ## Why evaluation is called the hardest part Everything above, restated The problem Seen here as 
 Wrong answers look exactly like right ones 90% completion, 50% accuracy 
 A test can only find what it was built to find ten lookups measure lookups, nothing else 
 Small samples cannot see small differences p = 1.00 on the comparison that mattered 
 Public benchmarks may already be in the training data the reason these tasks come from a private repository 
 The thing being measured changes underfoot the expected answer moved from 39 to 40 mid-chapter

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
The problem Seen here as 
 Wrong answers look exactly like right ones 90% completion, 50% accuracy 
 A test can only find what it was built to find ten lookups measure lookups, nothing else 
 Small samples cannot see small differences p = 1.00 on the comparison that mattered 
 Public benchmarks may already be in the training data the reason these tasks come from a private repository 
 The thing being measured changes underfoot the expected answer moved from 39 to 40 mid-chapter None of these are solved problems in the field. They are the reason two models can be a percentage point apart on a public leaderboard and obviously different in use — and the reason this project will trust its own small, checkable, private harness over a published number.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
They are the reason two models can be a percentage point apart on a public leaderboard and obviously different in use — and the reason this project will trust its own small, checkable, private harness over a published number. ## Part III, complete What the three chapters established Chapter Finding 
 20 An agent re-sends its whole conversation every turn — 4.6× waste on eight short turns. Ollama prefix-caches at up to 4.87× and Part I could not see it. 21 The small model failed loudly; the 8B model completed everything and got two thirds wrong. Both were read to 49× more than they spoke. 22 0%, 50%, 60% accuracy against 0%, 90%, 90% completion — and one of the two orderings is not statistically real.

title: 22 · Evaluation — the Hardest Part
text:
22 0%, 50%, 60% accuracy against 0%, 90%, 90% completion — and one of the two orderings is not statistically real. The instrument Part V needs now exists , along with a written list of what it cannot see. ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter 
 eval harness ground truth contamination completion rate accuracy pass@k statistical significance overfitting to a benchmark 
 A harness that ranks three models, and the honesty to say which third of that ranking it cannot support. Next: Part IV, the walls — quantizing the cache, how far context really goes, and speculative decoding, all measured against the instrument built here. Sources & further reading

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
# Quantizing the KV Cache The KV cache holds the keys and values worked out for every token so far, and it is measured here in a model quantized to Q4_K_M — a 4-bit quantization format. Chapter 07 derived the cache formula and pointed out that one term in it — bytes per value — is the only one we control. This finds out what happens when we turn that dial, and it is the first chapter that can score the answer instead of guessing. ## The one lever The cache size is a product of five numbers, and four of them belong to whoever designed the model. From chapter 07, with the ownership marked Term For Llama-3-8B Whose choice 
 2, for the keys and the values 2 fixed by the mechanism 
 layers 32 the model's architecture 
 key-value heads 8 the model's architecture 
 head dimension 128 the model's architecture 
 bytes per value 2 ours

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
Term For Llama-3-8B Whose choice 
 2, for the keys and the values 2 fixed by the mechanism 
 layers 32 the model's architecture 
 key-value heads 8 the model's architecture 
 head dimension 128 the model's architecture 
 bytes per value 2 ours At 8,192 tokens that product is 536,870,912 stored numbers . Storing each in one byte instead of two removes half a gigabyte, and nothing about the model has to change. The question is what it costs in quality, and until chapter 22 this project had no way to answer that. Now it does. ## The measurement Same model, same card, same ten tasks with computed answers. Only the cache precision moves. Measured · source/23_kv_quant.py · Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M · context 8,192 · 2026-09-14

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
Measured · source/23_kv_quant.py · Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M · context 8,192 · 2026-09-14 Cache Card holds Saved Correct Answered Text identical to 16-bit? f16 — 16-bit 5,737 MB — 5 / 10 9 / 10 baseline 
 q8_0 — 8-bit 5,257 MB 480 MB 5 / 10 8 / 10 yes — byte for byte 
 q4_0 — 4-bit 5,001 MB 736 MB 6 / 10 10 / 10 no ### The 8-bit row is the finding **Halving the precision of every cached number produced identical text.** Not similar — the same 96 tokens in the same order, on a generation long enough for a difference to show. And 480 MB came back. Why identical is plausible rather than suspicious 
 The cache holds keys and values, which are inputs to a softmax — a function that converts scores into weights that sum to one.

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
Why identical is plausible rather than suspicious 
 The cache holds keys and values, which are inputs to a softmax — a function that converts scores into weights that sum to one. Small perturbations in the scores mostly wash out in that normalisation. The weights themselves are already 4-bit in this model; the cache was the most precise thing in the pipeline, and it did not need to be. ### The 4-bit row is where chapter 22 has to be obeyed At 4 bits the text changed, and the score went **up** — 6 of 10 against 5. It is tempting to report that quartering the cache improved the model. It did not, and this project already proved it cannot tell 
 Chapter 22 measured two models one task apart and ran the test: p = 1.00 .

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
It did not, and this project already proved it cannot tell 
 Chapter 22 measured two models one task apart and ran the test: p = 1.00 . A one-task gap at ten tasks is exactly what chance produces. The same arithmetic applies here, to a result that happens to flatter the conclusion. The honest statement is "no difference detectable at this sample size" , and the harness's own limitations page says why: ten tasks, all lookups, one sample each. This is the discipline being tested on itself. The first chapter after the eval harness produced a number that looks like an improvement, and the harness's documented limits say it is not measurable. Reporting it as a win would have been the easiest paragraph in this guide to write.

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
Reporting it as a win would have been the easiest paragraph in this guide to write. ## The formula was slightly wrong, in a way worth knowing Chapter 07's formula predicted the 8-bit cache would save 537 MB. It saved 480. Predicted 805 for 4-bit; it saved 736. Both short by about 7%. Measured · source/23b_block_overhead.py — where the missing bytes are Type How it is stored Naive Actual Overhead 
 f16 2 bytes per value, no structure 1,074 MB 1,074 MB 0% 
 q8_0 32 values in 32 bytes, plus a 2-byte scale 537 MB 570 MB 6.2% 
 q4_0 32 values in 16 bytes, plus a 2-byte scale 268 MB 302 MB 12.5% A quantized number is not stored alone. Values are grouped into blocks of 32 that share one scale factor — the multiplier that turns small integers back into real numbers.

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
Values are grouped into blocks of 32 that share one scale factor — the multiplier that turns small integers back into real numbers. The scale is 2 bytes per block whatever the block holds, so it costs proportionally more the smaller the values get. That is why a 4-bit cache is not exactly half of an 8-bit one. Including the scales, the prediction lands within **4.6%** for both — and it is the same 4.6% both times, which suggests one small fixed allocation rather than an error in the reasoning. The corrected formula 
 Chapter 07's version is right about the values and silent about the blocks. For quantized caches, multiply by 34/32 for 8-bit and 18/32 for 4-bit rather than by 1 and 0.5. ## What this actually buys

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
## What this actually buys The same 8 GB card, spent differently Cache Cache at 8,192 tokens Context that fits in the same 1,074 MB 
 f16 1,074 MB 8,192 tokens 
 q8_0 570 MB ~15,400 tokens 
 q4_0 302 MB ~29,100 tokens Derived from the measured sizes above. An 8-bit cache is not a saving — it is a longer conversation , for free, on hardware that has not changed. Corrected by chapter 24 — the sentence above reaches one step too far 
 The table is arithmetic about the cache and it is right. The conclusion assumes the cache is what limits context, and chapter 24 measured that it is not: this model refuses any prompt beyond 8,192 tokens whatever the memory situation, because that is what it was trained on.

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text: The conclusion assumes the cache is what limits context, and chapter 24 measured that it is not: this model refuses any prompt beyond 8,192 tokens whatever the memory situation, because that is what it was trained on. A 12,000-token request was refused on a card with gigabytes free. So for this model, halving the cache freed 480 MB and bought zero additional usable context. The corrected claim: an 8-bit cache is a saving , and becomes a longer conversation only for a model trained on longer conversations. The original sentence is kept rather than quietly edited, because the gap between correct arithmetic and an over-reaching conclusion is the more useful thing to see. That reframes the whole chapter.

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
That reframes the whole chapter. The memory was never the point. The point is that the same card holds nearly twice the context at 8 bits, and almost four times at 4 bits, and at 8 bits the output did not change at all. The recommendation, with its evidence Setting Verdict Because 
 8-bit cache use it Byte-identical output, 480 MB back, nearly double the context. No measured cost of any kind. 4-bit cache defensible, unproven 736 MB back and four times the context. Output changes; whether quality changes is below this harness's resolution . ## The vocabulary you now own Terms from this chapter 
 cache quantization block scale factor block overhead q8_0 q4_0 below the resolution of the instrument 
 One lever, turned twice.

title: 23 · Quantizing the KV Cache
text:
Terms from this chapter 
 cache quantization block scale factor block overhead q8_0 q4_0 below the resolution of the instrument 
 One lever, turned twice. The first turn was free and the second is unmeasurable — which is a finding about the instrument as much as about the cache. Next: chapter 24, how far context actually goes — where the extra room bought here gets spent, and where it stops being usable. Sources & further reading

title: 24 · How Far Context Goes
text:
# How Far Context Goes The previous chapter ended by saying an 8-bit cache is not a saving but a longer conversation. This chapter tried to have that conversation, and the engine refused — which makes it a correction as much as a chapter. ## Two questions, and only one of them is about memory What "context" has to mean before it can be measured Question Kind of limit 
 How much conversation fits ? memory — the cache, which chapter 23 halved 
 How much can the model make sense of ? training — what lengths it was shown while learning 
 How much will it actually use ? behaviour — whether a fact buried in the middle is still reachable Three separate things that the phrase "context window" collapses into one number, and chapter 23 quietly assumed the first was the binding one.

title: 24 · How Far Context Goes
text:
Three separate things that the phrase "context window" collapses into one number, and chapter 23 quietly assumed the first was the binding one. ## What a long prompt costs Measured · source/24_context.py · Llama-3-8B at Q4_K_M (a 4-bit quantization), 8-bit cache · 2026-09-14 Prompt tokens Time to first token Per 1,000 tokens 
 256 131 ms 511 ms 
 2,416 871 ms 361 ms 
 7,216 2,167 ms 300 ms Reading the prompt costs about 0.3 ms per token and the rate improves with length — a longer prompt amortises the fixed startup better, exactly as chapter 05's launch-overhead argument predicts. The cost is real but it is linear and well behaved: a 7,000-token prompt takes two seconds to read before a single word comes back.

title: 24 · How Far Context Goes
24 · How Far Context Goes
text:
And the memory was not the reason — chapter 23 measured an 8-bit cache at 8,192 tokens costing 570 MB on a card with gigabytes free. The engine had said so at startup, in a line nobody reads: ```
W llama_context: n_ctx_seq (16384) > n_ctx_train (8192) -- possible training context overflow
I srv load_model: n_slots = 4, n_ctx_slot = 8192, kv_unified = 'true'
``` Two candidates in two lines: the model was **trained** on 8,192, and the allocation was being **divided between four concurrent slots**. Both would produce this refusal. Measured · source/24c_slots_or_training.py — one flag separates them Configuration Slots Context per slot 8,800-token prompt 
 default 4 8,192 refused 
 --parallel 1 1 8,192 refused

title: 24 · How Far Context Goes
text:
Configuration Slots Context per slot 8,800-token prompt 
 default 4 8,192 refused 
 --parallel 1 1 8,192 refused One slot, the entire allocation, and the per-sequence context is still 8,192. It was never the slots. llama.cpp clamps what one sequence may use to what the model was trained on, however much memory is handed to it. Rope scaling — the usual way to stretch a model past its training length — was tried and changed nothing here either. Which corrects the previous chapter 
 Chapter 23 concluded: "An 8-bit cache is not a saving — it is a longer conversation." 
 For this model that is wrong. The cache was never the binding constraint. Halving it freed 480 MB and bought zero additional usable context, because the model refuses to go past 8,192 whatever the memory situation.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
# Speculative Decoding The trick that makes a single stream faster, which chapter 08 proved nothing else can. It needs a second model meeting two conditions, and the two models on this box each meet exactly one of them. ## The problem it solves Decoding is serial. Each token needs the one before it, so a model produces them one at a time however much hardware is idle. Chapter 08 measured the consequence directly: **a single stream never gets faster**, 16.2 tokens per second at batch 1 and 15.7 at batch 64. Batching helps everyone else. It does nothing for the person waiting. The trick, in three lines Step 
 1 A cheap draft model guesses the next few tokens. 2 The expensive target model checks all the guesses in one pass — because verifying tokens it already has is a prefill, and prefill is parallel.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
2 The expensive target model checks all the guesses in one pass — because verifying tokens it already has is a prefill, and prefill is parallel. 3 Every guess that matches what the target would have said is kept. The first mismatch and everything after it is thrown away. The output is identical to what the target would have produced alone. A wrong guess costs time, never correctness — which is the property that makes the whole idea acceptable rather than a gamble. ## Two requirements, and they pull in opposite directions What a draft model has to be Requirement Why 
 The same vocabulary A guess is checked against the target's own probabilities for that token. Both models must mean the same thing by token number 4,721, or there is nothing to compare.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
Both models must mean the same thing by token number 4,721, or there is nothing to compare. Much cheaper Drafting n tokens costs n draft steps plus one verification. If the draft is not dramatically cheaper, that arithmetic loses before acceptance is even considered. The tension is that models sharing a vocabulary are usually from the same family and therefore similar in cost, while models that differ enormously in cost usually come from different families and different tokenizers. ## What this box actually has Measured · source/25b_why_no_speedup.py · 2026-09-14 Model Alone Vocabulary Usable as a draft for Llama-3-8B? Llama-3-8B, 8-bit — the target 13.4 tok/s 128,256 — 
 Llama-3-8B, 4-bit 74.5 tok/s 128,256 vocabulary yes , cost marginal 
 SmolLM2-360M 265.7 tok/s 49,152 cost ideal , vocabulary no

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
Llama-3-8B, 8-bit — the target 13.4 tok/s 128,256 — 
 Llama-3-8B, 4-bit 74.5 tok/s 128,256 vocabulary yes , cost marginal 
 SmolLM2-360M 265.7 tok/s 49,152 cost ideal , vocabulary no Each model satisfies exactly one requirement and fails the other. SmolLM2 is 20× faster and would be an excellent draft on cost alone; it cannot be one, because the two models do not agree on what any token number means. A caveat on that 13.4, stated before it is leaned on 
 The 8-bit model does not fit on one card, so it runs with 28 of 32 layers offloaded and the rest crossing PCIe ( Peripheral Component Interconnect Express ) every token — chapter 11's territory. Its 13.4 tokens per second is therefore a measure of partial offload as much as of precision, and the 5.6× gap to the 4-bit model conflates the two.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding

Its 13.4 tokens per second is therefore a measure of partial offload as much as of precision, and the 5.6× gap to the 4-bit model conflates the two. A fair like-for-like comparison is not available on this hardware. ## The pairing that was allowed, and what it did Measured · source/25_speculative.py · 160 tokens, same prompt Configuration Speed Speedup Output identical 
 8-bit target alone 13.6 tok/s 1.00× baseline 
 8-bit target, 4-bit draft 13.6 tok/s 1.00× yes Not slower. Not faster. Exactly the same , to three significant figures, with the draft model loaded and speculation enabled at its default depth of three tokens. The break-even arithmetic explains why it was always going to be close.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
The break-even arithmetic explains why it was always going to be close. Drafting 3 tokens with a draft 5.6× cheaper costs about **1.5 target-steps** of work to win at most 3 tokens — so roughly **51% of guesses must be accepted just to break even**. A 4-bit model drafting for its own 8-bit self should clear that easily. It did not produce a gain either way, which suggests the speculation is not engaging rather than engaging and failing. And the failure that worries me more 
 The mismatched pairing — SmolLM2 drafting for Llama-3, different vocabularies — was not refused . The engine loaded it, started, served requests, and produced correct-looking output at 13.5 tok/s : the target's own speed.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
The engine loaded it, started, served requests, and produced correct-looking output at 13.5 tok/s : the target's own speed. No error, no warning in the log that this pairing is impossible, and a result indistinguishable from having configured nothing at all. Somebody could run this in production believing speculation is on. This is chapter 21's lesson in a different costume. The dangerous failure is not the one that stops; it is the one that looks exactly like success. ## What this chapter did not establish Said plainly, because the result is a null one Not shown What would be needed 
 That speculative decoding does not work A valid pair: same vocabulary, an order of magnitude apart in cost.

title: 25 · Speculative Decoding
text:
Not shown What would be needed

Why the matched pair produced no change at all Acceptance-rate statistics, which this build does not report. Whether the draft ran and was rejected, or never ran, is unresolved. Any figure for a well-chosen draft Published work reports 2–3× on good pairings. Nothing here confirms or contradicts that. The honest summary is: Part IV's last wall is one this box cannot get over , not because the technique fails but because the ingredients are missing — and that is a fact about the model files available, not about the method.

title: 26 · What Training Actually Costs

# What Training Actually Costs Twenty-five chapters have been about running somebody else's model. This part makes one — and it opens by measuring the number that decides what "making one" is allowed to mean on this hardware. ## The claim being checked The calculator built alongside this guide states that a full fine-tune needs roughly **16 bytes per parameter**, against 2 bytes for running the same model. That figure is **derived** — standard published arithmetic, never run on this machine. Part V depends on it, so it gets measured. One training step on SmolLM2-360M, with memory sampled between each stage. Measured · source/26_training_cost.py · 2026-09-14 · one card Stage Card holds Added

 peak during the step: 7,436 MB

title: 26 · What Training Actually Costs
text:
Right total, different route — worth noticing 
 The calculator reaches 16 as 2 weight + 2 gradient + 8 optimizer + 4 master copy , which is the mixed-precision recipe. This run was pure 32-bit, so it reaches the same 16 as 4 + 4 + 8 and no master copy at all . Two different arrangements landing on the same total is a coincidence of this particular pair of recipes, not a law. The useful invariant is the ratio: training costs about eight times what running costs , however the bytes are arranged. The optimizer is the largest single item, at **8 bytes per parameter** — twice the weights themselves. Adam keeps two running averages for every number in the model, and neither of them is the model. ## How fast this box can train

title: 26 · What Training Actually Costs

## How fast this box can train Memory decides whether a run is possible. Throughput decides whether it is sane. Measured · one card, sequence length 512 Quantity Value

Training moves fewer tokens per second than inference does — and each of those tokens is doing a forward pass, a backward pass, and an optimizer update rather than just a forward pass. ## And then the arithmetic that decides Part V Derived from the measured 1,059 tokens/second Target Tokens One card Three cards, optimistically

A corpus measured in megabytes says very little about what it costs to train on , and for an agent-and-code project the conversion runs against you. ## What the data is actually for The obvious conclusion is that we need more data from somewhere else. The more useful conclusion is that **this data should not be trained on at all.** These 323,933 tokens are already doing a job 
 Chapter 22 's evaluation harness works because its questions are about this repository , which no public model has been trained on. That is what makes it immune to contamination and the reason it can be trusted over a published benchmark score. Training on this corpus would destroy that. A model fine-tuned on our files would answer questions about our files from memory, the harness would report a large improvement, and the improvement would be meaningless — and unfalsifiable, because we would have done to ourselves exactly what makes public benchmarks untrustworthy.

After that they separate and go in opposite directions — training loss towards zero, held-out loss climbing back up past where it was at step 500. ### It learned Before drawing the obvious conclusion, the first half of that table deserves its due. A model that guesses uniformly from a 49,152-token vocabulary has a loss of **10.803** and a perplexity of **49,152** — one in fifty thousand, every time. At its best, step 1,000 Perplexity Meaning 
 guessing at random 49,152 no information at all

title: 28 · The Run
text:
From random noise, in ninety-three seconds, on one second-hand graphics card: a model that narrows fifty thousand possibilities to about fifty. That is learning, and it is the thing this whole project was built to reach. ### Then it stopped learning and started memorising Chapter 27's number, made visible 
 By step 3,000 the model had seen 12,288,000 tokens drawn from a corpus of 93,337 . That is 132 complete passes over everything this project has written. Training loss of 0.103 does not mean it understands the text. It means it has memorised it. And the held-out column is what memorisation looks like from outside: the model got monotonically better at the 63 files it had seen and twice as bad at the 7 it had not.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text: # Choosing a Model in 2026 Twenty-nine chapters treated the model as given and the engine as the variable. This one inverts it. Choosing wrongly costs a day of downloading and nothing else moves — so the choice is made with arithmetic, before anything is fetched. Part I held one model fixed so the engines could be compared. That was the right experiment and it is finished. The question now is the one it deliberately excluded: of everything published, what should actually be run on 24 GB of graphics memory — and how is that decided without downloading ninety gigabytes to find out? ## What stopped working The old heuristic was *pick the largest model that fits*. Two things broke it. The first is in chapter 29: **size predicts cost, not quality**.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
The first is in chapter 29: **size predicts cost, not quality**. Measured on this box, a 2025 model activating 3.04 billion parameters per token matched a 2024 model activating 7.50 billion, on the same tasks and the same hardware. Ranking by parameter count ranks by nothing. The second is that *fits* stopped being a yes-or-no answer. A model four times larger than the graphics memory still runs, out of host memory, at a speed the arithmetic in chapter 29 predicts. The question is no longer whether it fits but what it will cost, and that is a number rather than a verdict. Two ceilings, and they are not the same ceiling This box Decides 
 Graphics memory VRAM, video random access memory 24 GB how fast 
 Host memory RAM, random access memory, on the motherboard 125 GB whether it runs at all

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
This box Decides 
 Graphics memory VRAM, video random access memory 24 GB how fast 
 Host memory RAM, random access memory, on the motherboard 125 GB whether it runs at all Confusing them is how people conclude a model is impossible when it is merely slow, or that one will be fine when it will not start. ## The host memory number, measured Everything about a model that does not fit turns on how fast host memory can be read, so that figure cannot be a specification. Eight gigabytes streamed past every cache, summed so the reads cannot be optimised away, across a varying number of threads: Host memory read bandwidth, best of three runs Threads 1 4 8 16 32 
 GB/s 7.4 23.3 23.4 21.8 18.3 **23.4 GB/s**, and it gets worse past eight threads — thirty-two threads are 22% slower than eight.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
**23.4 GB/s**, and it gets worse past eight threads — thirty-two threads are 22% slower than eight. The machine has 32 of them. Throwing every core at a memory-bound problem makes it slower, which is the sort of thing only measuring tells you. Against **1,344 GB/s** across the three cards, host memory is **57 times slower**. That ratio is the entire economics of running something too large. ## The procedure Four steps, none of which require downloading anything. ### 1 · Does the engine know the architecture? A model published last month may use attention this engine has never compiled. The download will be perfect and the load will fail. ```
strings engines/llamacpp/build/bin/libllama.so.0 | grep -i deepseek
```

```
strings engines/llamacpp/build/bin/libllama.so.0 | grep -i deepseek
``` `DEEPSEEK4` present, so `deepseek4` will load. Absent, and nothing else in this chapter matters. Which engine, and a correction 
 This page assumed llama.cpp, on the grounds that it is the only one of the four in Part I that will run a model larger than the graphics memory. That was wrong, and checking rather than assuming is the whole method here. All three production engines now offload: Engine Setting Offloaded weights are 
 llama.cpp -ngl N computed on the CPU , the central processing unit , reading host memory at 23.4 GB/s 
 vLLM cpu_offload_gb streamed to the card over PCIe , Peripheral Component Interconnect Express , at 4.9–5.8 GB/s 
 SGLang cpu_offload_gb the same, with layer grouping and prefetch

Engine Setting Offloaded weights are

The difference is not which engine is better but which road the bytes take: reading host memory is roughly four times faster here than crossing the bus, and vLLM's own documentation says its offload “requires fast CPU-GPU interconnect” — the link between the processor and the GPU , the graphics processing unit — which chapter 17 measured, and this box does not have.

So llama.cpp should win on this hardware, and chapter 31 will run all three rather than assert it. On a machine with NVLink — NVIDIA's direct card-to-card link, which this box does not have — the ordering could invert. ### 2 · Which quantization, from the sizes rather than the names A GGUF repository — GPT-Generated Unified Format , the single-file layout llama.cpp reads — typically holds a dozen quantizations of one model and the names sort badly.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
A GGUF repository — GPT-Generated Unified Format , the single-file layout llama.cpp reads — typically holds a dozen quantizations of one model and the names sort badly. Ask the API — Application Programming Interface , the machine-readable side of the Hugging Face site — for real sizes, summing the shards of split files: ```
curl -s ".../api/models/ / ?blobs=true"
``` For DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 that returns fifteen, from 82.5 GB to 161.9 GB. `UD-Q3_K_M` at 128.1 GB is past 125 GB of host memory and is not a candidate however much better it would have been. `UD-IQ2_M` at 90.9 GB leaves roughly 35 GB for the operating system, the page cache and the engine's working set. ### 3 · Read the header before the weights arrive

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
### 3 · Read the header before the weights arrive This is the step worth knowing about. A split GGUF's first shard is a few megabytes and holds the **entire header** — every architectural fact, hours before the weights finish downloading. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, read from 5.2 MB of a 90.9 GB model Layers 43 Experts 256 
 Width 4096 Active per token 6 + 1 shared 
 Attention heads 64 Key-value heads 1 
 Context 1,048,576 Label 256x8.4B One key-value head against sixty-four query heads is compressed attention, and it is why a million-token context is claimed at all — chapter 23 derived what an uncompressed cache that size would cost. Six experts of 256, plus one that always runs, is 2.7% of the model per token.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
Six experts of 256, plus one that always runs, is 2.7% of the model per token. The expert layers dominate the parameter count and can be counted exactly: 43 layers × 256 experts × 3 matrices × 4096 × 2048 is **277 billion** parameters — 96% of the whole model — of which seven experts' worth, **7.6 billion**, run for any given token. The label `256x8.4B` states 8.4 billion active. The count and the label agree. Which explains a download size that looked impossible 
 287 billion parameters at one byte each would be a 287 GB download. The original is 166.9 GB. The configuration says why: expert_dtype: fp4 . The published model already stores its experts at four bits — 277 billion of them at half a byte is 138.5 GB, plus roughly 10 GB for everything else, plus the block scale factors four-bit storage needs.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
The published model already stores its experts at four bits — 277 billion of them at half a byte is 138.5 GB, plus roughly 10 GB for everything else, plus the block scale factors four-bit storage needs. So quantizing this model is not the usual exercise of compressing a 16-bit original. Ninety-six percent of it arrived compressed, and choosing UD-IQ2_M goes below what its authors shipped — which is a thing worth knowing before blaming the model for what comes out of it. This was caught because the arithmetic disagreed with the download size. That disagreement is the only reason to do the arithmetic. ### 4 · Predict the speed Chapter 29's calculation, with the split between tiers included: ```
bytes per token = active parameters × bytes per parameter
seconds per token = share on the card / 448 GB/s + share in host RAM / 23.4 GB/s
```

text:
```
bytes per token = active parameters × bytes per parameter
seconds per token = share on the card / 448 GB/s + share in host RAM / 23.4 GB/s
``` DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 UD-IQ2_M, before it has run Total parameters ~285 B 
 Active per token 8.4 B 
 File size over total parameters 0.319 bytes/parameter 
 Read per token 2.68 GB 
 Layers that fit 24 GB ~10 of 43 
 From graphics memory 0.62 GB ÷ 448 GB/s = 1.4 ms 
 From host memory 2.06 GB ÷ 23.4 GB/s = 88 ms **Ninety milliseconds a token, or about 11 tokens per second**, and 98% of that wait is host memory. The cards contribute under a millisecond and a half between them — and since a layer split works them one at a time, the figure uses one card's bandwidth rather than three cards' summed, for the reason chapter 29 sets out.

The cards contribute under a millisecond and a half between them — and since a layer split works them one at a time, the figure uses one card's bandwidth rather than three cards' summed, for the reason chapter 29 sets out. The prediction, recorded before the run 
 Bandwidth arithmetic alone says 11 tok/s . It ignores compute, and the compute here happens on Xeons from 2012 with no AVX-512, doing expert matrix multiplications that the cards would have done far faster. So: 
 Prediction: 4 to 11 tokens per second, and closer to the bottom of that range than the top. Prefill will be far worse in proportion than decode, because reading a long prompt routes tokens to every expert and the saving that makes decoding cheap does not apply — measured at 4× worse on a model already in graphics memory, and host memory is 57× slower than graphics memory.

Chapter 31 scores this. This guide has published a 44.6× figure and a 1.5 µs latency that were derived and wrong; the rule since has been that a prediction is written down before the measurement and kept afterwards whatever it says. ## What this rules out, and why that is the useful part Applied to what was actually available Candidate Size Verdict

**The count agrees with the announcement**, which is the first thing worth checking about any announcement. Then the sizes, which decide it: Every published quantization, against 125 GB of host memory Quantization Size Verdict

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026

Four machines' worth of unified memory is the order of magnitude the 444.7 GB build needs; this box has one motherboard and 125 GB. The arithmetic and the field reports agree, which is the point at which it is safe to stop. What that leaves 
 V4-Flash-0731 at 90.9 GB is the largest DeepSeek this machine can hold, and it was already the one chosen. A newer, better model existing does not change what fits — and knowing why it does not fit, in numbers, is worth more than the disappointment. The next machine needs host memory, not graphics cards. ## What the choice does not settle Everything in this chapter is about cost. Nothing in it says whether the model is any good, and nothing in it can. The header gives layers, widths and expert counts; it does not give what the model was trained on, how long for, or what happened to it afterwards — and chapter 29 showed those are what decide the answer.

Which is the honest shape of the problem. The arithmetic tells you what you can afford to run. Only the eval harness tells you whether running it was worth doing, and building one that can still tell two good models apart is chapter 22's unfinished business. The vocabulary you now own 
 architecture support quantization ladder split GGUF header before weights compressed attention shared expert host memory bandwidth recorded prediction 
 And the habit worth keeping: the decision is cheap and the download is expensive, so spend an hour on the decision.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text:
The vocabulary you now own 
 architecture support quantization ladder split GGUF header before weights compressed attention shared expert host memory bandwidth recorded prediction 
 And the habit worth keeping: the decision is cheap and the download is expensive, so spend an hour on the decision. ## Five questions Why check strings on the engine binary before looking at model sizes at all? Because an unsupported architecture fails after the download, not before it. The check costs a second and can save ninety gigabytes. It is the only step that can invalidate every other step. A split GGUF's first shard is 5 MB and the other two are 45 GB each. What is in the small one, and why does it matter?

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text: What is in the small one, and why does it matter? The entire header — layer count, width, head counts, expert counts, context length. It arrives in seconds, so the architecture can be read and the speed predicted while the weights are still downloading. It also looks exactly like a failed download, and deleting it is a common way to waste an afternoon. Host memory measured 23.4 GB/s at eight threads and 18.3 at thirty-two. Why would more threads be slower? The bottleneck is the memory controller, not the cores. Past the point where the channels are saturated, additional threads add contention and cache pressure without adding bandwidth. On a memory-bound workload, the right thread count is the one that fills the channels and no more.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026
text: On a memory-bound workload, the right thread count is the one that fills the channels and no more. A 128.1 GB quantization was rejected on a machine with 125 GB of host memory and 24 GB of graphics memory, totalling 149 GB. Why? The two do not add up into one pool. Weights on the cards are loaded from host memory, and the operating system, the page cache and the engine's working set all need host memory too. A file larger than host memory alone has nowhere to be read from. The prediction is 4–11 tok/s with a wide range and a stated lean. Why not publish a single number? Because the bandwidth half is arithmetic and the compute half is a guess about 2012 Xeons running expert matrix multiplications.

title: 30 · Choosing a Model in 2026

Because the bandwidth half is arithmetic and the compute half is a guess about 2012 Xeons running expert matrix multiplications. Stating a range with the reasoning attached makes the prediction falsifiable in a useful way: if it lands at 12, the memory model is wrong; at 1, the compute assumption was. # A 90 GB Model on 24 GB Chapter 30 predicted, before the download finished, that DeepSeek-V4-Flash would decode at 4 to 11 tokens per second on this box, nearer the bottom. The download finished. It runs. It decodes at 1.45 . This chapter is about the three-fold miss, because the miss is more instructive than a hit would have been. Measured, on this box Model DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, UD-IQ2_M 
 Size on disk 90.9 GB (3 shards, byte-exact) 
 Layers on the cards 9 of 43 
 Layers on the CPU (central processing unit) 34 of 43 
 Graphics memory (on the GPU, the graphics processing unit) 7407 / 6401 / 4955 MiB  (~18.3 of 24 GB) 
 Host memory (RAM, random access memory) ~90 GB mapped into page cache 
 Decode 1.45 tok/s  (median of three) 
 First token 0.9 s warm, 3.3 s cold

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
Model DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, UD-IQ2_M 
 Size on disk 90.9 GB (3 shards, byte-exact) 
 Layers on the cards 9 of 43 
 Layers on the CPU (central processing unit) 34 of 43 
 Graphics memory (on the GPU, the graphics processing unit) 7407 / 6401 / 4955 MiB  (~18.3 of 24 GB) 
 Host memory (RAM, random access memory) ~90 GB mapped into page cache 
 Decode 1.45 tok/s  (median of three) 
 First token 0.9 s warm, 3.3 s cold ## It runs, and that part is not nothing A 552-billion-parameter model — a frontier release from four days before this was written — produced correct, coherent text on three second-hand gaming cards that cost less than one datacentre GPU. It is a reasoning model, so it emits its thinking and then its answer, exactly as chapter 30's arithmetic said it would fit.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
It is a reasoning model, so it emits its thinking and then its answer, exactly as chapter 30's arithmetic said it would fit. The header read out of the 5 MB first shard was right about everything: 43 layers, 256 experts, six active. Ninety gigabytes of weights sit in the host page cache and are pulled through as needed. This is the staircase from chapter 29 working as designed: the fast tier full, the rest spilled to the slow tier, and the whole thing running rather than refusing. It is also slow in a way the prediction did not see coming, and the honest work is explaining why. ## The prediction, scored Recorded in chapter 30, before the run 
 “Bandwidth arithmetic alone says 11 tok/s. It ignores compute, and the compute here happens on Xeons from 2012 with no AVX-512 … so: 4 to 11 tokens per second, nearer the bottom.” 
 Measured: 1.45 tok/s.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
It ignores compute, and the compute here happens on Xeons from 2012 with no AVX-512 … so: 4 to 11 tokens per second, nearer the bottom.” 
 Measured: 1.45 tok/s. That is not near the bottom of the range. It is a third of the bottom — the prediction missed low, by about 3×. Two of its assumptions were wrong and the third was right but not enough. **Miss one: fewer layers fit than assumed.** Chapter 30 estimated ~10 of 43 layers would fit in 24 GB. Loading at 10 (`-ngl 12` including the overhead layers) hit `cudaMalloc failed: out of memory` — a single layer's buffers wanted ~7.9 GB on an 8 GB card, more than was free. It loaded at **9**. So 34 layers ran on the CPU, not 33 — a small error on its own, but it points at the big one.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
So 34 layers ran on the CPU, not 33 — a small error on its own, but it points at the big one. **Miss two, the real one: the roofline priced reading the weights, not computing on them.** This is the mistake worth carrying out of this chapter. Why a bandwidth model breaks for CPU offload 
 Chapter 29's roofline works because on a graphics card , the arithmetic on a weight is almost free next to the cost of reading it — so the read is the whole story, and read speed predicts token speed. Chapter 30 applied that same model to the host-resident layers: 2 GB read from RAM at 23.4 GB/s, call it ~88 ms. But the CPU does not get the arithmetic for free. Those 34 layers are computed on the Xeons — the CPU — expert matrix multiplications, on 2012 silicon without the wide vector instructions modern math kernels lean on.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text: Those 34 layers are computed on the Xeons — the CPU — expert matrix multiplications, on 2012 silicon without the wide vector instructions modern math kernels lean on. The bottleneck for an offloaded layer is not reading its 2 GB, it is the CPU doing the multiply, and that is far slower than the read. The roofline counted the cheaper of the two costs and ignored the one that actually dominated. llama.cpp's own timing agrees to three significant figures: it reports 1.49 tok/s where the streamed measurement got 1.45. The number is not noise; it is what a 2012 CPU multiplying 34 layers of experts per token can do. **Miss three, correct but insufficient:** the prediction did say “nearer the bottom,” and it named the CPU compute as the reason the bandwidth number was optimistic.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text: **Miss three, correct but insufficient:** the prediction did say “nearer the bottom,” and it named the CPU compute as the reason the bandwidth number was optimistic. That instinct was right. It just did not go far enough — the compute did not shave the top off an 11, it dragged the whole thing to 1.45. Being directionally right and quantitatively wrong is still wrong, and the record says so. ## What 1.45 tokens per second actually is Two thirds of a second between words. A 128-token reply takes about a minute and a half. For an interactive chat that is unusable, and it is worth being plain about that rather than dressing it up: on this hardware, this model is a batch tool, not a conversation.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text: For an interactive chat that is unusable, and it is worth being plain about that rather than dressing it up: on this hardware, this model is a batch tool, not a conversation. You would point it at something overnight, not talk to it. But the number is a property of the *pairing*, not the model. The same weights on a machine that could hold them — the four DGX Sparks the field reports describe — run at the 2,000 tok/s prefill those reports quote. The model is not slow. It is slow *here*, because 34 of its 43 layers are being multiplied by a fourteen-year-old CPU. Change the tier the layers live on and the number changes with it. ## What this closes Part VI set out to run the best models of 2026 on hardware that has no business running them, and to be honest about what that costs.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
Part VI set out to run the best models of 2026 on hardware that has no business running them, and to be honest about what that costs. It costs this: the memory staircase is real and a 90 GB model genuinely runs on 24 GB of graphics memory — and the price, measured rather than guessed, is a token every two-thirds of a second, because the slow tier is not just slower memory, it is a slower processor doing the math. The arithmetic that priced the fast tier so well underpriced the slow one, and now the record says by how much. The vocabulary you now own 
 CPU offload compute-bound offload roofline breakdown page cache residency -ngl layer count prediction scored batch tool vs interactive 
 And the correction worth keeping: a bandwidth roofline predicts a GPU because there the read is the cost.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
The vocabulary you now own 
 CPU offload compute-bound offload roofline breakdown page cache residency -ngl layer count prediction scored batch tool vs interactive 
 And the correction worth keeping: a bandwidth roofline predicts a GPU because there the read is the cost. It underpredicts a CPU-offloaded model, because there the math is the cost, and the math on old silicon is slow. ## Five questions The roofline predicted 11 tok/s from bandwidth and the model ran at 1.45. Where did the missing time go? Into CPU compute. The roofline priced reading the 34 host-resident layers' weights (~2 GB at 23.4 GB/s ≈ 88 ms) but not the cost of multiplying by them on the Xeon. On a GPU that multiply is nearly free next to the read; on a 2012 CPU without wide vector units it is the dominant cost, and it is far larger than the read time the roofline counted.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text: On a GPU that multiply is nearly free next to the read; on a 2012 CPU without wide vector units it is the dominant cost, and it is far larger than the read time the roofline counted. Loading at 10 GPU layers OOM'd; 9 worked. Why would one more layer overflow an 8 GB card that was only ~7.4 GB full? A layer is not just its weights — loading it also allocates its share of the compute buffers and KV (keys and values) cache on that card, and one layer's buffers wanted ~7.9 GB of contiguous allocation that was not free. The free-memory headroom has to hold the largest single allocation, not just the average. Host "used" memory was only ~3 GB but ~119 GB sat in buff/cache. Where are the 90 GB of weights?

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text: Where are the 90 GB of weights? Memory-mapped into the page cache. llama.cpp mmaps the GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format) file, so the offloaded layers' weights live in the operating system's file cache (buff/cache), not in the process's resident set. It is real residency — the pages are in RAM — just accounted under cache rather than "used". The prediction said "nearer the bottom" and named CPU compute as the risk. It was still wrong. Why keep it in the guide? Because being directionally right and 3× off is still a miss, and hiding it would make every other prediction in the guide less trustworthy. The point of recording a prediction before the measurement is that the measurement can overrule it in public.

title: 31 · A 90 GB Model on 24 GB
text:
The point of recording a prediction before the measurement is that the measurement can overrule it in public. A guide that only shows its hits is advertising, not a record. The same model reportedly runs at 2,000 tok/s prefill on four DGX Sparks. If the weights are identical, why is this box 1,000× slower? Because speed is a property of the pairing, not the model. On hardware that holds all 90 GB in fast unified memory, every layer computes on capable silicon at memory speed. Here, 34 of 43 layers are multiplied by a fourteen-year-old CPU. The model is not slow; this tier is. Sources & further reading

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
# When a 0.5B Beats a 30B A note from X claimed the sellable thing now is not software but SLMs — small language models — fine-tuned for one job and licensed like a service. That is a testable claim, and this box is built to test it. So: three narrow tasks, one 0.5-billion-parameter model fine-tuned for each, measured against a general model sixty times its size. The tuned model wins two of the three. The one it loses is the most useful result of all, because the pattern of wins and losses tells you exactly when to build one and when not to bother. Measured, on this box — tuned 0.5B vs a 30B, on held-out data Task Metric base 0.5B tuned 0.5B 30B 
 1 · extraction exact-match, strict schema 4.2% 99.5% 17.8% 
 2 · text→SQL execution, forgives surface 36.5% 99.5% 89.5% 
 3 · classification macro-F1, open-ended 32.0% 86.8% 99.0%

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
Task Metric base 0.5B tuned 0.5B 30B 
 1 · extraction exact-match, strict schema 4.2% 99.5% 17.8% 
 2 · text→SQL execution, forgives surface 36.5% 99.5% 89.5% 
 3 · classification macro-F1, open-ended 32.0% 86.8% 99.0% Base and tuned are both Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct; the tune is a LoRA (low-rank adaptation) adapter trained in three to seven minutes on one card. The large model is Qwen3-Coder-30B, served locally as the stand-in for a frontier API (application programming interface). Every score is on an out-of-distribution set — phrasings the tuned model never saw in training. ## The claim, and the honest version The pitch is seductive: fine-tune a tiny model, and it “beats a state-of-the-art model on specific use cases — drop API costs by ninety-five percent, five times faster, hosted privately.” The first thing to do with a claim like that is refuse to believe the flat version of it and find the true, narrower one.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: The pitch is seductive: fine-tune a tiny model, and it “beats a state-of-the-art model on specific use cases — drop API costs by ninety-five percent, five times faster, hosted privately.” The first thing to do with a claim like that is refuse to believe the flat version of it and find the true, narrower one. The narrow version, which these three tasks confirm, is this: **a fine-tuned small model wins when the task is about obeying a convention, not understanding the world.** When what you need is a specific output shape produced the same way every time, a tiny model that has been shown the shape beats a giant one that merely understands your request. When what you need is open-ended judgement about inputs you did not anticipate, the giant's breadth wins and the tune cannot buy its way there on a narrow diet.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
When what you need is open-ended judgement about inputs you did not anticipate, the giant's breadth wins and the tune cannot buy its way there on a narrow diet. ## Three tasks, one tiny model Each task is scored by code, not by a judge, so “beats” is a number and not an impression. Each has a training set, and each has a separate *hard* set drawn from a different generator — new vocabulary, new phrasings, deliberate distractors — so a high score means the concept was learned, not the templates memorised. What each task measures, and why the metric matters 
 Task 1 — extraction. A messy message becomes strict JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): {intent, time, amount, ref, person} . Scored by exact match on all five fields.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: Scored by exact match on all five fields. This metric is unforgiving: "$199" instead of 199 , or "#4471" instead of 4471 , is simply wrong. Task 2 — text to SQL. A question becomes an SQL (structured query language) query, scored by execution : run the predicted query and the gold query against a real database and compare the rows. This metric forgives surface differences — a differently-written query that returns the same rows counts as correct. Task 3 — classification. A support ticket is routed into one of twelve categories, scored by macro-F1 — the average per-class F1, so a model cannot coast on the common classes. The categories are close cousins: a defect versus a technical bug versus an outage.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: The categories are close cousins: a defect versus a technical bug versus an outage. ## Where it wins, and where it loses Read the table down the tuned column and it looks like a rout — 99.5, 99.5, 86.8, every one a large jump from the base model. Read it against the 30B and the real shape appears. **It wins decisively on extraction (99.5 vs 17.8).** The 30B is not confused by the text — it reads the time and the amount fine. It loses because it will not obey the schema: it writes "#29117" where the schema wants the bare 29117 , and it guesses a different intent taxonomy than the one asked for. Understanding the message was never the problem; producing exactly the demanded shape was, and a fine-tune bakes that shape in where a prompt would have to spell out every convention and still drift.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: Understanding the message was never the problem; producing exactly the demanded shape was, and a fine-tune bakes that shape in where a prompt would have to spell out every convention and still drift. **It wins modestly on SQL (99.5 vs 89.5).** Here the metric forgives surface form, so the 30B's genuine competence shows through — it writes working queries that return the right rows most of the time. The tuned model still wins, but the gap is a tenth of what it was on extraction, precisely because the score stopped punishing convention and started rewarding correctness, which the big model has. **It loses on classification (86.8 vs 99.0).** This is the honest one. Routing unseen phrasings across twelve adjacent categories is open-ended semantic judgement, and the 30B's world knowledge generalises to phrasings nobody trained it on.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: Routing unseen phrasings across twelve adjacent categories is open-ended semantic judgement, and the 30B's world knowledge generalises to phrasings nobody trained it on. The 0.5B, trained on a handful of templates per class, learned those well and stumbles on the genuinely novel ones. No amount of shrinking the model fixes that; the fix is a wider net of training examples — which is the lesson of this whole guide wearing different clothes. ## The miss that proves the rule The extraction model did not start at 99.5 on the hard set. It started at **23%**, and the collapse was concentrated in one field: intent, at 34%. The hard set used verbs the training set never contained — phone , settle , ship — and the model had learned intent as a lookup from the *training* verbs, not as a concept.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
The hard set used verbs the training set never contained — phone , settle , ship — and the model had learned intent as a lookup from the *training* verbs, not as a concept. The fix was not a bigger model or a longer tune. It was widening the training data to cover the range of verbs, after which intent went to 100% and the whole task to 99.5%. The correction worth keeping 
 The number that moved capability was never the parameter count. It was the coverage of the training data. Task 3 loses for the same reason task 1 first scored 23%: the corpus did not span the inputs. Size predicts how fast and how cheap the model is; the data predicts whether it is right. This is chapter 30 's rule — capability is training, not size — arriving from the training side instead of the serving side.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: This is chapter 30 's rule — capability is training, not size — arriving from the training side instead of the serving side. ## What you would actually sell The extraction model, merged and exported, is a **507 MB** GGUF (GPT-generated unified format) file that decodes at **434 tokens per second** on one second-hand RTX 3060 Ti, and scores the same 99.5% through that quantised file as it did in full precision. That is the product the note on X was describing, made concrete: a single small file, served privately, at no marginal cost per call, that beats a rented frontier model on the one job it was cut for. But the table also draws the boundary of the business, and drawing it is the honest service.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
But the table also draws the boundary of the business, and drawing it is the honest service. You sell a custom small model for the **narrow, convention-bound task** — the fixed output shape, the house schema, the format that a general model keeps almost getting right. For open-ended semantic work you rent the big model, because there its breadth is the product and your narrow tune cannot match it. The idea captured in idea/1_custom-slm-monetization.md is real; it is just not universal, and knowing which side of the line a task falls on is the whole skill. The vocabulary you now own 
 LoRA adapter fine-tune vs prompt exact-match metric execution accuracy macro-F1 out-of-distribution set schema adherence convention vs comprehension GGUF export 
 And the boundary worth keeping: a fine-tuned small model wins where the task is obeying a convention, and loses where the task is understanding a world it was not trained on.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
The vocabulary you now own 
 LoRA adapter fine-tune vs prompt exact-match metric execution accuracy macro-F1 out-of-distribution set schema adherence convention vs comprehension GGUF export 
 And the boundary worth keeping: a fine-tuned small model wins where the task is obeying a convention, and loses where the task is understanding a world it was not trained on. ## Five questions On extraction the tuned 0.5B scored 99.5% and the 30B 17.8%. Does that mean the 0.5B is the smarter model? No. The 30B reads the message correctly — its per-field accuracy on the amount was 99.5%. It fails the exact-match metric because it will not obey the output convention: it keeps the # on a reference the schema wants bare, and picks its own intent labels.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: It fails the exact-match metric because it will not obey the output convention: it keeps the # on a reference the schema wants bare, and picks its own intent labels. The tune's advantage is schema adherence, not comprehension, and the metric happened to punish exactly the thing the big model would not do on command. Why is the gap between the tuned model and the 30B so much smaller on SQL (99.5 vs 89.5) than on extraction (99.5 vs 17.8)? Because the SQL metric is execution accuracy — it compares the rows returned, not the query text — so it forgives the surface differences that sank the big model on extraction. When the score stops rewarding exact convention and starts rewarding correct results, the general model's real competence shows, and the specialist's edge shrinks to the margin.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: When the score stops rewarding exact convention and starts rewarding correct results, the general model's real competence shows, and the specialist's edge shrinks to the margin. The tuned model lost task 3 (classification) 86.8 to 99.0. What would actually close that gap — a bigger small model, or something else? Something else: more and broader training data. The loss is a coverage gap — twelve adjacent categories with only a handful of phrasings each, tested on novel phrasings — not a capacity limit. Growing the 0.5B would not help much; widening the corpus so it spans the range of ways people describe each category would. Capability is training, not size. The extraction model first scored 23% on the hard set, driven by intent at 34%.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: The extraction model first scored 23% on the hard set, driven by intent at 34%. What had it actually learned, and what fixed it? It had learned intent as a lookup from the specific verbs in the training set, not as a concept, so unseen verbs ( phone , settle , ship ) broke it. The fix was widening the training data to cover the range of verbs, not enlarging or retraining a bigger model. Afterwards intent was 100% and the task 99.5%. Given the three results, when is a custom fine-tuned small model the right thing to sell, and when is it not? It is right for a narrow, convention-bound task — a fixed output shape or house schema a general model keeps almost getting right — where a 507 MB file at 434 tok/s on one card beats a rented API at no marginal cost.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text:
It is right for a narrow, convention-bound task — a fixed output shape or house schema a general model keeps almost getting right — where a 507 MB file at 434 tok/s on one card beats a rented API at no marginal cost. It is wrong for open-ended semantic work on unpredictable inputs, where the large model's breadth is the product and a narrow tune cannot reach it. Sources & further reading 
 LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models — Hu et al., 2021 The method used for all three tunes here — freeze the base weights and train small low-rank matrices — which is why a 0.5B fine-tune fits one 8 GB card and finishes in minutes. Qwen2.5 Technical Report — Qwen Team, 2024 The base model family for the tuned models, and the Apache-2.0 licence that makes a sold adapter clean — the point of picking a licence-clear base rather than the largest one.

title: 33 · When a 0.5B Beats a 30B
text: Qwen2.5 Technical Report — Qwen Team, 2024 The base model family for the tuned models, and the Apache-2.0 licence that makes a sold adapter clean — the point of picking a licence-clear base rather than the largest one. Spider: A Large-Scale Human-Labeled Dataset for Text-to-SQL — Yu et al., 2018 The source of execution accuracy — scoring a query by the rows it returns, not its text — which is exactly why the SQL task forgives surface form and narrows the specialist's lead.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
# Past the Wall A model larger than your graphics memory still runs. Chapter 07 said so in one line and pointed at chapter 11, which then demonstrated it with a model 8.5 GB in size. This page is the part that was owed: what the second tier of memory costs, and how to predict the speed before spending a day downloading. The gap this page closes 
 Two kinds of memory are in play throughout, and the abbreviations for them differ by one letter. RAM is Random Access Memory , the main memory on the motherboard. VRAM is Video Random Access Memory , the memory on the graphics card itself. This page is about what happens when a model needs more of the second than exists, and borrows the first. Chapter 07 ends its budget table with a row reading “70B Q4 · 3 cards + system RAM · 40 GB needed · does not fit — and is run anyway” , and promises that chapter 11 runs it.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
Chapter 07 ends its budget table with a row reading “70B Q4 · 3 cards + system RAM · 40 GB needed · does not fit — and is run anyway” , and promises that chapter 11 runs it. Chapter 11 spills three layers of an 8.5 GB model and measures the cost of doing so, which is a different and much smaller claim. The 40 GB run was never made. Worse, the framing left VRAM looking like a wall with a small crack in it, when it is really the top of a staircase. ## Three tiers, and the gap between them Weights have to be read to be used. Where they are read from decides everything: Where a weight can live on this box Tier How much How fast Source 
 Graphics memory 24 GB (3 × 8) 448 GB/s per card vendor spec for GDDR6 on a 256-bit bus 
 Host memory 125 GB tens of GB/s DDR3 on a 2012 Xeon 
 Disk 879 GB hundreds of MB/s not a place to read weights from

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
Tier How much How fast Source 
 Graphics memory 24 GB (3 × 8) 448 GB/s per card vendor spec for GDDR6 on a 256-bit bus 
 Host memory 125 GB tens of GB/s DDR3 on a 2012 Xeon 
 Disk 879 GB hundreds of MB/s not a place to read weights from The jump from the first row to the second is roughly a factor of ten, and it is the only number that matters when a model does not fit. A layer living in host memory is not unavailable; it is slow. The engine reads it across PCIe — *Peripheral Component Interconnect Express*, the bus connecting the cards to the motherboard — measured on this box at 4.87–5.81 GB/s in chapter 17. Both models below are Q4_K_M — four bits per weight, stored in the
 K -block format, at the M edium size within that family.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
Both models below are Q4_K_M — four bits per weight, stored in the
 K -block format, at the M edium size within that family. It is the
quantization this guide uses by default, for the reason chapter 11 gives. ## The one calculation worth memorising Producing a single token reads the weights that token needs and does almost no arithmetic with them. That makes decoding a *bandwidth* problem, not a compute problem, and bandwidth problems can be predicted: ```
tokens per second = memory bandwidth / bytes read per token
``` Run it backwards on a measurement and it becomes a diagnosis. Multiply the tokens per second you observed by the bytes each token reads, and compare the result to what the memory can do.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
Multiply the tokens per second you observed by the bytes each token reads, and compare the result to what the memory can do. The percentage tells you what to fix. Measured, on this box, at one stream Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M dense, 1 card Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4_K_M mixture of experts, 3 cards 
 File on disk 4.9 GB 18.6 GB 
 Decode 76.8 tok/s 110.7 tok/s 
 Parameters, total 7.50 B 30.22 B 
 Parameters, active per token 7.50 B 3.04 B 
 Read per token 4.92 GB 1.87 GB 
 Bandwidth reached 388 GB/s 202 GB/s 
 Of one card's 448 GB/s 86.6% 45.1% 
 Card utilisation 80.4% 26.7 / 24.9 / 29.6% The larger model is **faster**, and that is not the interesting part. The interesting part is the last two rows. The 8B is at its ceiling.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
The 8B is at its ceiling. It reads its entire 4.9 GB for every token it produces, reaches 86.5% of the rated bandwidth, and keeps the card 80% busy. Nothing about the software will improve it. A faster card would; a smaller model would; better code would not. The 30B is nowhere near its ceiling: 45% of what one card can read, against the 8B's 87%. It is faster than the 8B in spite of the hardware rather than because of it, and the headroom says plainly that something other than memory is the limit. A correction, and the reasoning that forced it 
 This table first divided by three cards' bandwidth, 1,344 GB/s, and reported the 30B at 15%. That ceiling does not exist. The split used here is by layer, so the layers run in order and exactly one card reads weights at any instant while the other two wait.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text: The split used here is by layer, so the layers run in order and exactly one card reads weights at any instant while the other two wait. Three cards hold the model; one card at a time is what moves it. What forced the correction was a third model. A dense 27B spread over all three cards measured 380 GB/s — 28% of a three-card ceiling, which would mean idle hardware, but 85% of one card's, which means saturated. Its card utilisations were 28.8, 28.4 and 31.2 per cent: that is not three cards working at a quarter tilt, it is one card working and two waiting , averaged. The dense 8B on a single card, with nothing to wait for, sat at 80%. So the ceiling for a layer split is one card's bandwidth, and the numbers line up the moment that is used: both dense models saturate it (87% and 85%) no matter how many cards they are spread across, and only the mixture of experts has room to spare.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text: So the ceiling for a layer split is one card's bandwidth, and the numbers line up the moment that is used: both dense models saturate it (87% and 85%) no matter how many cards they are spread across, and only the mixture of experts has room to spare. ## Why a mixture of experts changes the arithmetic A **mixture-of-experts** model stores many parameters and reads few. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B holds 30 billion and activates about 3 billion per token — the *A3B* in the name. The file is 18.6 GB; the bytes actually pulled through memory per token are a fraction of that. Those active-parameter figures are counted, not taken on trust. A GGUF header — GPT-Generated Unified Format , the single-file layout llama.cpp reads — states the layer count, the width, the head counts, and for a mixture of experts how many experts exist and how many run per token; adding up the matrices a token touches gives 3.04 B of 30.22 B, or 10%.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
A GGUF header — GPT-Generated Unified Format , the single-file layout llama.cpp reads — states the layer count, the width, the head counts, and for a mixture of experts how many experts exist and how many run per token; adding up the matrices a token touches gives 3.04 B of 30.22 B, or 10%. The model's own name says A3B . The arithmetic and the label agree, which is the only reason to believe either. This is the whole reason a 30B model out-decodes an 8B one here. It is not better engineering meeting better hardware. It is a model that asked memory for less. And it does not help the other half 
 Reading the prompt is a compute problem, not a bandwidth one, and there every expert gets used: Prefill, 3,250-token prompt Rate 
 Llama-3-8B, 1 card 8,696 tok/s 
 Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, 3 cards 2,194 tok/s

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
Prefill, 3,250-token prompt Rate 
 Llama-3-8B, 1 card 8,696 tok/s 
 Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, 3 cards 2,194 tok/s Four times slower, on three times the hardware. Routing spreads a long prompt's tokens across all the experts, so the saving that makes decoding cheap does not exist while the prompt is being read. A mixture of experts is fast to talk and slow to listen . ## The formula has a batch size in it, hidden Measured on the same two models, streams running at once: Total throughput by concurrency Streams Llama-3-8B, 1 card Qwen3-30B-A3B, 3 cards 
 1 65.1 tok/s 87.6 tok/s 
 4 158.9 tok/s 183.0 tok/s 
 16 167.2 tok/s 185.5 tok/s At four streams the 8B produces 158.9 tokens per second. At 4.9 GB each that would be 778 GB/s — from memory rated at 448.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text: At 4.9 GB each that would be 778 GB/s — from memory rated at 448. The arithmetic is impossible, and the impossibility is the lesson: **the weights are read once per batch, not once per token.** Four streams share one read. Bytes-per-token falls as the batch grows, which is why the roofline calculation above is only valid at a single stream, and why batching is the one free improvement in serving. It is also why both models stop improving between 4 and 16. Past that point the reads are no longer the constraint. ## Choosing a quantization, on this box The tiers give a decision procedure. Weights that fit the cards run at card speed; the remainder runs at host speed; anything that does not fit host memory either does not run or thrashes.
