Weights that fit the cards run at card speed; the remainder runs at host speed; anything that does not fit host memory either does not run or thrashes. 24 GB of graphics memory, 125 GB of host memory Size on disk Where it lives What to expect

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
`UD-IQ2_M` at 90.9 GB leaves roughly 35 GB of host memory spare for the operating system, the cache and the engine's own working set. That is the one to fetch, and the reasoning took a minute against a download that takes hours. Not yet measured 
 Every number above was measured on this box. The DeepSeek row is arithmetic, not a result — the file was still downloading when this page was written. Its predicted speed is deliberately absent: this guide's own history includes a 44.6× figure and a 1.5 µs latency that were derived, printed, and wrong. text: To say which is better would need harder tasks, which this guide does not yet have — and chapter 22 is about why that is the hardest part. ### Where the gain actually comes from Three mechanisms, none of which appear anywhere in a model's size: Training far past compute-optimal. The 2022 Chinchilla result gave the compute-optimal ratio for a *training* budget and the field read it as a recipe. Accounting for inference changes the answer: if a model will serve many requests, it pays to train something smaller for much longer. Hoffmann's successors put the useful ratio into the thousands of tokens per parameter, far past where Chinchilla stops. A smaller model trained longer is cheaper to run *and* better than the size suggests.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
A smaller model trained longer is cheaper to run *and* better than the size suggests. Distillation from a stronger teacher. A large model's outputs become a small model's training data. Recent work reports distilled students beating same-size models trained with reinforcement learning alone by a wide margin — and the modern recipe is stranger still: train a separate expert per domain, then distil all of them into one student while it generates its own attempts. Data quality over data volume. The scarce resource stopped being compute and became good tokens. This is the mechanism with the most leverage and the least glamour. Which is why the dataset is the thing to build 
 If capability comes from the corpus rather than the parameter count, then the leverage on this box is not in finding a bigger file to download.

 If capability comes from the corpus rather than the parameter count, then the leverage on this box is not in finding a bigger file to download. It is in building the data — and building it per model , because a distillation set is only as good as the teacher it came from and the student it is aimed at. That is what Part V is for. Chapter 26 prices what this hardware can train, chapter 27 counts the tokens actually available and gets the count wrong twice on the way, and chapter 28 trains something from noise. Read after this page, they are the only part of the guide that touches the variable that matters. ## What this means for the wall There is no wall. There is a staircase with a steep first step, and a calculation that tells you the height of the step before you take it. A 90 GB model on a machine with 24 GB of graphics memory is not a stunt; it is the second tier doing its job, slowly, as predicted — and chapter 31 measured just how slowly, and by how much the speed guess missed. The mistake is not running a model that does not fit. The mistake is not knowing what it will cost. The vocabulary you now own 
 memory tier roofline bytes per token bandwidth-bound compute-bound active parameters prefill vs decode batch amortisation overtraining distillation 
 And two numbers worth carrying.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text:
The vocabulary you now own 
 memory tier roofline bytes per token bandwidth-bound compute-bound active parameters prefill vs decode batch amortisation overtraining distillation 
 And two numbers worth carrying. At a single stream, a dense model reads its whole self for every token it says. And the size of a model tells you what it will cost, never what it will be worth. ## Five questions A 13B dense model at 4-bit runs at 60 tok/s on a card rated 448 GB/s. Is it bandwidth-bound? About 7 GB per token × 60 = 420 GB/s, which is 94% of rated. Yes, and decisively. No software change will help; the only levers are a smaller model or a faster card. Why can four concurrent streams exceed the bandwidth the single-stream calculation says is available?

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text: Why can four concurrent streams exceed the bandwidth the single-stream calculation says is available? Because the weights are read once per batch step and used for every stream in it. Bytes-per-token falls as the batch grows, so the single-stream roofline stops applying. It is the same reads doing more work, not faster reads. A mixture-of-experts model is three times the size of a dense one and decodes faster. Where does it lose? Prefill. Routing sends a long prompt's tokens to all the experts, so reading the prompt uses the whole model. Measured here: 2,194 tok/s against the dense model's 8,696 on the same 3,250-token prompt. Both cards sit at 25% utilisation while a model runs across three of them.

title: Past the Wall — Running What Does Not Fit
text: Both cards sit at 25% utilisation while a model runs across three of them. What does that rule out? It rules out the cards being the constraint. Idle silicon cannot be the bottleneck. Look at what feeds them: a layer split runs one card at a time by design, and per-token overhead at batch size one is fixed cost that no amount of graphics memory addresses. Model A has 30 billion parameters and model B has 8 billion. Which answers a question better? Unanswerable from those numbers. They predict speed and memory, not quality, and the gap between them is a year of training practice, not architecture. Measured here on the same four tasks, a 2025 model with 3.04 billion active parameters matched a 2024 model with 7.50 billion.

title: PCIe vs NVLink — the deep reference
text:
# PCIe vs NVLink PCIe — Peripheral Component Interconnect Express — is the general-purpose slot standard every expansion card plugs into. NVLink , NVIDIA Link , is a dedicated wire running from one card directly to another. This box has the first and not the second. Here is every route on it, measured, plus the part chapter 18 found that spoils the easy conclusion. What this page is for 
 Chapter 17 establishes the headline: these cards talk at about 5 GB/s, and a single card reads its own memory at 423.9. This page is the reference behind that sentence — the full pair matrix, the fixed per-crossing cost, the arithmetic that predicts the two-hop rate, and what each parallelism strategy actually pays.

title: PCIe vs NVLink — the deep reference
text: This page is the reference behind that sentence — the full pair matrix, the fixed per-crossing cost, the arithmetic that predicts the two-hop rate, and what each parallelism strategy actually pays. It also carries the correction that matters more than the headline. On this box the link is not the dominant cost of tensor parallelism. Chapters 18 and 19 measured that, and a reference page that repeated "the interconnect is the bottleneck" would be repeating something this project has already disproved on its own hardware. --- ## 1 · Two different things called an interconnect They are not two speeds of the same idea. They are different topologies, and the topology is what sets the price. The two links, structurally

title: PCIe vs NVLink — the deep reference
text:
The two links, structurally PCIe NVLink 
 What it is A general slot standard. Graphics cards, network cards and drives all use it. A proprietary point-to-point link between cards of the same vendor. Route a byte takes card → motherboard → destination. Everything shares the root complex. card → card. The motherboard is not involved. Who else is on it Every other device in the machine, including drives and network cards. Nothing. The wire exists for this pair. Designed for Attaching an arbitrary device to a host. Making several cards behave like one larger card. On this build yes — three cards, 16 lanes each no — every figure quoted here is external The middle row is the whole difference. PCIe was never meant to carry card-to-card traffic; it was meant to attach a card to a host.

PCIe was never meant to carry card-to-card traffic; it was meant to attach a card to a host. Card-to-card works, but it is a route the standard permits rather than a route it was built for. card 0

That is an 8.8% penalty for arriving at card 0 , which is the socket crossing showing through — small, consistent, and the only place the topology is visible in the numbers at all. The 33% is the number to sit with. Sixteen lanes of Gen 3 carry about 15.75 GB/s, and a card-to-card copy gets a third of it. That is not a tuning failure; sections 2.4 and 2.5 show it is arithmetic. ### 2.3 Latency — the fixed price of any crossing Bandwidth describes a large transfer. A small one pays something else entirely: a fixed cost before a single useful byte moves. Measured · tiny transfers, the fixed cost alone

The fixed cost is dominated by software and driver work, not by the distance travelled. Two measurements — a rate and a fixed cost — set the size at which one stops mattering and the other starts. The crossover is where the fixed cost equals the transfer time: $$S^{*} = L \times B$$ Every symbol in that formula Symbol Means Value here

Above it, the crossing is genuinely bandwidth-bound. A card-to-card copy on this box is two host transfers back to back, so the host leg is worth measuring on its own. **Pinned** host memory is memory the operating system has promised not to relocate; the card can read it directly. Ordinary *pageable* memory must be staged through a buffer first, so the bus is paid twice for one hop. It also settles the diagnosis — a single hop done properly reaches 75% of theoretical, so the slot, the lanes and the board are not the problem. ### 2.5 Why a third: the two-hop model One good hop is 11.75 GB/s. A card-to-card copy measures 5.81 GB/s on the same script. That ratio is almost exactly one half, which is the signature of doing the same thing twice. $$B_{\text{pair}} \approx \frac{B_{\text{hop}}}{2}$$ Every term, and where it came from Term Means Value Status

title: PCIe vs NVLink — the deep reference
text:
Measured · asking the driver for a direct path 
 cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess returns 217 — cudaErrorPeerAccessUnsupported . Every pair, both directions. Peer access is one card reading another's memory without going through host memory. GeForce hardware has it disabled in the driver. It is the feature line that separates a consumer card from a data-centre card, a product decision rather than a limit of the slot or the lanes . The bus would carry it — section 2.4 shows one hop reaching 75% of theoretical. The driver declines to route it. This single refusal is responsible for more of Part II's results than any other fact about the hardware, and it propagates in three separate directions: What error 217 costs, downstream

text:
What error 217 costs, downstream Consequence Effect Where it shows up 
 Copies route through host memory Two hops instead of one: 11.75 GB/s becomes 5.81 every figure on this page

 Host memory bandwidth is now in the path Card-to-card traffic competes with everything else the host is doing, including the drives and the network not isolated — see section 7 The second row is the expensive one, and it is easy to miss. It is not that transfers got slower; it is that the algorithm everyone writes about is unavailable, and the fallback moves twice as much.

Three cards delivering exactly one card's throughput, on more total work than the row that overlapped perfectly. It is not the amount of work and it is not the link — chapter 19 also deleted the transfer entirely and the timing did not move. It is a single thread issuing many small programs, one at a time, and never getting far enough ahead for the cards to run concurrently. Stated as a hypothesis, because it was not isolated 
 Tensor parallelism issues many small programs per layer, which is the shape that serialises in the table above. That makes kernel-issue serialisation the plausible home of the 0.62× residual in section 5's decomposition. It has not been measured as such — no experiment in this project attributes that residual directly — so it is written here as the leading candidate and nothing more.

 Pin every host buffer 2.10× outbound and 3.21× inbound, for an allocation flag. The easiest thing on this list to forget and the largest free gain measured anywhere in the project. Make the programs bigger before blaming the wire One 4096 × 4096 multiply overlaps across three cards at 1.04×. Two hundred small ones serialise at 3.01×, with the transfers deleted. Never read link state from an idle machine It reports Gen 1 — a quarter of the truth — and the panic that causes is entirely avoidable. Six of these eight cost nothing but knowing them.  No NVLink hardware was available Every NVLink figure here is external. Two transfer sizes, not a sweep 256 MB copies and tiny transfers. The 233 kB crossover is derived from those two points, not observed as a curve, and the true knee is likely a region rather than a value. One copy at a time, never three at once All six pairs were measured in isolation.

It would shrink on a wider model; the bandwidth term would not. The 0.62× residual is unattributed Section 5.2 names the leading candidate and does not claim it. title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
# Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model The arena's engine selector greys out vLLM and SGLang for every model on this box, and lets you pick them for exactly one. That is not a bug or a licence check. It is a hard fact about file formats that no amount of configuration gets around, and this page is the whole of it, laid out as who, what, when, where, why, and how. The one-line version 
 A model is stored in one of two formats — GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format) or safetensors. llama.cpp reads one of them; vLLM and SGLang read the other. Neither reads both, so the engine you can use is decided by the file you have — not by which engine is “better.” ## WHAT — the two formats GGUF and safetensors are not two flavours of the same thing

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
GGUF and safetensors are not two flavours of the same thing GGUF safetensors (HF) 
 Made by the llama.cpp project Hugging Face 
 Shape one binary file tensors + a JSON header, plus separate config and tokenizer files 
 Holds the tokenizer? yes, baked in no — it sits in sibling files 
 Built for quantized local and CPU (central processing unit) inference training, distribution, direct GPU (graphics processing unit) serving 
 On this box models/gguf/ models/hf/ GGUF ( GPT-Generated Unified Format ) is a single file that bundles the weights, the tokenizer, and the metadata together, with the low-bit quantization schemes — the Q4, IQ2 of earlier chapters — native to it. safetensors stores only the raw tensors behind a small JSON header, and leaves the tokenizer and the architecture config in separate files beside it.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
safetensors stores only the raw tensors behind a small JSON header, and leaves the tokenizer and the architecture config in separate files beside it. The one holds everything in itself; the other is a set of parts that expect their siblings. ## WHO — which engine reads which The split is clean, and it is the whole reason for the greyed options Engine Reads Built for 
 llama.cpp · Ollama GGUF one machine, one or a few users, CPU or a small card 
 vLLM · SGLang safetensors a datacentre GPU serving many requests at once These grew up on opposite sides. llama.cpp is a C++ engine with its own tensor library and its own quantization; GGUF is its native format and it reads nothing else. vLLM and SGLang are built on PyTorch and load the safetensors a model is trained and published in.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text: vLLM and SGLang are built on PyTorch and load the safetensors a model is trained and published in. The format each reads is not a setting — it is what the engine was written against. ## WHEN — the moment it bites At load time , and nowhere else. A model downloads fine, sits on disk fine, and looks like a model — the mismatch only appears when an engine tries to open a file it was not built to read. The arena moves that failure earlier, to the moment you pick the engine: the selector greys the options that would fail, so you never wait through a load that was doomed at the first byte. ## WHERE — and why your dropdown looked broken Every model this project downloaded is GGUF, because GGUF is what makes a 30B model fit on an 8 GB card.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
Every model this project downloaded is GGUF, because GGUF is what makes a 30B model fit on an 8 GB card. They all live in models/gguf/ . Until this was fixed, the arena's model list only scanned that folder — so every model in the dropdown was GGUF, so vLLM and SGLang were correctly greyed for all of them, and the one safetensors model that would have lit them up was invisible because it lived in models/hf/ , which the list never looked at. The engines were never the problem. The list was showing half the disk. What the fix does 
 The model list now reads both folders. A GGUF offers llama.cpp; a safetensors model offers vLLM and SGLang; each engine is presented only for the format it can actually open.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
A GGUF offers llama.cpp; a safetensors model offers vLLM and SGLang; each engine is presented only for the format it can actually open. Pick a .gguf and llama.cpp is your engine; pick an HF model and the other two wake up. ## WHY — the reason it cannot simply be made to work This is the part worth understanding, because the obvious question is “so add a GGUF reader to vLLM.” It has been tried, and it was demoted to an experimental plugin, for three reasons the projects state plainly — and this box measured the first of them by accident. Three walls, one of them felt here 
 1. The tokenizer. A GGUF has the tokenizer baked in, in llama.cpp's own layout; vLLM and SGLang expect it as separate Hugging Face files.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text: A GGUF has the tokenizer baked in, in llama.cpp's own layout; vLLM and SGLang expect it as separate Hugging Face files. Converting one to the other is, in vLLM's own words, “time-consuming and unstable, especially for some models with large vocab size.” When this project pointed SGLang at a bare .gguf , it loaded the weights and then aborted looking for a tokenizer repo — the exact failure the docs warn about, reproduced without meaning to. 2. GGUF is not a serving format. Its throughput under concurrency is poor next to a vLLM-class stack — it was built to run one conversation on a laptop, not a thousand at once. Bolting it onto a throughput engine gives up the reason to use that engine, which is covered in chapter 14 .

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
Bolting it onto a throughput engine gives up the reason to use that engine, which is covered in chapter 14 . 3. New architectures lag. A brand-new model has to be taught to the convert_hf_to_gguf.py script before any GGUF of it can exist at all. safetensors is what a model ships in on day one; its GGUF appears later, when someone converts it. A frontier release is servable by vLLM before a single GGUF of it exists. ## HOW — to cross the divide when you need to You do not configure your way across it; you convert or you re-download. Two directions, two costs You have You want What it costs 
 safetensors to run llama.cpp convert_hf_to_gguf.py then quantize — minutes to an hour, and it shrinks 
 GGUF to run vLLM / SGLang download the safetensors original — much larger, because it is unquantized (an 8B is ~16 GB, a 30B ~60 GB)

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
You have You want What it costs 
 safetensors to run llama.cpp convert_hf_to_gguf.py then quantize — minutes to an hour, and it shrinks 
 GGUF to run vLLM / SGLang download the safetensors original — much larger, because it is unquantized (an 8B is ~16 GB, a 30B ~60 GB) The second direction is the expensive one, and it is why this box runs GGUF for the big models: the whole reason a 30B model fits here is the quantization that GGUF carries and that a raw safetensors download would undo. To compare all three engines fairly you download a small safetensors model and accept that it is small — which is exactly what the one HF model in models/hf/ is for. The vocabulary you now own 
 GGUF safetensors embedded tokenizer format-native quantization route by format convert_hf_to_gguf serving vs local format 
 And the sentence that ends the confusion: the engine you can use is decided by the file you have, and the file you have is decided by whether you needed it small (GGUF) or needed it fast under load (safetensors).

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text:
The vocabulary you now own 
 GGUF safetensors embedded tokenizer format-native quantization route by format convert_hf_to_gguf serving vs local format 
 And the sentence that ends the confusion: the engine you can use is decided by the file you have, and the file you have is decided by whether you needed it small (GGUF) or needed it fast under load (safetensors). ## Five questions The engine selector greys out vLLM for a Qwen GGUF. Is that a limitation of the app? No. vLLM cannot read GGUF at all — it reads safetensors. The selector is reporting a fact about the file, not a choice the app made. Point it at a safetensors model and vLLM becomes available. Why does a GGUF need no tokenizer files beside it, but a safetensors model does?

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text: Why does a GGUF need no tokenizer files beside it, but a safetensors model does? GGUF bakes the tokenizer into the single file; safetensors stores only tensors and keeps the tokenizer and config in sibling files. Move a lone .safetensors without its tokenizer.json and config.json and no engine can load it; move a .gguf alone and it still works. SGLang loaded a GGUF's weights and then crashed. On what, and why was it predictable? On the tokenizer. It found the weights but then went looking for a Hugging Face tokenizer repo, because its code path expects the tokenizer as separate files, not baked into a .gguf . vLLM's docs call GGUF tokenizer conversion “time-consuming and unstable” — the crash was that warning, made real.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model
text: vLLM's docs call GGUF tokenizer conversion “time-consuming and unstable” — the crash was that warning, made real. A frontier model was released today. Which engine can serve it first, and why? vLLM or SGLang, from the safetensors the model ships in. A GGUF cannot exist until the architecture is added to convert_hf_to_gguf.py and someone converts and quantizes it — which lags the release. safetensors is the day-one format. You want to run one of this box's 30B GGUF models on vLLM. What is the real cost, and is it worth it? Downloading its safetensors original, which is unquantized and roughly three to four times larger (~60 GB for a 30B). It is worth it only to measure vLLM's throughput under concurrency; for single-user chat, the GGUF on llama.cpp is smaller and faster, so there is usually no reason to pay it.

title: Why an Engine Can't Run Every Model

It is worth it only to measure vLLM's throughput under concurrency; for single-user chat, the GGUF on llama.cpp is smaller and faster, so there is usually no reason to pay it. Sources & further reading

title: The Harness — where every number came from
text:
# The Harness This guide says "measured by the same harness" thirty-eight times across eight chapters and never once shows it. Every number here rests on this code, so here it is. Why this page exists 
 A measurement is only as trustworthy as the thing that took it. Citing a harness as authority while keeping it out of sight asks the reader to believe rather than check — which is the opposite of what this project claims to be for. There are two, and they answer different questions. The two instruments File Asks Used by 
 serving bench/run.py , 273 lines How fast, how much memory, what text? chapters 10–15, 18 
 agent source/22_eval.py , 150 lines Was the answer right ? chapter 22 Both are standard library only.

title: The Harness — where every number came from
text:
Both are standard library only. Nothing is installed to take a measurement, because a dependency is one more thing that can differ between runs. --- ## 1 · The serving harness ### It watches two kinds of memory, not one Every guide quotes video memory. An engine written in Python with a deep learning framework behind it can hold **gigabytes of host memory** — ordinary *Random Access Memory* on the motherboard — that never appears in `nvidia-smi` at all. Sampling only the card reports a C++ binary and a Python server as comparable when they are not. ```python
class GpuWatch:
 """Polls memory in the background, BOTH kinds. peak VRAM per card, from nvidia-smi
 peak_rss resident system memory of the engine process tree, from /proc
 """

title: The Harness — where every number came from
text:
peak VRAM per card, from nvidia-smi
 peak_rss resident system memory of the engine process tree, from /proc
 """ def _poll(self):
 while not self._stop.is_set():
 out = subprocess.run(
 ["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=index,memory.used",
 "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"], ...).stdout
 for line in out.strip().splitlines():
 i, mb = [x.strip() for x in line.split(",")]
 self.peak[int(i)] = max(self.peak.get(int(i), 0), int(mb)) # Sum resident memory across the engine's WHOLE process tree. # These servers fork workers, and the parent alone understates it. rss = subprocess.run(["bash", "-c",
 f"ps -eo rss,comm,args --no-headers | grep -E '{self.match}' "
 "| grep -v grep | awk '{{s+=$1}} END {{print s+0}}'"], ...).stdout
 self.peak_rss = max(self.peak_rss, int(rss or 0) // 1024)
```

text:

 Sample in a background thread , five times a second, and keep the maximum Peak memory is transient. A reading taken after the run is over shows the engine at rest, which is not the number that decides whether a model fits. Sum the whole process tree , not the parent vLLM and SGLang fork worker processes. The parent alone reported a fraction of the truth. Record all three cards , always Part I is single-card by constraint .

title: The Harness — where every number came from
text:
Record all three cards , always Part I is single-card by constraint . Watching every card is what proves the constraint held instead of assuming it — a run that quietly spread is visible in the results. ### It gets token counts from the engine, never from the text The error this exists to prevent 
 The first version estimated tokens as characters ÷ 4 , the usual rule of thumb. Measured against the engine's own count, the real figure for this model was 5.71 characters per token — the estimate was wrong by 1.43× . It would have inflated every tokens-per-second number in Part I by 43%, consistently, across all five engines — so every comparison would still have looked right, and the error would have survived to the end of the project.

A stored answer key would have silently started grading against the wrong number. ### The tasks are private Every question is about files in this repository, which no public model has been trained on. A benchmark made of public questions cannot separate a model that reasons from one that memorised — **contamination**, and it is unfalsifiable from outside, because nobody can prove what was in a training set. ### Grading is mechanical No model judges another. The answer is a number or a yes, normalised and compared: ```python
def normalise(s):
 s = s.strip().strip(".").strip()
 low = s.lower()
 if low.startswith("yes"): return "yes"
 if low.startswith("no"): return "no"
 m = re.search(r"-?\d[\d,]*", s) # accept 1,234 and 1234 alike
 return m.group(0).replace(",", "") if m else low[:40]
```

The rules the harness enforces on itself Rule Why 
 Every run writes bench/results/<run-id>.json No file, no run. A number quoted from a terminal that has scrolled away is not evidence. The label, level, quantisation and a free-text note go in the file Six months later, "which one was this?" has an answer.
